blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
Hsia Yan, a.k.a. Hsia Zuxiang. He went to Taiwan in 1949, and co-founded one of the first modern art groups that advocated innovation in the region, namely the “Ton Fan Art Group,” which was viewed as an experimental and open-up stance against the conservative painting world. To take a more active part in the development of the avant-garde, Hsia left for Paris and New York at the age of 31. Inspired by this experience, he gradually deviated from his original style of mystical abstraction with calligraphic characters, and switched to concerns regarding existentialism and subjective experience. His signature style, “fuzzy man,” took its initial form from these rushing figures composed of quivering lines, suggesting a restlessness intrinsic to human existence. In the following decades, Hsia brought multiple pictorial themes and motifs and the experience encapsulated into the “fuzzy” universe. He refused to attribute his periodic subject matter to globalization or the local environment, believing that “painting itself is a ‘philosophical’ act that comes from what the visual enables the heart to see.” The “fuzzy man” created by the artist, is both a blurry shadow projected on the canvas and a dual mode of observation that blurs the reality and the reconstructed fantasy. Featuring the variations of the “fuzzy man,” the exhibition examines the different stages of Hsia’s radical and still evolving artistic career.

Currently Hsia used to study painting with Li Chun-Shan in Taiwan and thus played an important role in the regional modernization of painting. His solo and group exhibitions include: “Hsia Yan: Journey to Art”, Taipei Fine Arts Museum (2018); “The 8th Shanghai Biennale,” Shanghai Art Museum (2010); “Work Exhibition of Six Painters in Taiwan,” National Art Museum of China (1984); “Urban Aesthetics”, Queens Museum of Art, New York (1976) ; The 5th Sao Paulo Art Biennial, Brazil (1959).

title: History of Chemistry II Excessively Restrained Mountaineering Enthusiasts

raw.title: History of Chemistry II Excessively Restrained Mountaineering Enthusiasts

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Lu Chunsheng’s highly distinctive feature length film History of Chemistry II is staged in vacant spaces where the protagonists seem lost or detached from reality, wandering around like somnambulant sleep-walkers. Correspondingly, the most significant aspect of the film is its absence of any clear narrative, instead the film is structured around repetition: In Beckett-like absurd scenes we witness the characters repeating actions that make no obvious sense. The performances are perfectly synchronized to the sound score composed by B6. The film’s odd charisma clearly plays homage to the surrealist works of Fellini and Bunuel.

blocks.body:
born.1968; lives and works in Shanghai.


Lu Chunsheng was graduated from the Department of Sculpture at China National Academy of Fine Arts. He currently lives and works in Shanghai. A particularly generative aspect of his work is the way it breaches the boundary between documentary and fiction. His conceptual and methodological coherence broadens and extends the inquiry into everyday life rather than merely illustrating it. He is now focusing on photography and video art, articulating a surrealistic and neutral attitude in his videos. Using fixed camera positions, endless drawn-out shots and unprofessional shooting techniques, he documents human behavior in bizarre situations. Exhibitions include "Perspectives: Lu Chunsheng", Arthur M. Sackler Gallery, Washington D.C, U.S.A. (2011); " The Materialists are All Asleep, A Retrospective of Lu Chunsheng", The Red Mansion Foundation, London, U.K. (2008); 10th International Istanbul Biennial "Not only Possible, But also Necessary-Optimism in the Age of Global War", Istanbul, Turkey (2007); etc.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
Zhang Ding's double channel video installation Boxing 1 & 2 features the artist hitting a punching bag composed of three round cacti, in a dark space.


The first video consists of various angles and close-ups of the man and his bleeding clenched fists as he repeatedly hits the spiky cacti, while the collapsed thorns are covered with blood.


The second video, in a vertical format, presents a static shot of the artist during the whole process as he unceasingly boxes the cacti punching bag.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1980, Gansu Province; lives and works in Shanghai.


His practice often consists of large scale projects including installations, sculptures, videos, paintings, frequently animated with live performances. These works presented as a whole and with a strong performative, musical, dramatical nature, explore notions related to human perceptions, the collective consciousness, conflicts of wills, the power as well as psychological and physical manipulations. Zhang Ding's exhibitions and projects reflect on alienations taking place in a social and political context, and stage scenes with confrontational and chaotic natures. His works have been presented internationally in institutions and biennales such as the 7th Guangzhou Triennial (Guangzhou, 2023); Astrup Fearnley Museum of Modern Art (Oslo, Norway, in 2017 and 2007); the Biennale of Lyon (Lyon, France, 2013); The Contemporary Art Museum in Houston (U.S.A., 2012) among others.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Great Era is a surrealistic narrative video work in which a man is presented riding a horse-headed bicycle through various scenes representative of certain customs in Shanghai, with circus-like music playing in the background. With his unusual mount, the protagonist appears at first before a red velvet theatrical curtain unveiling a night postcard view of Shanghai. He wanders around empty streets of the city, discovering objects on the way, bathing, dancing and dining, before going back through the curtain again, which closes as he walks away. What is on the other side of the curtain, and where the man come from remain unknown.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
Co-founded in 1984 by brothers Fernando (1961-2022) and Humberto (1953) Campana, the Campana studio has achieved international recognition for its furniture design and intriguing pieces. In 2024, the studio celebrates its 40th anniversary acknowledged as a pioneer of disruptive design, which led them to create a groundbreaking language in their field. Deeply rooted in Brazilian culture and traditions, their work carries universal values at its core, such as freedom and human dignity, creating their identity through life experiences. By incorporating the idea of transformation and reinvention, their creative process raises everyday materials to nobility. Brazilian characteristics - such as the abundance of colors, mixtures, and creative chaos - bring the triumph of simple solutions, poetically.


Based in São Paulo, Campana is constantly investigating new possibilities within Design: from furniture making to architecture, landscaping, fashion, scenography, and more. Bridging disciplines and encouraging the exchange of expertise among communities and artists are vital sources of inspiration, fresh repertoire, and free-thinking. Working with multiple brands and industries allows them to combine the best of craftsmanship, sustainable production practices and state-ofthe-art technologies.

blocks.body: Established in 1984 by Brazilian design duo Humberto Campana (b.1953) and Fernando Campana (1961-2022).

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Yu Youhan's artistic journey over five decades has traversed figuration, Pop art, and abstraction. In his later years, he returned to the abstract style he first explored in the 1980s, immersing himself in a spiritual realm where external distractions are shielded and the mind wanders freely. "Circle" is a recurring motif in Yu Youhan's abstract works. Within circular compositions, the artist traces the trajectories of flowing dots and lines, evoking the movement of stars, the flow of energy, and the footprints of life - a continuous process without beginning or end, distant yet interconnected. Created in 2016, The Big Pill is an exceptional piece among Yu Youhan's abstract creations. Unlike his typical abstract works, which rarely bear figurative titles, this piece, referred to as "pill," prominently features a geometric form at its center - a rare symbolic element in his abstract works. This departure from pure abstraction echoes the spontaneity of his Pop art style creations from the 1990s. The artist abandoned purity, absorbing external elements and incorporating them into his "circle" that embodies circularity, coherence, and integration. Moreover, in Yu Youhan's vision, the circle exists not only within the canvas but also beyond its boundaries.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1943, Shanghai; b. 1943, Shanghai; d. 2023, Shanghai.


Yu Youhan graduated from Central Academy of Arts & Crafts, and taught at the Shanghai Arts & Crafts College. After studying the techniques of modern Western painting, he tried to express China's profound national culture and spirit through such techniques and created his own artistic style. His signature works include “the Circle” Series, “Ah! We” Series, etc. In the early 1990s, Yu Youhan gained international attention as a political pop artist, and was invited to participate in the exhibition “China's New Art, Post-1989” (1993), the 45th Venice Biennale (1993) and the 22nd São Paulo Biennial (1994). He is one of the first Chinese contemporary artists active in the international art scene.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
For the project Crazy English Camp, Zhou Xiaohu invited a Chinese "Crazy English" teacher to London to train native English-speaking volunteers in the Chinese "Crazy English" method, with each volunteer interviewed immediately after the session.


Zhou views the educational action project Crazy English Camp as a social installation imbued with complex emotional undertones, entirely reliant on the teacher and the "Crazy English" pedagogy—both acting as "pan-readymades" that propel the work autonomously. By bringing the "Crazy English" teacher to London to instruct native English-speaking British volunteers in a Chinese-developed approach to their own language, Zhou displaces the inherent relationship between education, site, and subject. Through this dislocation of context and target, the fundamental attributes and purpose of the educational task are stripped away, revealing its constructed nature.


The collective training action of Crazy English Camp evokes the imagery of a "cultural filter": this shared, almost frenzied, experiential passion relies on a linguistic tool originally from the West—now repurposed and filtered through another cultural context. The historical absurdity of such an exchange becomes embedded within a site-specific journey of cultural adventure.


More importantly, the work’s intent is not merely to “liberate the audience” through passionate engagement or to reiterate interactive performance. Instead, it seeks to use the event as a catalyst for questioning—turning the artistic act into a starting point for broader discourse and triggering social observation.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
born.1960 in Changzhou, Jiangsu Province; lives and works in Shanghai.


A pioneering figure in Chinese contemporary art, Zhou has used the computer in art-making, including stopframe animation, video installation, and other experiments. His works span various media, including animation, video installation, sculpture, painting, and action art projects. Adopting pan-readymade and "automatic writing" as his approach, Zhou aims to build an energy theater for integrated art, push the boundaries of art, and deepen anthropological exploration. His art is characterized by the multi-dimensional pictorial interaction between images and physical objects, with a focus on possible life in the digital age, questioning how truth and history are misinterpreted, amplified, omitted, and recorded. He has attended group exhibitions inlcuding the 3rd Shanghai Biennale (2000), the 5th Asia Pacific Triennial of Contemporary Art (2006), the 8th Gwangju Biennial (2010), No Soul For Sale, Tate Modern, London (2010), Asia Triennial, Manchester (2014), the 2nd Bangkok Art Biennale (2020), the 14th Shanghai Biennale (2023), and many others.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: This video installation consists of eight sections, each derived from the training sessions of Amway employees in China, which is appropriated in the artwork as "pan-readymade." The artist collaborated with an acrobatic troupe to stage a theatrical performance. Employing electrical props, the performers were suspended on stage and the set was constructed in an inverted manner. In this upside-down state, the performers performed the eight Amway training sessions. The image of the filmed performance was then reversed in post-production to create the illusion of a standard, upright training session.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
My college years coincided with China’s Enlightenment Era — a period when intellectual circles were widely engaged with existentialist thought. I was drawn to related plays and scripts, and that reading deeply influenced my later work.


Take, for example, my video piece Shui Diao Ge Tou (to the tune of ‘Prelude to Water Melody’), which was exhibited at the 2000 Shanghai Biennale. It can be seen as an observation of the human condition from an existentialist perspective, focusing on the psychological space of the individual within a public environment. I filmed swimmers — especially those who couldn’t swim — in a pool, capturing their helplessness and constant struggle: always on the verge of sinking, yet always potentially buoyed by others nearby. My focus wasn't underwater photography per se, but on expanding the expressive possibilities of video art.


Later, I placed a spherical fish tank in front of a monitor playing that footage. Looking through the water-filled tank created a double-convex lens effect, distorting and inverting the images. The swimmers appeared trapped inside a vessel, tumbling and struggling in a confined, anxious state. Thus, the core visual of the final work was achieved through this secondary, mediated filming process.


Talk Show can be considered my first true video work. It was also created through a two-step, layered recording process. First, I filmed myself performing in front of the camera, reciting Chinese chengyu (four-character idioms) in an escalating sequence starting from the number “one” — from yi ma dang xian (taking the lead) to shi quan shi mei (perfect in every way), bai fa bai zhong (every shot hits the target)… all the way to wan ma ben teng (ten thousand horses galloping). My delivery grew increasingly exaggerated.


Next, I filmed the act of blowing up a balloon, while projecting the footage of my reciting face onto the balloon’s surface. As the balloon inflated, you could initially see me blowing it, but soon my face was completely obscured by the expanding balloon, which now displayed the full, reciting visage. Finally — pop! — the balloon burst. The controlling power of these traditional linguistic forms seemed to vanish with it. The title Talk Show carries this dual meaning: it aims to reinterpret or break through the authority of traditional culture using a less serious, absurd, and non-mainstream medium.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Painting, an ancient form of art, holds a special place in my heart, always evolving yet perpetually enduring. Despite speculation that AI may one day replace traditional painting, I firmly believe otherwise. While my paintings may exhibit minor color loss in certain areas over time, the overall composition and proportion remain unchanged. Where there is disappearing, there is also a revealing of what lies beneath. The heavy paints may resist drying for decades, yet the dryness evolves gradually, much like the shifts in the contours of aging skin. Indeed, change is the eternal verity of life. I think AI can create things that are beyond humans’ ability, while humans can create certain things that are beyond AI’s ability. However, it’s possible for AI and humans to work together and it’s interesting for them to collaborate in creation.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
born.1950 in Shanghai, works and lives in Shanghai.


Hu Xiangcheng's artistic journey began with random scribblings on his father's discarded paper ledgers, followed by acts of copying the Manual of the Mustard Seed Garden. After graduating from primary school, he went to Shanghai’s Yuanfeng Woolen Mill as a work-study practitioner, where he worked as a wood-molding operator, sand-casting operator, and cook after only three days of classroom study. In 1970, Hu Xiangcheng studied sketching with Meng Guang. Following graduation from Shanghai Theater Academy in 1976, he taught successively at the academy and Tibet University, before going to Japan to study Japanese at a commercial Japanese language school in 1986 and graduating from Musashino Art University in 1991. In the same year, he started to visit cities and villages in Africa, Europe, and the United States to conduct research and experiments on folk craft and contemporary art. In 1996, he participated in the establishment of the Shanghai Biennale, serving as a member of the biennale’s academic committee for several terms. In 2000, he initiated a decade-long practice of rural construction around Shanghai, before serving as the art director of the United Africa Pavilion at the 2010 Shanghai Expo.

 

Across decades of artistic career, Hu Xiangcheng has carried out experiments in many different fields. His works have been included in local and international exhibitions such as the San Paulo Architecture Biennale, the International Sculpture Exhibition in Venice, the Contemporary Sculpture from China Exhibition in Hague, the Arts, Accumulation and Objects in Asian Megacities exhibition at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, the Shanghai Biennale, the Yokohama Triennale, and the Guangzhou Triennial. He has also engaged in and organized a large number of activities such as contemporary art, performances, country bands, literati gathering, folklore protection and improvement, etc. in public locations such as abandoned rural factories and seaside spots.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
born.1950 in Shanghai, works and lives in Shanghai.


Hu Xiangcheng's artistic journey began with random scribblings on his father's discarded paper ledgers, followed by acts of copying the Manual of the Mustard Seed Garden. After graduating from primary school, he went to Shanghai’s Yuanfeng Woolen Mill as a work-study practitioner, where he worked as a wood-molding operator, sand-casting operator, and cook after only three days of classroom study. In 1970, Hu Xiangcheng studied sketching with Meng Guang. Following graduation from Shanghai Theater Academy in 1976, he taught successively at the academy and Tibet University, before going to Japan to study Japanese at a commercial Japanese language school in 1986 and graduating from Musashino Art University in 1991. In the same year, he started to visit cities and villages in Africa, Europe, and the United States to conduct research and experiments on folk craft and contemporary art. In 1996, he participated in the establishment of the Shanghai Biennale, serving as a member of the biennale’s academic committee for several terms. In 2000, he initiated a decade-long practice of rural construction around Shanghai, before serving as the art director of the United Africa Pavilion at the 2010 Shanghai Expo.

 

Across decades of artistic career, Hu Xiangcheng has carried out experiments in many different fields. His works have been included in local and international exhibitions such as the San Paulo Architecture Biennale, the International Sculpture Exhibition in Venice, the Contemporary Sculpture from China Exhibition in Hague, the Arts, Accumulation and Objects in Asian Megacities exhibition at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, the Shanghai Biennale, the Yokohama Triennale, and the Guangzhou Triennial. He has also engaged in and organized a large number of activities such as contemporary art, performances, country bands, literati gathering, folklore protection and improvement, etc. in public locations such as abandoned rural factories and seaside spots.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Painting, an ancient form of art, holds a special place in my heart, always evolving yet perpetually enduring. Despite speculation that AI may one day replace traditional painting, I firmly believe otherwise. While my paintings may exhibit minor color loss in certain areas over time, the overall composition and proportion remain unchanged. Where there is disappearing, there is also a revealing of what lies beneath. The heavy paints may resist drying for decades, yet the dryness evolves gradually, much like the shifts in the contours of aging skin. Indeed, change is the eternal verity of life. I think AI can create things that are beyond humans’ ability, while humans can create certain things that are beyond AI’s ability. However, it’s possible for AI and humans to work together and it’s interesting for them to collaborate in creation.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Utilizing a trumpet, the percussion instrument, Shanghai dialect rap, and a hand-operated mechanical device, I collaborated with three musicians, Hu Danfei, Zhang Zujing, and Xia Fei, to complete an alternative experiment. Through interaction via music and dynamic installation, we attempt to offer people a fleeting moment of joy and solace amidst the unsettling consequences resulting from global ecology, warfare, and the advancement of artificial intelligence. Additionally, we seek to demonstrate the crisis of small and regional languages facing rapid disappearance worldwide, and hope that the hidden languages of each region will be revitalized after experiencing multiple values.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Fluorescent colors began to increasingly dominate Ding Yi’s canvas since 1998, as an attempt to capture the metropolitan exuberance and vitality of Shanghai and the infinite tension emerging from the intersection of reality and illusion. If the grid compositions in Ding Yi’s “Appearance of Crosses” paintings calls to mind architectural drawings of urban planning, the “Fluorescence” series, on the other hand, bestows this towering landscape with a magical radiant aura. Creation of the “Fluorescence” series continued until 2010. Like the artist’s works of public sculpture and architecture, these paintings respond to Shanghai’s urban spirit, and can be seen as carriers of Shanghai’s urban sensibility in highly concentrated form.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: New exhibitions are often one of the main external sources of Ding Yi’s creative motivation. This work, Appearance of Crosses 2018–B3, was created specifically for the exhibition The Challenging Souls: Yves Klein, Lee Ufan, Ding Yi. Taking three months to complete, the painting is an experiment on a new painting surface—Xuan paper. This choice of material not only echoes Ding Yi’s experience studying traditional Chinese painting at Shanghai University in the late 1980s, it also summons the “East-West contention” that concerned the entire art scene at the time. Such discussion remains relevant today, and this artwork can be seen as the artist’s experiment in the contemporary expression of “Orientalism.”

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Reflection on Chinese and Western cultural conditions and directions runs through Gao Huijub's "The Landscape" series of works. His paintings follow traditional methods, and the landscape in his work presents a twilight texture. His creation conveys the poetry of Chinese traditional landscape painting and Western surreal aesthetics through exquisite brushstroke and multi-layers space layout. There suddenly occurs a little bird without tail feathers in the picture, standing blankly on a cloud without any direction. This action, losing its original flying ability and having to be helped by an external force, comes from the artist's observations on the current conditions of Chinese traditional cultures and arts. He alludes to reality by exhaling the old and inhaling the new in the paintings, so as to keep self-awareness and summon cultural return. The dilemma in contemporary reality enables him to keep sober about cultural critique. Therefore, in front of tradition or reality, the artist can always be free and deliberate in his artistic expression so as to "take nutrients from daily life and transcend beyond the reality."

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1966, Baoding; lives and works in Beijing

 

Freelance artist, selected as one of the Outstanding Artists of China Art Fair with Zhu Dequn Cheng Jungle in 1995, and one of the Top Ten Freelance Artists of China in 2004. He held more than ten solo exhibitions in Singapore, Shanghai, Beijing, Paris, Taiwan and Japan from 1995 to 2018, and took part in more than thirty domestic and international exhibitions during the same period. His works have been collected in art museums and cultural enterprises of many countries, the latest collection being Tsinghua University Art Museum and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the People's Republic of China. Heshang-Gao Huijun Studio has received many national leaders’ visit and encouragement. He is the representative artist of neoclassical landscape painting.

As the strength imbued with traditional essence among contemporary art groups, his neoclassical landscape painting “Xishan Qingyuan Tu” entered the Chinese national collection in 2018.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
The last link in the chain of "city-building-structure" from macro to micro is Yuna's most varied and fundamental creation - irregular structure. Just as matter is composed of molecules, and molecules are composed of atoms, the discovery and study of atoms has become the basis for human understanding of the properties of matter. After proposing the concept of mobile buildings and aerial cities, Yuna's later work focused on the invention and experimentation of different forms of irregular structures.


Yuna made the following distinctions between the subtly related concepts of "irregular", "arbitrary" and "uncertain": when the deployment of the constituent elements of a pattern cannot be defined by convention, it is considered "irregular"; when the constituent elements have no obvious combination rules, it is considered "arbitrary"; "uncertain" patterns or systems, their internal structure not only appears "disordered", but also their constituent elements have no combination rules. In Yuna's architectural system, the details of the architectural object are uncertain, even if they can be defined by statistical approximations, just as thermodynamics and chaos theory presuppose, although the details are unstable, the whole will lead to equilibrium.


Mobile buildings can be composed of a single irregular structure or a mix of different types of irregular structures, such as partition chain structure, protein chain structure, container structure, Möbius structure...

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: At the end of the 1950s, Yona Friedman was in his thirties. The Hungarian proposed his "Mobile Architecture" theory at CIAM then. He believed that residences and urban planning should be decided by residents, and publicly questioned both Le Corbusier's assertion that residents should adapt to the building and the individualism of the Team 10, which evoked much controversy within the architectural circle. For more than half a century, Friedman has retained a distance from mainstream architecture. His theory doesn't just go beyond architecture, but examines the nature of architecture, the identity of residents, and the mechanism of civil society in terms of philosophy, sociology and psychology. His concepts not only represented a challenge to the urban planning of the time, but also inspired a new way of thinking for later architectural design, and have had far-reaching practical influence on urban planning in developing countries. Being in his nineties, Friedman has few realized works. He has however created a unique hand-drawn visual language, and is known as a utopian architect. His architectural concepts and visual expression have had important impact on UK's Archigram and Metabolism movement in Japan. Yona has created a legend through years of self-deviation: how a naturalist constructs sentences through trial and error, how to record the evolution of free will in waiting.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Instead of the variability of architecture noumenon, Friedman's central theory, "Mobile Architecture", is to explore how to develop a framework of architecture that could respond to or contend with the varied social system.The theory echoes with the inhabitants' self-consciousness and free-expression of their spatial needs, highlighting that the existence of a city is to meet human's aspiration for changes. Hence, Yona is above all against the so-called privilege of an architect. To him, the architect is rather a technology provider and popularizer, a problem solver, sometimes a problem performer as well.Friedman describes his unrealized projects as a parabola. His autonomy world ensconced between art and legend indicates a brand new way of life in civil society.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1975, Yiwu; lives and works in Paris, Shanghai and Hangzhou


From 1999 to 2005, using her birth name Chen Lingyang, she was active in the avant-garde art scene in China. Her work Twelve Flower Months was considered a landmark work in the development of contemporary feminist art in China.

 

From 2005 to 2020, Chen Lingyang continues to conduct an art experiment: she actively left the operating system of the art industry, abandoning her identity as an artist,and allowing art to become an entirely private matter.

 

In 2018, she quietly put forward Positive Art Research Center (PARC), which aims to research, practice, and promote art that brings positive force to human beings and society. In 2020, she returned to the art world after publicly announcing that using the name Alice Chen, she would re-assume her identity as an artist. All of Alice Chen's works in the art field will be carried out under the overarching title of "Positive Art Research Center, "whether in the form of creating personal works, initiating projects, curating, or coordinating.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Artistic creation always originates from the artists' inner feelings. It is the transformation of consciousness after the occurrence of concrete reality. In southern China, people have the custom of eating toads. They usually peel them first and then make smoked toad meat, stew, or toad hot pot. This seemingly disgusting creature has a unique taste. Since its glands are poisonous, according to the philosophy of "counteracting one toxin with another", it is used to make a medication called Liu Shen Wan. In 2003, when the artist witnessed hawkers selling toads on the roadside and in the wet market, he was touched by the bloody toad skins they tore off and tossed aside. So the artist decided to go to the wet market every day to pick up those blood-stained skins, take them back home to wash and process them, and use them in a series of works themed "Soul Expiation" and "Life Release". Furthermore, this is also a way to record the artist's life in Jiangnan's picturesque canal towns and his concern and reflection on the relationship between man and nature, cultural customs, and current ecological issues. It is a work of abstract realism.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1958, Shanghai; lives and works in Shanghai


Zhou Yunxia is one of the artists of the “’85 New Wave” generation who grew up with the reform and opening up. He has always been highly sensitive to the reality of life and constantly presents his inner feelings, struggles and thoughts through his works. His first solo exhibition was held at the gallery of Beijing Concert Hall in 1991 and was featured on Beijing TV’s foreign channel and in the overseas edition of China Daily. His solo exhibition “Anesthesia” at Beijing Art Archives Warehouse in 2007 was a record of his experience of living in the Yangtze River villages, and since 2002, his works have reflected a kind of nihility. For example, his work A Request to Heaven (2003–2006) collected by White Rabbit Gallery is his reflection on the ultimate existence. In 2016, he held a solo exhibition “In Between the Times” at The Shanghai Gallery of Art to consolidate and organize his art activities in the past 30 years.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
The footage cited in the work documents Paul Getty II, the grandson of an American oil magnate, being found by the police on the highway south of Salerno on 15 December 1973, five months after his abduction. The starving boy who lost his right ear in the freezing winter was returned to his mother in Rome. After a debriefing with the police, he was sent to a private hospital for a medical examination, which confirmed that he was physically assaulted.

 

The story is one that the artist Charlotte Gyllenhammar heard about as a young girl. What she cannot forget -- more than the chilling plot -- is the sensuality of the teenager Paul Getty as he appeared on the street and the sensuality of the crowd of bystanders at the time. The artist has placed seven sculptures of children wrapped in winter clothing in the audience, as a reenactment of the scene and a reflection on the present.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1963, Goteborg; lives and works in Stockholm.

 

Charlotte Ullenhammar is a renowned Swedish contemporary artist who graduated from the Royal College of Art. Her early works were in the form of paintings, which quickly changed to sculpture, mixed-use installations and video. Her public art works have attracted considerable attention both nationally and internationally, and have made her one of Sweden's most influential sculptors. 1993's public art work "Die for You", created in the centre of Stockholm, made a statement on the environment, society and the individual's situation, and influenced many of her later creations. In 2014, her work "The Spectators" made its debut in China for the 10th Shanghai Biennale. The work was first created in 2003.

title: The New Sutra of the Mountains and the Oceans I

raw.title: The New Sutra of the Mountains and the Oceans I

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
When I was studying in Germany, I kept thinking about a question — what kind of work could express how I feel about today’s real world, and also continue the core narrative of traditional Chinese culture? Seeing the beast illustrations in The Classic of Mountains and Seas, I knew that it was exactly the perspective I was looking for. In the unknown eyes before the Flood, creations in the civilized modern world that we take for granted would become stranger beasts. In 2004, when I came back to China to work in Shanghai, I started the series creation of The New Classics of Mountains and Seas. To begin with, I employed the traditional Chinese painting technique, Baimiao, to draw the beasts with fine ink outlines on paper. It was quite an interesting process to conceive these exotic beasts. On one hand, the modelling of the beasts should be consistent with the prototypes so that the audience can guess what they are at first glance. They also should have the characteristics of real animals so that they do appear alike. On the other hand, the description of their functions should be compatible with the original features and also contain new definitions. When the first group of “beast” drawings were accomplished, I came up with a plan to animate them, and wondered how to form a reasonable thread of narration. In the first animation, I centred the story around energy conflict. Energy was at the core of conflicts of national interests worldwide in the last century, and these “beasts” are products closely related to energy. The basic theme of the first animation was so developed. I employed ink and wash as the visual language to present the animation. It fits well with the entire concept, and is also my personal preference and method of doing works. Zhang Qing, one of the curators of the 2006 Shanghai Biennale, was very interested after seeing my proposal, and determined to include this work in the exhibition. Thus, I took the opportunity and completed the first animation work of The New Classic of Mountains and Seas series.

 

Qiu Anxiong

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b.1972, Sichuan Province; works and lives in Shanghai.


Qiu Anxiong graduated from the Kunsthochschule Kassel in 2004. His creation involve animation, installation, video, painting and other cross-media forms. As a representative artist of water-and-ink animation, Qiu's representative works include the ink animation "The New Sutra of the Mountains and the Oceans", "Minguo Landscape", "Temptation of The Land", and video installation "Staring into Amnesia", etc. His series "The New Sutra of the Mountains and the Oceans" trilogy depicts the technological wonders and existential crises of modern society through the lens of the ancients. Reflecting on the utility of myth in the developmental process of civilization, this trilogy once again places ancient mythological scenarios and tropes under the gaze of a modern society obsessed with technology.

title: “Bend It Like Yoga”  Furniture Series Roll Back Chair

raw.title: “Bend It Like Yoga”  Furniture Series Roll Back Chair

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
“Bend It Like Yoga” Furniture Series comes from the first exhibition of the psD - "In the Name of Architecture". The exhibition, presented through seven mediums – architecture, furniture, product, apparel, jewelry, video, and publication – explores the possibilities of pan-design that comes from an architectural way of thinking.


Starting with materials and structural forms, and pushing specific furniture-making techniques, like curved glulam, to the ultimate limits.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b.1956, Beijing; lives and works in Boston and Beijing


AIA, Founder, Principal Architect of Atelier Feichang Jianzhu, Professor, Tongji University. 

 

Originally from Beijing, Chang received a Master of Architecture degree from the University of California at Berkeley in 1984. He has been practicing in China since 1992 and established Atelier Feichang Jianzhu (FCJZ) with Lijia Lu in 1993. He has won a number of prizes, such as First Place in the Shinkenchiku Residential Design Competition in 1987, a Progressive Architecture Citation Award in 1996, the 2000 UNESCO Prize for the Promotion of the Arts, and the Academy Award in Architecture from American Academy of Arts and Letters in 2006.

 

He participated in many international exhibitions of art and architecture, including five times in the Venice Biennale since 2000, and curated/co-curated the 1st West Bund Biennale of Architecture and Contemporary Art in Shanghai in 2013, the China Pavilion at Venice Biennale in 2008, the 1st Shenzhen Biennale of Urbanism and Architecture in 2005. He has taught at various architecture schools in the USA and China; he is presently a professor at Tongji and MIT where he served as the head of Architecture Department from 2005 to 2010, founded the Peking University Graduate Center for Architecture in 1999, and was the Kenzo Tange Chair Professor at Harvard in 2002 and the Eliel Saarinen Chair Professor at Michigan in 2004. In 2009 he was bestowed the honorary membership by AIA Hong Kong. Since 2011, he became a Pritzker Prize Jury member.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: The artist is adept at combining ink and oil to create different effects according to shifts in his mood, environment, and the weather. In this work, the mixture of ink and oil causes granules to appear on the surface of the painting. Natural cracks emerge at some parts, like cracks in porcelain.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1946, Shanghai; lives and works in Lausanne and Sainte Croix in Switzerland.


Franklin Chow attended the Académie de la Grande Chaumière in Paris. Having been born into an influential family which has fostered lots of outstanding talents and been raised in a paternal education encouraging an appreciation for art, Chow grew up with fine artistic sensibility and taste. His upbringing, as well as rich life and work experience contributed to his multicultural awareness, and was reflected in his artistic creation. His art practice combines the form of traditional Chinese art with the vision and concept of Western contemporary art. His works were exhibited in Switzerland, France, and Singapore, and collected by private collectors and art institutions in Switzerland, France, Germany, the UK, including the Teo Jakob art foundation (Bern), the Inez & Yves Oltramare Foundation (Geneva), and Rolex S.A. (Geneva).

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
The series was initially started in mid 2012 by MadeIn Company (Xu Zhen®) when the artists came to observe an alternative effect from an art historical point of view (or more specifically abstractionism), a whiff of provocativeness largely attributed to the application of tools other than brushes. Then they went on to produce more pieces which were almost monochromic. Their unusual resemblance with satellite view of cityscape when seen from distance, as well as the visual haziness caused by the creamy movement, finally evolve into the birth of series title, "Under Heaven".

 

Under the magnificent title of "Under Heaven", the series works are the dense cream flowers that make people dazzle - strawberry red, grape purple, pineapple yellow, matcha green, milk white, and chocolate black like a thick layer of piping cream on a freshly baked cake, all these mouth-watering food colors and cream flower shapes, stirred and blended in the baroque carved from the forest, due to the exaggeration of the size to present an excessive density and excessive carnival.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
1977 Born in Shanghai, China. Currently lives and works in Shanghai.


Xu Zhen’s practice covers various media such as installations, video, painting and performance, etc. His works displayed in the 49th Venice Biennale in 2001, and won the prize for ‘Best Artist’ at the china Contemporary Art Award in 2004. Aside from being an artist, Xu Zhen is also a curator. He-curated together with other artists major exhibitions in Shanghai and was one of the initiators of Art-Ba-Ba in 2006. In 2009, Xu Zhen established “MadeIn Company”, a contemporary art creation corporate, focused on the production of creativity, and devoted to the research of contemporary culture’s infinite possibilities. In2013, MadeIn Company launched XUZHEN® which is committed to art creation and cutting-edge culture development. In 2014, MadeIn Companyestablished MadeIn Gallery and in November 2016 launched the first “Xu Zhen Store” in Shanghai.

title: Landscape Cosmos-3
medium: Oil on canvas and mixed media

raw.title: Landscape Cosmos-3
raw.medium: Oil on canvas and mixed media 170×220cm

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Chinese landscape painting has long been a critical vehicle for men of letters throughout the history to relieve their feelings and emotions. Though ink is not among the media for Landscape Cosmos-3, Hu Xiangcheng deems that the inheritance of art should be more focused on the essence. So, combining mankind’s current understandings of the world he innovates and goes beyond the usual. In this work these seven violent and intense lines resemble traditional hanging-scroll style, cutting the dynamic landscape into seven images; the flowing mountains and the split planets seem to demonstrate the energy dynamics where objects keep flowing during solidification and get animated during vaporization, just like people can feel and hear the invisible Qi (spirit) and Yun (consonance). The life that has created all this is on the other hand hidden within, its mystery leaving us imagination to explore the past and the future.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
born.1950 in Shanghai, works and lives in Shanghai.


Hu Xiangcheng's artistic journey began with random scribblings on his father's discarded paper ledgers, followed by acts of copying the Manual of the Mustard Seed Garden. After graduating from primary school, he went to Shanghai’s Yuanfeng Woolen Mill as a work-study practitioner, where he worked as a wood-molding operator, sand-casting operator, and cook after only three days of classroom study. In 1970, Hu Xiangcheng studied sketching with Meng Guang. Following graduation from Shanghai Theater Academy in 1976, he taught successively at the academy and Tibet University, before going to Japan to study Japanese at a commercial Japanese language school in 1986 and graduating from Musashino Art University in 1991. In the same year, he started to visit cities and villages in Africa, Europe, and the United States to conduct research and experiments on folk craft and contemporary art. In 1996, he participated in the establishment of the Shanghai Biennale, serving as a member of the biennale’s academic committee for several terms. In 2000, he initiated a decade-long practice of rural construction around Shanghai, before serving as the art director of the United Africa Pavilion at the 2010 Shanghai Expo.

 

Across decades of artistic career, Hu Xiangcheng has carried out experiments in many different fields. His works have been included in local and international exhibitions such as the San Paulo Architecture Biennale, the International Sculpture Exhibition in Venice, the Contemporary Sculpture from China Exhibition in Hague, the Arts, Accumulation and Objects in Asian Megacities exhibition at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, the Shanghai Biennale, the Yokohama Triennale, and the Guangzhou Triennial. He has also engaged in and organized a large number of activities such as contemporary art, performances, country bands, literati gathering, folklore protection and improvement, etc. in public locations such as abandoned rural factories and seaside spots.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Wailing Requiem, the final installment of The Northeast Tetralogy, follows the life of the "migrant worker assassin" in the city before he returns home to seek revenge, as shown from the perspective of his roommate, a fellow laborer. In the city their alienated identities initially formed a barrier between them, but as they travel to their respective hometowns, a connection grows between their spirits. Driven by emotions between the two of them that they can neither define nor clarify, the workers comprehend anew this narrative that transcends individual revenge, and realize that personal emotions may have an unconscious, irrational link with macrohistory. As the tetralogy concludes, reality and fantasy intertwine, past and present tenses antagonize each other, and fragments of China's modern history make fleeting appearances.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
Born 1984; lives and works in Beijing.


Born and raised in Changchun, China, Wang Tuo currently lives and works in Beijing. Wang Tuo employs various mediums and a process that combined interview, reality show and the theatre of absurd to construct a maze of melodrama. Through his performative manipulation on individuals’ lived experiences and intervention in intellectual legacies such as literature, film, theatre and art history, Wang’s practice attempts to examine the unreliable relationship between the contemporary human status, myth and cultural archive. In the self-referential environments that he constructs, dramatic, often humorous as well as absurd aspects of the concept of society are exposed. Wang’s practice also seeks to develop a discourse on how present ideology is derived from its historical context continues to adapt to changing condition. Wang has recent solo shows at Present Company, New York, Salt Project, Beijing, Taikang Space, Beijing. In 2021, Wang Tuo will have his first institutional survey at UCCA Beijing.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
The work "Home" is inspired by my recent experience of viewing houses. I have to find new place for my studio due to unstable situation. I feel almost lost during that process. The speed of urban expansion far exceeds my imagination. There are constantly new housing estates being built with new names. These names are highly similar with words such as Hao (豪), Yu (御), Di (帝), Zun (尊), Jing (晶) appearing frequently. They all point to a kind of expectation of the "luxury", the "prestige" and the "high-end" for home.

However, the fact is that most of them are located at the edge of the city with sparse population and inconvenient traffic, and not suitable for living. The reality and the imagination form an absurd vision.

I collect the names of these housing estates by taking a massive number of pictures of these golden characters usually placed in flowerbeds. With them I build a database from which a random new name can be generated every second through computer program. No beginning, no end and never repeat.

This is an imaginary machine that creates "homes". It is like a perpetual motion machine that continues producing names indefinitely with materials from life. In the meantime, when we are watching the "homes" being freshly created, the homes also look at us from afar.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1990, Shanghai; lives and works in Shanghai.


Hu Weiyi graduated from the China Academy of Art. Committed to new media art, he focuses on the exploration of the unknown and the melancholic moments in life, while staying curious about the nature and bodily harm. He reversed the randomness and naturally-generated relationship to a subjective expression, and preset the audience's trajectory. Like many mature artists, he has a good grasp of space, concepts, and outreach information. His main exhibitions include the solo exhibition “Flirt” (2014) at M50 Art Space in Shanghai, the opening exhibition “Multiverse” (2014) in the Shanghai 21st Century Minsheng Art Museum, the second CAFAM Future Exhibition (2015), and “No Express” (2015) at Ullens Center for Contemporary Art, Beijing.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: In Smoke and Fire, Wang Tuo portrays the image of a migrant worker who exists simultaneously in both worlds of a two-part intertwined reality. In one world, this migrant worker is in a warehouse of movie props with an extremely vague sense of time and space. By reading tales of the miraculous and the legendary, he is projecting himself into multiple texts, “practicing” it again and again in reality or in his imagination. In the other world, the artist is conducting a sample observation of this migrant worker in a small town in Northeast China—recording his daily life, his emotions, and his journey back home. The documentation has slowly turned into a dramatic “rehearsal” of a recent violent incident in China that has been widely discussed. In this narrative on revenge, healing the deep-seated wound seems to have become a ritual that needs to wait. Through these embodied corporeal “counterattacks”, the artist implies a rupture between social and internal identities, as well as the latent contradiction between the individual trauma and the monstrous yet powerless reality.

blocks.body: “A play of Exploration” is a mixed-media installation created by Christophe Demaitre for exhibition "Snacks" held at the Power Station of Art in 2015. He experimented with a subtle and small "construction", as he said: I realized that PSA is a huge museum, so I decided to make a miniature museum in it.

blocks.body:
b.1968 in Kortrijk；lives and works in Shanghai


Christophe Demaitre studied plastic art first in Kortrijk and then in Gent, Belgium. When he traveled through Europe and Asia, his work became oriented towards photography research. In 2006, he was invited by Island 6 Arts Center in Shanghai where he develops his new creation using multimedia technologies.

title: The Temple
medium: Silk, barbed wires, cocoons, polycarbonate sheet, resin corrugated sheet, steel-frame structure

raw.title: The Temple
raw.medium: Silk, barbed wires, cocoons, polycarbonate sheet, resin corrugated sheet, steel-frame structure  3000×1170×1030cm

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
The Temple is a monumental installation that bridges notions of eternity, ritual and redemption across religions and cultures. Amidst a darkened interior, a glowing tower is flanked by two rows of silk-covered pyramids beaming light above. The shadows cast by their metal vertebrae onto the ceiling evoke moving clouds and constellations, while the pyramids below are like monuments linking heaven and earth.

 

Liang created these pyramids by placing his silkworms on their iron understructures, allowing them to shroud the metal in their silk, symbolically embodying life and the sediments of time. The cold metal brings to mind artifice, industry and modernity, and its contrast with the natural softness of the silk brings to mind the Taoist stratagem of conquering the mighty through the weak. The sharp knots interlaced throughout resemble Christ’s crown of thorns from the Crucifixion. This religious connotation is echoed in the iconology of silk itself, which in China contains references to self-sacrifice, generosity, transubstantiation and resurrection. It is further underscored in the layout of the installation, which resembles that of a church interior. Having studied the philosophies of East and West for many years, The Temple and Liang’s other works touch upon themes present across civilizations, reflective of humanity’s shared fate.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
1945, born in Shanghai, China. Currently lives and works in Taizhou, Zhejiang Prov, China.


From 1986 to 1989, Liang Shaoji studied soft sculpture from Maryn Varbanov at China Academy of Art who was one of the world's leading tapestries. In the late 1980s, Liang started experimenting with silkworms. For more than thirty years, he has been indulged in the interdisciplinary creation in terms of art and biology, installation and sculpture, new media and textile. His Nature Series sees the life process of silkworms as creation medium, the interaction in natural world as his artistic language, time and life as the essential idea. His works are fulfilled with a sense of meditation, philosophy and poetry while illustrating the inherent beauty of silk.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: The idea of this work comes from the silk garment excavated from King Ma’s Mound. The silk garment, as thin as cicada’s wings, tells all the memories and history. This piece of circular silk is created upon the artist’s acquaintance of the biological clock of the silkworm, the span of its spinning activity and the regularity of how it piles silk up. The light casts a dim shadow from the silk on the wall, floating, and then leaks away. It seems to depict a tunnel expanding infinitely.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: In 2014, I went to the disaster area to collect the bricks, stones and cement boards of the ruins.The silkworms were spinning to wrap them. The organic life materials comforted the “spirit” in the inorganic materials. Then all “spirits”came back to nirvana.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Liang’s practice often involves using silkworms to wrap or cover distinct objects. The power of this simple action is focused and magnified in Whirl. Liang refers to these round stones wrapped in silk as “Origin” stones. Differing from the work The Origin of Cloud - Wenchuan Stones, which used stones with very specific histories, Whirl uses anonymous, round river stones, sculpted into the forms we see today by what Taoists refer to as the “regular” and “irregular” forces of nature. Silkworms, with their lifespan of only a few weeks, have used their small but seemingly eternal actions to bind the stones, in a gesture that seems to warm them against the desolate cold of eternity. In this work, Liang applies the least amount of manual intervention to illustrate the power of the principle wuwei [letting things run their course.] Dozens of “Origin” stones are arranged into a spiral, a static form hinting at principles of movement in life and the universe.

title: Notebook Shrine
medium: Wood, iron, stone, architect series notebook

raw.title: Notebook Shrine
raw.medium: Wood, iron, stone, architect series notebook 29.7x61x60cm

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
The reusable bags, skateboards, bookmarks, or notebooks sold in the DODODO store are all derivatives of PSA's previous exhibitions. Suppose the source of these derivatives - "those exhibitions that have passed"- embodies human spiritual activity. In that case, designing products for exhibitions is a work that transforms spiritual activity into a practical level.


What we, Birdhead, have done in this project is to dismantle, collage, and appropriate-reassemble the process of removing the usefulness of these exhibition derivatives and giving them spirituality again.


"Bag adult" and "notebook shrine" are our stage practice of understanding and responding to PSA in a "bird's head" way.

-- Bird head

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: Birdhead produces mainly street photography, capturing the everyday minutiae of the city or their birth place, Shanghai. Their huge and growing archives of photographs (both colour and black & white) constitute a portrait of a modern city that is both personal and original.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Ding's appreciation of African woodwork and Chinese folk images along with their symbolic significance is palpable in this series of wood sculptures on display. In the 1960s, having relocated to Shanghai for his career, Ding came into contact with a wider art world, and often attended gatherings at the residences of artists Guan Liang and Liu Haisu. It was in Liu's library Ding first encountered Chinese woodblock print illustrations and catalogues on African folk art, during a time magazines or exhibitions on the subject was scarce. Even though Ding did not follow a certain precedent style, he was greatly encouraged by his teachers' affirmation of his unconventional artistic preference.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
Born to a liberal gentry family in Haimen, Zhejiang, Ding Liren embraced the enlightenment of arts in his childhood, as the family always had artists and opera masters on the guest list. Even at a young age he had a taste for painting; the initial material for his paintings included the opera performances in his hometown, and the stories told by his nanny. Later on, these legendary popular stories became the prototype for the theme of his artwork on many occasions. Although Ding barely had much formal professional training in art, he was a natural student who tended not to acquire artistic knowledge by confining himself to genres. Instead, he drew inspiration equally from various schools of painting as well as folk cultures. After graduation, Ding’s interest led him to work in places including an insect research institute, a toy factory, a furniture factory, etc. It not only expanded his artistic view to a broader range of life experience, but also initiated his journey to the vast realm of folk art. Ding has always been fascinated by the richness of tradition and ritual knowledge sealed in folk cultures. He once discovered some hearth paintings during farmland insect sampling in suburban Shanghai in the late 1950s, and recorded the local architectural styles in Lanzhou, Shaanxi, western Hunan, Shandong, etc. during his visits, just to name a few. The spontaneity of such art along with the underlying narrative coherence deeply influenced the way he produced his artwork. Similarly, case studies on Ding reveal an endogenous growth pattern of modernity embedded in native China.

 

Currently Ding Liren lives and works in Shanghai. He once studied at the Department of Biology, Nanjing University; the Department of Fisheries, Shandong University; and the Department of Painting, East China Branch, Central Academy of Fine Arts (now China Academy of Art). Important solo and group exhibitions include: “Two Insects,” Platform China (2021); “A Southbound Trip of the Journey to the West: Ding Liren’s Solo Exhibition”, Guangdong Museum of Art (2020); “Group Exhibition of Chinese Contemporary Painting,” Liu Haisu Art Museum (1998); “Ding Liren’s Fine Art Exhibition,” Gallery at Central Academy of Fine Arts (1989); “Ding Liren’s Work Exhibition,” Shanghai Chinese Painting Academy (1980).

title: Journey to the West series 100 Send Away the Child

raw.title: Journey to the West series 100 Send Away the Child

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Growing up, Ding Liren held opera performance as one of the dearest art forms to his heart. His parents founded an amateur Peking Opera troupe at home in Taizhou. The vivid imagery of the rehearsals deeply imprinted in Ding's mind first inspired his 70s paintings on the subject. A Journey to the West can be regarded as a continuation of such theater paintings. The composition draws from the aesthetic tradition of stage scenery, which does not highlight a single element but comprises multiple narrative frameworks. It was Ding's nanny who first told him the fables from "A Journey to the West," which initially inspired him to pick up a paintbrush and remains a prototype subject in his future oeuvre. While revisiting his childhood memories, Ding constructed "A Journey to the West" into a "myth" of personal singularity and revealed a most inventive aspect of his memory-making process.

The vivid imagery of the rehearsals deeply imprinted in Ding's mind first inspired his 70s paintings on the subject. A Journey to the West can be regarded as a continuation of such theater paintings. The composition draws from the aesthetic tradition of stage scenery, which does not highlight a single element but comprises multiple narrative frameworks. It was Ding's nanny who first told him the fables from "A Journey to the West," which initially inspired him to pick up a paintbrush and remains a prototype subject in his future oeuvre. While revisiting his childhood memories, Ding constructed "A Journey to the West" into a "myth" of personal singularity and revealed a most inventive aspect of his memory-making process.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
Born to a liberal gentry family in Haimen, Zhejiang, Ding Liren embraced the enlightenment of arts in his childhood, as the family always had artists and opera masters on the guest list. Even at a young age he had a taste for painting; the initial material for his paintings included the opera performances in his hometown, and the stories told by his nanny. Later on, these legendary popular stories became the prototype for the theme of his artwork on many occasions. Although Ding barely had much formal professional training in art, he was a natural student who tended not to acquire artistic knowledge by confining himself to genres. Instead, he drew inspiration equally from various schools of painting as well as folk cultures. After graduation, Ding’s interest led him to work in places including an insect research institute, a toy factory, a furniture factory, etc. It not only expanded his artistic view to a broader range of life experience, but also initiated his journey to the vast realm of folk art. Ding has always been fascinated by the richness of tradition and ritual knowledge sealed in folk cultures. He once discovered some hearth paintings during farmland insect sampling in suburban Shanghai in the late 1950s, and recorded the local architectural styles in Lanzhou, Shaanxi, western Hunan, Shandong, etc. during his visits, just to name a few. The spontaneity of such art along with the underlying narrative coherence deeply influenced the way he produced his artwork. Similarly, case studies on Ding reveal an endogenous growth pattern of modernity embedded in native China.

 

Currently Ding Liren lives and works in Shanghai. He once studied at the Department of Biology, Nanjing University; the Department of Fisheries, Shandong University; and the Department of Painting, East China Branch, Central Academy of Fine Arts (now China Academy of Art). Important solo and group exhibitions include: “Two Insects,” Platform China (2021); “A Southbound Trip of the Journey to the West: Ding Liren’s Solo Exhibition”, Guangdong Museum of Art (2020); “Group Exhibition of Chinese Contemporary Painting,” Liu Haisu Art Museum (1998); “Ding Liren’s Fine Art Exhibition,” Gallery at Central Academy of Fine Arts (1989); “Ding Liren’s Work Exhibition,” Shanghai Chinese Painting Academy (1980).

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
From 1959 to 1965, Ding Liren worked at the Shanghai Institute of Entomology. His careful observation of insect specimens under the microscope for a long time gave him a different insight into the movement laws of micro-organisms and the mysteries of life. This experience also made Ding Liren's first exposure to stove painting in the countryside of Shanghai, and since then he has been attracted by the vivid forms of folk art that are not limited to traditional paradigms. Ding Liren once compared his interest in single-celled organisms to his interest in folk and primitive art; Although single-celled organisms do not have a central nervous system, they are perfectly capable of digestion, movement, and eating, as if guided by an invisible system, he said. This is in line with his understanding of the integrity of the internal meaning system of folk art and the continuity with local customs and belief systems.


The "Insect Collage" series includes Ding Liren's fictional models based on two categories: locusts and 䖬 insects. Most of the collage materials come from the fashion magazines he scour at garage sales, and the high-quality pictures and grotesque shapes provide him with a steady flow of creative inspiration. These insects seem to contain a strange world full of modern images, but also reminiscent of the artist's own rich life experience.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: In this work, Hsia Yan depicts a lady holding a cat in her arms, with a serene aura that seems to harbour the artist's plain memory of the past. Art scholar Liu Yung Jen concluded, "'Figure' is one of Hsia Yan's most important subjects. Even plants and animals show traces of anthropomorphism ... The playfulness in approaching art and the loyalty to self are inherently contrastable and intriguing, filling the picture with a vibrant modernity."

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
Hsia Yan, a.k.a. Hsia Zuxiang. He went to Taiwan in 1949, and co-founded one of the first modern art groups that advocated innovation in the region, namely the “Ton Fan Art Group,” which was viewed as an experimental and open-up stance against the conservative painting world. To take a more active part in the development of the avant-garde, Hsia left for Paris and New York at the age of 31. Inspired by this experience, he gradually deviated from his original style of mystical abstraction with calligraphic characters, and switched to concerns regarding existentialism and subjective experience. His signature style, “fuzzy man,” took its initial form from these rushing figures composed of quivering lines, suggesting a restlessness intrinsic to human existence. In the following decades, Hsia brought multiple pictorial themes and motifs and the experience encapsulated into the “fuzzy” universe. He refused to attribute his periodic subject matter to globalization or the local environment, believing that “painting itself is a ‘philosophical’ act that comes from what the visual enables the heart to see.” The “fuzzy man” created by the artist, is both a blurry shadow projected on the canvas and a dual mode of observation that blurs the reality and the reconstructed fantasy. Featuring the variations of the “fuzzy man,” the exhibition examines the different stages of Hsia’s radical and still evolving artistic career.

Currently Hsia used to study painting with Li Chun-Shan in Taiwan and thus played an important role in the regional modernization of painting. His solo and group exhibitions include: “Hsia Yan: Journey to Art”, Taipei Fine Arts Museum (2018); “The 8th Shanghai Biennale,” Shanghai Art Museum (2010); “Work Exhibition of Six Painters in Taiwan,” National Art Museum of China (1984); “Urban Aesthetics”, Queens Museum of Art, New York (1976) ; The 5th Sao Paulo Art Biennial, Brazil (1959).

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: “Accordion Book” is one of Ding Yi's few albums. This traditional Chinese form of painting allows viewer to appreciate the painting in a way similar to reading. In the process of flipping through pages, the pattern composed of the crosses as a unit unfold sequentially. Interrelated and independent, they challenge the possibility of change within the limited size.

raw.title: Light as Fuck II

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: “Light as Fuck II” is based upon a conviction that the lightness of the isolated exterior or interior is a source of interesting material. Artist arranged the video of cityscape along the bund upside down and presented unexpectedly an acrobatics performance. Beneath the appearance of urbanization, Yang realized the changes in weight of the city and therefore decided its weightlessness as descriptive element in this piece by holding the crucial construction upside down. In this very series, "light" and "easy" encourage the awareness accompanied by significance. They smash inside and outside previously separated from each other and produce a drama which is both amusing and thought-provoking.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b.1968, Hangzhou; works and lives in Shanghai.


Yang Zhenzhong has been working with various art forms such as photography, installation, video, multimedia, and interaction since 1994. He is adept in analyzing the relationship between people, space and their living conditions in a straightforward and sarcastic attitude, and satirizing moral values in modern Chinese society. With metaphors and paradoxes, he tries to question the spirit of the times, and condemn a host of problems people have to face in modern society in a humorous manner.

title: The Equinox
medium: Installation, video, images；Willow: , mulberry: 150 × 210 × 290 cm; Video 4'

raw.title: The Equinox
raw.medium: Installation, video, images；Willow: 220 × 180 × 346 cm, mulberry: 150 × 210 × 290 cm; Video 4'

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Yang Zhenzhong continues to crack his jokes in the work The Equinox. The natural growing direction of the trees is altered due to human intervention: their intertwined roots are exposed nakedly towards the sky, while the crowns are almost brutally forced into cement pots, replacing the roots’ function to expand deep into the soil instead of sprouting from the branches. As a paradoxical spectacle rooted in reality, the work conveys a profound analysis of people’s living conditions in today’s society. When the orientation of the world’s development is reversed, can all of us overcome the reality like a tree does with support from its inner vitality, and re-discover a way to survive?

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
Born to a liberal gentry family in Haimen, Zhejiang, Ding Liren embraced the enlightenment of arts in his childhood, as the family always had artists and opera masters on the guest list. Even at a young age he had a taste for painting; the initial material for his paintings included the opera performances in his hometown, and the stories told by his nanny. Later on, these legendary popular stories became the prototype for the theme of his artwork on many occasions. Although Ding barely had much formal professional training in art, he was a natural student who tended not to acquire artistic knowledge by confining himself to genres. Instead, he drew inspiration equally from various schools of painting as well as folk cultures. After graduation, Ding’s interest led him to work in places including an insect research institute, a toy factory, a furniture factory, etc. It not only expanded his artistic view to a broader range of life experience, but also initiated his journey to the vast realm of folk art. Ding has always been fascinated by the richness of tradition and ritual knowledge sealed in folk cultures. He once discovered some hearth paintings during farmland insect sampling in suburban Shanghai in the late 1950s, and recorded the local architectural styles in Lanzhou, Shaanxi, western Hunan, Shandong, etc. during his visits, just to name a few. The spontaneity of such art along with the underlying narrative coherence deeply influenced the way he produced his artwork. Similarly, case studies on Ding reveal an endogenous growth pattern of modernity embedded in native China.

 

Currently Ding Liren lives and works in Shanghai. He once studied at the Department of Biology, Nanjing University; the Department of Fisheries, Shandong University; and the Department of Painting, East China Branch, Central Academy of Fine Arts (now China Academy of Art). blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: The series of “Water System Refuge” focuses on the impacts of local policies and post-disaster reconstruction after the 2008 Sichuan earthquake. Taking old tents, building materials of ethnic Qiang people, and the post-earthquake museum as our research objects, this project discusses how frequent disasters in the upper stream of the Minjiang River (which is not a human-centered area, with its complex geological structure) are related to the urgent need for collective experiments beyond the region,and the need for thinking about the diversity of local traditions, local plants and ancient wisdom.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
Cao Minghao, born 1982, and Chen Jianjun, born 1981

Working collaboratively since 2010; based in Chengdu.


The practice collaborated by Cao Minghao and Chen Jianjun is based on research and focuses on processes and multiple ways of collaboration. The two artists make efforts to explore new social relationships between ecological materials and human society; they particularly look at the river basins which have not been re-recognized and the water systems which have been outside the real orders, to explore the changes of ecology history and the ways of re-imagining the future. Their works include researching about the disappearing countryside, the connection of migrant workers in the South, the new narratives of specific water systems and the public installations of water refuge. Their works create the power of connection between all things through different visual narratives. Their projects have been shown at a number of exhibitions, including COSMOPOLIS #2.0：Repenser l’humain in Centre Pompidou (Paris, 2019), COSMOPOLIS #1.5: Enlarged Intelligence (Chengdu, 2018), The 7th Bi-city Biennale of Urbanism/Architecture (Shenzhen, 2017), etc.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Tong Wenmin “grafted” Shanghai's endemic plants into the bodies of the performers - different plants are allocated to different performers based on the postures and characteristics of each performer - and built a “forest” at the Power Station of Art Shanghai(PSA). The muscles tired from staying in the same position for a long time, accompanied by the slight ups and downs of an individual’s breathing. The relationship between a tree and a forest, and human beings and the environment are re-examined here.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b.1989, Chongqing; works and lives in Chongqing.


Tong Wenmin's work often focuses on the intersection between individual perception and the external environment, stimulating visual poetry, inspiring action, and exploring wild thinking as well as the meaning of modern life through behaviors that at first seem counter-intuitive. Through often simplified or regulated movements, her work hints at the allegorical character of the body and action within a semantically rich context.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
Christian Boltanski was born in Paris in 1944, and is a French visual artist that works with mixed media installations. From story to History, Boltanski emerges as one of the leading artists in the contemporary art scene since the early 1970s, exhibiting in the most important museums worldwide. Preoccupied with themes of remembrance, mortality, childhood and the passing of time, his artworks, which include photography, sculpture, painting and installation, often work as narratives that reflect both social spectrums and personal features. Christian Boltanski's work draws on history, from the most universal to the most intimate, as a way of challenging the present. Since the beginning of his artistic career in the 70s and 80s, he has recorded and tracked human drama as the subject of his work, in an effort to bring the memory of forgotten tragedies and struggles to the forefront of the here and now.

 

The events of Christian Boltanski’s birth and childhood - the end of the last world war and the liberation of Paris from German occupation - have marked his work. After having dropped out of school early, at age 13, he began to paint large expressionist paintings he exhibited in 1968 with "The impossible life of Christian Boltanski", first film among many others that he created until 1974. 

 

He exhibited his work very early, at the Sonnabend Gallery in 1971, at the Documenta in Kassel in 1972, then in a large series of exhibitions in the United States that started in 1987 and went through New York, Chicago, Los Angeles, and then in the 1990s in many European museums.

 

He worked more and more with the light and shadows and created the series of "Monuments" and "Reservations". "Lessons Of Darkness" sums up this time in this title. In the early 2000s, he turned to very large installations and participated in musical performances. His installations were then becoming more complex using sound as the movements as well. The works of C. Boltanski fall under the category of ‘Total Art’.

 

In the last few years, he mainly favoured huge installations such as "Personnes" in the series Monumenta at the Grand Palais in Paris, No Man's Land at the Armory in New York, 2010 or even Chance at the French Pavilion of the Venice Biennale in 2011. Next to these ephemeral projects, he realises permanent works that constantly increase such as “The Archives of the Hearts” in the island of Teshima in Japan or “The life of CB” on the island of Tasmania in Australia. Christian Boltanski has taught a large part of his life and has produced more than 100 artist’s books. He lives and works in Malakoff near Paris but spends most of his time traveling to create new projects around the world. He is represented by the Kewenig, Marian Goodman and Albarran Bourdais galleries.
