blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Boltanski presents four works created with shadows. In each case, the shadows of tiny figurines are projected onto the gallery walls. One depicts a small theatre of the macabre, another is the image of a hanged man, the third is the angel of death in flight, and the fourth is a mysterious dancer who turns ceaselessly. This kind of phantasmagoric imagery is part of a tradition heritaged from the Middle Ages until the 19th century. These mysterious shadows arevisible through small windows outside the room.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: For Animitas - Chili, Boltanski made this 13-hour video in Chile’s Atacama Desert. With hundreds of small bells attached to long stems of convallaria majalis, he has recreated a map of the sky. This work was abandoned in the desert and has probably since been destroyed. This video is the only remaining testimony of its existence.

blocks.body: In this installation comprised of three consecutive videos shot in Patagonia, Argetina, Boltanski aimed at communicating with the whales through horns in the hope of their response. In Native American culture,whales know the beginning of time. For Boltanski, this is the quest for unattainable knowledge.

title: Feel Just Like a Fish in Water

raw.title: Feel Just Like a Fish in Water

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: An old wooden dinghy is stranded on the white salt beach. Live fish swim around inside the boat, which is surrounded by scattered blue glass sculptures of various shapes. Like a Fish in Water was first exhibited at Arnolfini Gallery in Bristol, UK, in 2001, home to one of the world's oldest seaports. The glass sculptures with connotations of colonial trade—perfume bottles, vases, fish bones and candle holders—were all commissioned by the artist at local traditional glassmaking studios during her residency in Bristol. The simple, pure color tone is drawn from the famous International Klein Blue. At first, the world was drawn closer together by trade. As history unfolded, the original trade products no longer circulated on the markets, but the mutual aesthetic influences between cultures run deep.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1959, Xianyou, Fujian Province; lives and works in Paris.


Shen Yuan is one of the earliest Chinese contemporary artists to gain international recognition. In the early 1980s, she studied in the Chinese Painting Department of the Zhejiang Academy of Fine Art (now the China Academy of Art), and expanded on experimental arts as led by the trend at the time. She experienced changes of living environment and a discontinuity of cultures as she moved to France in the early 1990s, which provoked her reflection on language and identity issues. Shen is skilled at using daily objects to create art installations, and has a preference for those that dissolve shortly and are difficult to use. She contends that “it is the responsibility of an artist to endow new value upon things.” Materials like knitting, embroidery, hair and shoes appear constantly in her artworks, reflecting the simple scenes of women’s everyday life as well as the complex feminist discourse. Her recent artworks demonstrate a closer association with her peripatetic experience travelling around the world, which exhibits her acute perception towards the dramatic changes that are taking place around us.

title: La Jardin
medium: Iron, fabric, wire, fishing net, mixed materials ,  380 x 230 x 550 cm

raw.title: La Jardin
raw.medium: Iron, fabric, wire, fishing net, mixed materials 600 x 500 x 320 cm,  380 x 230 x 550 cm

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: The artwork is a site-specific installation created by Shen Yuan for the exhibition "HON: Niki de Saint Phalle & Shen Yuan" held at the Power Station of Art in 2018. The title of the work continues the artist's suspicion and dismantling of the language. The “garden” was originally a masculine noun in French and was modified to be negative here. The work is divided into two parts: the British style corset is divided into two parts: a part of the style is simple, shaped like a female upper body, up to 5.5 meters, the audience will be immediately exposed to the glare of the lights and surveillance cameras, become a "transparent person"; The other part is 3.5 meters high and has a rich interior. It is strewn with sewing machines, flower pots, fishing nets, spring eyes and other objects, depicting a self-sufficient picture of farming life.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
In "Light of a Thousand Autumns 2," one of five works presented at the 2012 Shanghai Biennale, our portraits are separated from each other, with the six photos in the middle covering everyday landscapes and our playfulness with friends. The "Thousand Autumn Light" series was shot between 2010 and 2012, and the name comes from a type of oil fume ink. For us, naming the work is as random as naming the group Birdhead - the names themselves are meaningless, like an empty bottle, and how the two members think and work constitutes the world of Birdhead. In 2011, for a job opportunity, we went to Datong in Shanxi Province with a team that was searching for and recording folk music, then to Inner Mongolia, northern Shaanxi, and then to Ordos. This trip was like a switch for us, the blood of the interest in traditional culture and the early years of the arts and crafts school of enlightenment mixed together to awaken a wonderful return. When we return to the familiar urban landscape for a new self-exploration, this "return" is reflected in the work along with the moment of pressing the shutter.


-- Bird head

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: Birdhead produces mainly street photography, capturing the everyday minutiae of the city or their birth place, Shanghai. Their huge and growing archives of photographs (both colour and black & white) constitute a portrait of a modern city that is both personal and original.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: In his later years, Chen Fushan maintained a free state of creation, was good at controlling the accidental factors, expressed his wonderful ideas in the accidental, and pursued the true meaning of life. The imaginary picture is transformed into lines and color blocks that are smooth and blocked, relaxed and tight, transparent and heavy, and become the nerve endings of the artist's body, emotion and cognition, expressing the yearning and pursuit of freedom.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: Luis Chan born in 1905 in Panama, Chan moved with his Cantonese family to Hong Kong five years later. He spent the rest of his life in the city, watching it change and devoting his life to making art that reflected those transformations. He began as a realist painter in the English style, capturing day-to-day scenes around Hong Kong with such verve and skill until his 40s that he earned him a reputation as the ‘Watercolor King’ and was considered one of the “Three Musketeers” of Hong Kong painting alongside with Li Bing and Yu Ben. After the 1950s, Chan devoted himself to experimenting different emerging painting techniques, including Abstraction and Illusionism. blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: This work is from the late 1960s to the 1980s "City of People" series. In the picture, all kinds of people, different ages, different genders, different professions, the head is surging, the look is different, and the stage is turned. Chen Fu-shan's paintings are like a multi-prism, showing a kaleidoscope of human conditions with strange composition and absurd images. Building a Hong Kong with an inclusive attitude; With a broader mind, in different latitudes with brushstrokes to express the changes in the current situation, social issues, with the strength of color to restore the metaphor of urban life.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
In the picture of "New Year", the plants, characters, animals, and the mountains and rocks are one, floating in the water and the air. The small people in the stone island dressed in bright clothes, with red and white top hats, smiling at each other, the crowd is happy, permeated with a festive atmosphere. "New Year" uses a traditional Chinese hanging pattern, which Chen Fu Shan once called his modern Chinese painting. This pattern is very common in the "Fantasy landscape" series, through the use of traditional ink media, with magnificent fantasy as the theme, began a series of vivid modern Chinese painting creation.


After bidding farewell to realistic painting, Chan Fu Shan's performance of scenery is more to depict his imagination of Hong Kong, as well as surreal dream wonders. In addition to the common elements of landscape, plants, flowers, people, animals, etc., the seasonal solar terms are added as the theme. The characteristics of the city organism grow in nature, and the grandeur of nature and the rhythm of life appear on the paper. With a surreal approach, Chan has built a peaceful and tranquil "fantasy home" for himself and for the people of Hong Kong.

title: Ocean No.9
medium: Mixed Media and Collage on Paper

raw.title: Ocean No.9
raw.medium: Mixed Media and Collage on Paper 76×56cm

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: The collage series, which took place in the mid-1970s, is a more experimental product created by Chan Fu Shan after he re-cut, deconstructed and freely reorganized old paintings when he was sorting them out. Sketching paintings, Western album pictures, newspaper and magazine pictures created in the early years were freely reorganized. In this attempt, Chen Fushan builds the fantasy space in his mind on paper, and the memory and the past are structurally extended, radiating a different kind of interest.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Untitled is a watercolor work created by Chan Fu-shan in 1970. In the center of the picture, a number of small people without faces appear. The bodies and hair of the small people are integrated with the green mountains and tree trunks in the background, which is clever and interesting. Using the blank space to add painting elements in the freehand landscape is a creative technique that Chen Fushan used to use after mastering the technique of single plate rubbing. We can find some clues in a large number of art magazines that Chan Fu-shan subscribs to, and he often carries out "graffiti adding" style of secondary creation in various Chinese ink albums, Monet, Picasso and other master albums. This practice of dialogue with the classics, through its abundant free imagination and expression talent to grow, the accumulation of inspiration and thinking into a strange creation.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
Chan's art world is full of rich and diverse images, from fish and crabs living underwater to dragons swimming in the sky. These seemingly fantastical visions are based on the feelings and thoughts he has accumulated in his life. When intention and logic intermingle, the two clear springs converge, flow to the unknown, but also out of a unique, deep, vast field.


Compared with the realistic period in the early years, Chen Fushan used colors in the transformation period more cheerful and bold, and often used high-saturation colors that stimulated the senses. In "Underwater", Chen Fu Shan's creation has a clear spray painting and single plate rubbings skills, which marks a great turning point in his painting career, "non-geometric abstract painting" has taken shape, and the work is quite a bit of the shadow of the "fantasy landscape" in the later period.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: During the 1960s and 1970s, when Hong Kong was transformed from a colonial city into an international metropolis, the ideology of The Times catalyzed the transformation of art forms. After deciding to bid farewell to realism, Chen Fushan continuously tried surrealism, cubism, pop collage, spray painting and other styles and techniques, trying to find his own vocabulary in the dazzling modern art style. These two oil paintings on wood were created during this period, and the abstract level relationship different from the realistic period is deduced from different themes.

During late 1960s, the fantasy landscape he eventually embraced later became his signature, showcasing strange creatures and imaginative scenes that span from heaven to seafloor. Such paintings revealed Chan’s free and brave surreal world, especially with bright colors and fluent lines, and brought back his childhood innocence. Led by his subconscious, they created a direct psychological state of Chan’s response to the myriad people of Hong Kong as it was metamorphosed from a colonial city to a global metropolis, and the sophisticated collective mind they had to confront. A painter as well as an art critic, Chen had been active in Hong Kong’s cultural circle, and significantly contributed to the development of local art. From his first solo in 1933 to his last in 1993, he hosted a total of 47 solo exhibitions throughout his more-than-50-year-long career, and published a rich number of literature that helped introduce contemporary art. With Chan’s creative mentality that always focused on both the landscapes and the mindscapes of Hong Kong, his paintings became strong psychological [spiritual] and artistic witnesses to not just China’s modernization process, but also his rise as a first-generation artist in the country’s modern art movement.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: In his early years, the realistic style of figure oil paintings shows the influence of his western painting training and the western painting art atmosphere in Hong Kong at that time. In 1952, Chan was elected president of the Hong Kong Fine Arts Society, and in the following years, he published a number of monographs, such as "On Painting" and "How to Draw a Portrait", which systematically explained to the public his grasp of realistic techniques and artistic concepts.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
“Smear” is the conception of “write-in” and “mop-up”. During the process where mRNA sends the DNA hereditary information to the protein processor, it is modified by a series of chemical signs (including “read-in”, “mop-up”, “write-in”) which it tell the cell which gene should be expressed and silenced.


For the exhibition at the Power Station of Art in Shanghai in 2017, I am preparing to make a work using genetically modified maize. The core idea of this work is, through the process of CRISPR-casq genome editing, to lift the inhibiting mechanism of gene expression of the maize in order to reactivate the dormant ancient genes. By doing so, the maize is forced to return to exhibiting its original traits. This is done by guiding the casq by means of gRNA and executed to the point where the specific ancient gene resides inside the maize genome, thus knocking off the two inhibitory genes Tb1 and Tu1 and relieving the enzyme-bind and its fixed location. The maize will then exhibit the teosinte and hermaphroditic trait.


Gene editing and Gene splicing

CRISPR-CAS9, which was introduced in the early 1990s, can be used as a tool for gene editing to modify the DNA of almost all organisms. At present, scientists of various countries are constantly improving the tools for gene editing. Gene editing changes the molecular sequence, and gene splicing changes the structure of the molecule itself. Both can make the gene product a new structure and function, although the methods are different. Splicing is an event in the initial stage of transcription. The same gene leads to different mRNA and protein products because of different splicing methods. Editing is a post-transcriptional modification which involves insertion deletion of bases and nucleotide substitution. By changing the information characteristics of the transcriptional products, gene editing will lead to changes both amino acid sequences of coding protein, codon meanings, as well as whole reading frame due to the gene moving location to change the gene products. At present, the biological art creation method is still in the stage of gene editing and gene splicing, and the conditions for going to the artificial genome are not yet available. The work "Smear" is a corn trait constructed by deleting two genes, Tb1 and Tu1, by using the CRISPR-cas9 editing tool. There are many ways to use gene editing, such as deleting, inserting, inverting, repeating, and translocating DNA fragments. Artists can make choices based on the needs of the program.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1942, Lanxi, Hei Longjiang Province; lives and works in Shanghai.


Li Shan studied at Heilongjiang University in 1963 and attended the Shanghai Theatre Academy in 1964. At a very young age, Li managed to avoid the bayonets of the Japanese invading army. During his study at the university, he was completely swept over by the “Cultural Revolution”.


He started to practice contemporary art in the late 60s, and created some important works during that period, i.e. the “Propagation” series and the “Rouge” series, both of which were selected for the China/Avant-Garde Art Exhibition (1989), the 45th Venice Biennale (1993), and the 22nd Sao Paulo Biennale (1994). He was one of the earliest Chinese artists to participate in the Venice Biennale, and a seminal figure in the '85 New Wave Movement (1984-1985).


As a pioneer of BioArt, he turned his artistic thinking to issues related to life science in 1993, and began to amass the scientific knowledge for the defining and creation of BioArt in 1995. In early 1998, with molecular biology as the scientific foundation, he finished the first BioArt proposal in art history at the genetic level, Reading. In 2000, he published the article on BioArt, The Story of Fish and Butterfly. In 2007, his live BioArt work, The Pumpkin Project, was completed and exhibited at the ShanghART Gallery. In 2012 and 2017, his large solo BioArt exhibitions were held in the Museum of Contemporary Art in Taipei and Power Station of Art in Shanghai, respectively.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: This video work, supervised by Li Shan, presents and describes the fundamental concepts of molecular biology. It delves into the structure and function of proteins, nucleic acids, and other macromolecules, highlighting their roles in information transfer. The piece also explores the composition, properties, and interactions of these molecules, as well as the biochemical processes of molecular transformation and energy conversion that are essential to life.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: "Reading Notes" intuitively shows the transformation of Li Shan's biological art creation from "theory" to "practice". It includes sketches of Recombination, The Pumpkin Project, Encounter, and The Error of Translation, as well as the process of making the Butterfly and the Fish in the Reading series, the operation of implanting human brain stem cells into a mouse's fertilized egg, and even the process of recombining Li Shan's own phenotypic genes with those of a frog.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Li Shan transformed the standard Holy Bible he purchased from a church by adding to the book cover the images of his own works and the title ‘Li Shan’s Bio-art Laboratory.’ This work concisely and forcefully eliminated the opposition and division between ‘creationism’ and ‘evolutionism’, stating the artist’s perspective of “all lives being equal and the same.”

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: The artist has restructured images in order to illustrate that characteristics of living things can produce different phenotypes by transforming, substituting, or mixing genetic information. God created men as in His image, Li Shan extended this spirit to all species, such as frogs, mantis, or bees. Substituting or pasting the genetic codes from his own mRNA, he have virtually created various creatures possessing human lips, skin, organ tissues, and other feature.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: The 33 photographic images of new-variety pumpkins successfully bred by The Pumpkin Project and some drawings related to this project. The Pumpkin Project is a set of biological art completed by Li Shan and Zhang Pingjie with the assistance of professors from the Shanghai Agricultural College in 2007.This is also the first artwork produced by bio-genetic engineering in China. It is the brainchild of two artists sharing the same concept: in the end, bio-art should present works with life. Compared to regular breeding experiment of flowers and plants, pumpkins have a visual impact on shape, which through gene conversion can be changed drastically, even being unrecognizable, and become a completely new artistic style .In this expriment, the artists focused ont eh shape of variation of pumpkins, Although the new life result of artificial transformation might be fragile, the diversity and innovation in form and the freshness and extraordinariness of limbs were very exciting to the two artists. However, the possibility and impact of manipulation of life have inevitably caused much controversy in respect to law, philosophy ,and morality. Therefore,bio-art of Li Shan and Zhang Pingjie can also be considered a metaphorical experiment touching on the future of social topics.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: In the process of reading, skipping words, misreading, or mispronunciation are inevitable.For Li Shan, these are indeed the most charming and meaningful incidents.If they are connected to the behavior of reading in life, a new definition of life and the creation of alternative art can be spawned. Reading Series 08 seems to be a conceptual sketch of a biologist before he carries out an experiment. An unfinished work of art, it records the traces of the artist’s thinking and is garnished with conflicting elements and contradicting vocabulary. In fact, can be regarded as an embodiment of Li Shan’s bio-art concept in a panel painting. The painting juxtaposes tiger, human, dragonfly, sperm, and other symbols of life, presenting a progressive state of information exchange in genetics. As Li Shan has uttered, “I provide that symbols and present them to you. I have reached this goal!”

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1946, Shanghai; lives and works in Lausanne and Sainte Croix in Switzerland.


Franklin Chow attended the Académie de la Grande Chaumière in Paris. Having been born into an influential family which has fostered lots of outstanding talents and been raised in a paternal education encouraging an appreciation for art, Chow grew up with fine artistic sensibility and taste. His upbringing, as well as rich life and work experience contributed to his multicultural awareness, and was reflected in his artistic creation. His art practice combines the form of traditional Chinese art with the vision and concept of Western contemporary art. His works were exhibited in Switzerland, France, and Singapore, and collected by private collectors and art institutions in Switzerland, France, Germany, the UK, including the Teo Jakob art foundation (Bern), the Inez & Yves Oltramare Foundation (Geneva), and Rolex S.A. (Geneva).

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: A layer of chicken wire is added over the grey hessian and marouflaged with Xuan paper and varnish, faintly resembling a grid. A small African woodcarving is affixed onto the chicken wire at the bottom portion. The work is divided into upper and lower portions. The line across the middle appears like an expansive horizon, pulling the viewer into a lingering story.

title: Shadow, Banner
medium: Ink, glaze and oil on unmounted canvas

raw.title: Shadow, Banner
raw.medium: Ink, glaze and oil on unmounted canvas

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: This installation is a tribute to the artist’s mentor, the renowned French journalist and art historian Pierre Daix. The ‘Banner’ alludes to the Super Étendard fighter aircraft developed in the 1970s, as a symbol of the brutality of war and as a metaphor for Daix’s tenacity and fighting spirit. The installation consists of a 10 metre-long canvas painted in black, and figurines of people created from scorched Xuan paper mounted on wire, scattered over a wooden frame. The burnt figurines commemorate death, and even more so, express compassion for the predicament of the living. The work is the artist's reflection on the irony of human nature: ‘The darkness is represented by the figures marouflaged with Xuan paper, and the light is the black painting on canvas, unmounted as a throwaway.’

medium: Xuan paper on wire frame, scorched and varnished

raw.title: Paper Dragon - Icarus
raw.medium: Xuan paper on wire frame, scorched and varnished

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: This work is the artist’s introspection. Xuan paper is mounted on a wire frame and then scorched and varnished. The installation takes the shape of a coiled dragon with three sets of legs, clutching its tail in its mouth. Icarus is a character in Greek mythology and his story is a metaphor that one should heed the advice of not flying too close to the sun or he will get burnt and end up going down in flames, even if he was a favourite son. To the artist, vanity brings destructive consequences and kills one’s creativity, because he yearns to hear applause rather than his inner voice.

His upbringing, as well as rich life and work experience contributed to his multicultural awareness, and was reflected in his artistic creation. His art practice combines the form of traditional Chinese art with the vision and concept of Western contemporary art. His works were exhibited in Switzerland, France, and Singapore, and collected by private collectors and art institutions in Switzerland, France, Germany, the UK, including the Teo Jakob art foundation (Bern), the Inez & Yves Oltramare Foundation (Geneva), and Rolex S.A. (Geneva).

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
To find light weight simple functional stool for the studio preferably done by local craftsman with locally available materials Prof. Doshi designed the stool.

It was made by the carpenter of Prof. Doshi using a single pipe bent. To give it stability two supports were added, one vertical pipe at the rear side and one horizontal pipe in the front that became the foot rest.

Another derivative was made of the same stool by adding a back rest (again a simply bent metal pipe) 。The seat was then made with the local method of braiding of the jute ropes by local craftsman.

The main objective of designing this stool was to design the cheapest light weight high drafting stool (for architectural drafting tables) & low sitting stool using locally available crafts.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
Prof. Balkrishna Doshi was a Fellow of the Royal Institute of British Architects and a Fellow of the Indian Institute of Architects. After studying at the JJ School of Architecture, Bombay, he worked for four years with Le Corbusier as Senior Designer (1951-1954) in Paris, and four more years in India to supervise his projects in Ahmedabad. He was also associated with Louis Kahn as the local architect for IIM in Ahmedabad, which indeed is an architectural landmark. Prof. Doshi had been a jury member for several international and national competitions, including the Indira Gandhi National Centre for Arts, the Aga Khan Award for Architecture and the Pritzker Prize.


Apart from his international fame as an architect, Prof. Doshi is equally known as an educator and institution builder. He has been the founder and the first director of the School of Architecture, Ahmedabad (1962-72), founder and the first Director of the School of Planning (1972-79), founder and the first Dean of the Centre for Environmental Planning and Technology (1972-81), founding member of Visual Arts Centre, Ahmedabad, and founder and the first Director of the Kanoria Centre for Arts, Ahmedabad. Prof. Doshi has been instrumental in establishing the nationally and internationally known research institute Vastu-Shilpa Foundation for studies and research in environmental design which has undertaken pioneering work in low cost housing and urban planning.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
“They destroyed our houses, they stole our possessions, they burned our clothes, they took our animals, they razed the corn, they persecuted us night and day.”

——Case 5339 (male Achíwitness) Plan Sánchez, Baja Verapaz, 1982.

Volume 1. Third Chapter. REMHI (Recovery of Historical Memory).

 

During the war in Guatemala, as part of a scorched earth military strategy, the corn was cut, it was burned, it was destroyed by the National Army with the intention to destroy indigenous communities that were considered guerrilla bases. The peace was signed in 1996. The corn resisted. The villages resisted. In 2014, the Congress of the Republic passed the Ley de Proteccion de Obtenciones Vegetales, popularly known as Ley Monsanto. This law put at risk the future of the corn and, thus, the future of the self-sustainability of the country. It was the indigenous villages that were the most resistant to the law, eventually achieving its repeal.

 

In the film, the artist remains hidden within a cornfield. Four men wield machetes to cut down the corn stalks until she is fully exposed. For a few minutes, she stands among the fallen corn stalks.

 

The work was created in Chotacaj Village, Totonicapán, Guatemala, in November 2014.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: B. 1974, Guatemala City. In her practice, Regina José Galindo situates her own body in a public dimension to speak of the violence and sadism of political events and personal disgrace. She was invited by Harald Szeemann to the 49th Venice Biennale, and awarded the Golden Lion for best under-35 artist in the 51st Venice Biennale. Galindo has participated in innumerable shows across the world, in the Istanbul, Prague and Tirane biennales, and in major international institutions in London, New York and Paris.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: The artists assemble tools from workers and farmers in Longshui into a cellular form, suggestive of growth and multiplication. The genius of Longshui’s cottage industry of tool making, and its form of life, stand in uneasy confrontation with the industrial production of tools over the last two decades. The work draws its name from a Chinese proverb, “You can take enough pains to grind an iron rod into a needle”, which metaphorically links labour, perfection and liberation.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: Estd. 2011, Chongqing. Cell Art Group was founded by Than Young (b. 1980) and Dong Xun (b. 1984) to engage in cultural study and artistic production. The group draws its inspiration from cells - how they reproduce, infect, mutate and regenerate - and sees this as an analogy for the relationship between artists and the society.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: The circular-shaped lamp can be expanded or collapsible thanks to photo reflector structure. The light emits from LED strip, which is located inside the edge of the spring steel flame towards the centre of the circle. As a result, the extended surface of the complete circle illuminates itself like a full moon. Colour of the light can be changed by the full colour LED to obtain different hues and ambiances.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
Kazuhiro Yamanaka graduated in Interior Design at Musashino Art University, Tokyo (1992-95 BA (Des.)) followed by Royal College of Art in London for Postgraduate studies (1995-97 MA (Des.) RCA). He set up Kazuhiro Yamanaka Office in London after his graduation. He participates in different aspects of design: from furniture design to lighting design, and lighting installation.


Kazuhiro Yamanaka was awarded Design Report Award 2004 (Milan) as the best young talented designer at the Milano Salone, making him the first Japanese designer to win this award. His creation belongs to a collection of MoMA (New York). Since 2004, he has been judging international design competitions and giving lectures and presentations to students and companies, and since 2011, he has expanded his activities to include the interior design of commercial spaces. He was appointed as an associate professor at Musashino Art University in Tokyo since 2014.

blocks.body: Small, open box with big eaves on a steep slope. Floor is articulated in response to the sloped site, forming the spatial composition. Connected stacked skip floors and gentle stairs create a soft space. The interior space is expanded by the big eaves and connected with the exterior space. blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: Kazunari Sakamoto graduated from the Department of Architecture at Tokyo Institute of Technology in 1966. In 1971, he became a full-time lecturer at Musashino Art University after completing his doctoral program at Tokyo Institute of Technology. In 1977, he served as an associate professor at Musashino Art University, an associate professor at Tokyo Institute of Technology in 1983, a professor at Tokyo Institute of Technology in 1991, and a professor emeritus at Tokyo Institute of Technology in 2008. In 1990, he won the Architectural Institute of Japan Award for House F, and in 1991, his work Common City Hoshida won Togo Murano Memorial Prize Award.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: “Cockroaching - Beetle Works”, is a kinetic visual experiment in which Nikl Petr brings together robotic insects, vibrating toothbrushes and other objects to help create impromptu large-format drawings. The genesis of each drawing has the nature of a game or performance in which the artist spontaneously intervenes in the chaotic movement of the endlessly gyrating mechanical objects.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: Nikl Petr remain active on the stage since the 1980s. He is not only an artist, but also an actor, singer, puppeteer, writer, publisher and performer. In the early 1990s he was a member of the artistic group Tvrdohlaví, and founder of the puppet troupe Medehaha. In 1995, he was awarded the Jindřich Chalupecký. In 2000, he undertook the curator of exhibition Nests of Games at the Galerie Rudolfinum, Prague. In 2005, Pieter Nickel represented the Czech Republic at Expo 2005 Aichi Japan. His mother is Libuše Niklová, the Czech queen of plastic toys.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
1. I designed the Map of Reactivation as a conceptual map specifically for the Shanghai Biennale. I hope that the map is able to convey certain messages to the co-curators, the participating artists as well as members of the audience, and to elicit discussions about certain

issues. Based on the feedback from everyone, we need to repeatedly redraw this map. After all, an accurate map is made possible only by the incremental experience of generations of travelers over time. The foundation of my work as a curator is the production of a series of

maps and their accompanying notes.

 

2. The entire map is based on the system renovation of a thermal power station. Situated in the top right are the parts about ‘resources’. Here there are three fuel feed inlets, through which natural resources, spiritual resources and community resources enter. Natural resources enter the stomach. Spiritual resources enter the nervous system. Community resources enter the lungs. After preliminary transformations, they enter the Reform Boiler. The bottom ash after combustion becomes the so-called art works with material form before going through the precipitator. Some of them enter the museum and exert an impact on daily life. Others return to society at large via the flue gas stack and become reintegrated into the resources, thereby completing a mini-cycle of resources.

 

The upper section of the Reform Boiler consists of pipes. Water coming from the stream of ‘everyday life’, which is the equivalent to the audience’, turns into steam after entering the Boiler. This is the process of artistic experience. Then it enters the turbine engine, which is the generator on the right hand side of the picture.

 

Water / Audience enters a series of lakes of Revisit. These are processes of reflections, revisits and activation of everyday life, and eventually return to the streams of everyday life, thereby completing a water cycle.

 

The energy generated by the generator is the renewal of social consciousness, which first enters the transformer before getting connected to the transmission network. Some part of the power generated centers the community and is immediately transformed into new energies.

The rest is transmitted to the city at top right of the picture. The city itself is also exporting energy. On top of the picture, the lightening tesla coils provide a wireless means of transmitting power, connecting city, brain and community resources while renewing the spiritual resources. Therefore a cycle of energy transmission is complete.

 

3. All forms of natural energy are but variations of solar energy. The gravity of the sun pulls the earth into an orbit, hence we have wind power. The moon is indirectly responsible for tidal power. Changes in climate give rise to water circulation, which makes possible hydropower. The top left corner of the picture shows the so-called green energies. To the right of the mountain range in the middle, solar energy is transformed into plant energy through photosynthesis. The latter either combusts or turns into coal over eons of years of geologic change, or into the food of animals, before transforming itself into petroleum and natural gas over eons of years of geologic change. This is what we term as black fossil fuel.

 

Crude means of extracting energy in pre-modern times were subject to geographical, climactic and energy limitations. Since modern times, man has turned to the faraway areas for energy. Man has ceaselessly been exploring, enclosing, excavating, distributing and expending energy further away and deeper. At present these remain the most mainstream method of extracting energy and have caused numerous wars on energy. Search for new energy, although superimposed by an environmentalist narrative, is not exempt from the unequal distribution of resources. What is crucial is the fact that man sticks to the path of looking for energies outside of himself, in deeper geologic strata and further ocean beds, and even in outer space that is further away, and integrating them into the orbit controlled by capital.

 

Part of these energies are poured into the funnel marked ‘natural resources’, the rest channeled into the lake of ‘energy war’ (left to the resources funnel). In the end, they have to be channeled into the smog of energy recycling, where there is another apparatus resembling a coal transmitter. The reclamation of endmost wastes.

 

4. Right to the Isle of Natural Resources lies the Isle of Spiritual Resources, i.e., inner energies. Way ahead of an energy shortage, the Far East has already seen the earliest development of an energy extraction method characterized by introspection. The Oriental sages looked for the potential energies within, in contemplative approaches such as qigong and yoga. In contrast to ‘natural resources’, here we are more concerned with ‘capacity’. Just as every natural resource comes from the sun, every spiritual resource has its root in education. The mountain range in the middle separates the wise from the foolish, dividing what the Buddha terms as ‘top’ and ‘low’ quality seeds. Left of the mountain range are fools like me, who can develop a ‘consistent ability’ by way of education, enlightenment, attention, study, belief, following, motivation and concentration, finally reaching the phase of ‘intelligence’ (or wisdom).

 

On the right hand side of the mountain range, the wise can swiftly reach understanding and intelligence and gain insight by way of platonic memory. With the inner approaches to energy, such as qigong and yoga, this is further transformed into passion. Two paths then converge, and with the help of the power of interest, can be transformed into the power of the will and of the imagination. Learning to wait for and seize opportunities as they come, they finally transform themselves at the lower section of the island into creativity and effective action.

 

5. Further to the right, an island lies almost horizontally due to its attachment to the power grid. It is in fact a peninsula. The local map is almost an exercise in philological research, which is intended to elicit discussions on community relationships.

 

The philological exercise starts with two nodes. On the right we see two traditional Chinese characters, 開kai, and 關guan. Guan is both a ‘Gate’, and a ‘Closure’. When justaposed, kaiguan means ‘switch’, which, when activated, will generate power that leads to ‘the Centre’, and connects to the city on top right.

 

At the foot of the Tesla Tower, artificial lightning creates the hieroglyphic 系xi in the seal script which depicts a handful of silk threads. From there four roads have emerged, one of which is marked 繫xi, which means the state in which everybody is bound together by given relationships and becomes a prisoner deprived of any possibility of exchange with the external world, just like a basin encircled by mountain ranges. Given relationships imprison man in his identity. Yet, identity can also become a choice suggesting voluntary moral responsibilities.

 

We are then brought back to the character 系xi in the seal script. Another road leads us to 係xi with a radical signifying ‘man’. This character means ‘relationship’. Turning left from the middle, it leads to intersubjectivity and awareness of the energy of distance and difference. Man starts with dialogue, which may make sense, or lead to the cul-de-sac of misunderstanding. Therefore, the more effective approach is to ‘travel together’ and ‘work together’, so that people become fellow cooperators.

 

The stray path under 係xi highlights the significance of ‘genealogy’, which includes the relationship between different clans and generations. It winds its way leftward along the foot of the mountain range and evokes the relationships of relay and inheritance, where schools and traditions start to appear. Tradition forms the basis of ‘prior understanding’. Lastly, it converges with the path of ‘fellow cooperators’ at the point of ‘affinity’, where they enter the funnel of ‘community resources’. Here we try to emphasize the collective responsibility crystalized in the narrative. We must mention yet again other sources of energy, i.e., to seek energy in community relations, just as we rely not only on the fireplace but also on each other for warmth in winters of our childhood. Energy is by no means a treasure trove waiting to be discovered, but rather something that originates from a communal awareness. Symbiosis is a kind of energy.

 

6. Let’s return to the character 系xi in the seal script. From here rightwards there extend two paths. The one on top right accentuates the value of silk threads as a ‘link’ connecting ‘the Other’, especially its sensitivity the faraway ‘Other’. Such sensitivity is called 仁ren, humanity, otherwise it’d be insensitive inhumanity. For this reason, those who are 仁ren, i.e., humane, must accommodate the ‘Other’. Here the concern, or ‘closure of hearts’, as suggested by the Chinese word 關心guanxin, converges with the path of initiative, and gets connected to the ‘possibility of the stranger’. ‘The Other’ is a treasure trove.

 

Here, community awareness gives rise to an outward-looking responsibility and concern. ‘Treat with the reverence due to age the elders in your own family, so that the elders in the families of others shall be similarly treated’. (from Mencius, James Legge’s translation)

 

The road extending downward and rightward from the character 系xi highlights the role of silk threads as ‘intertexture’ while implying ‘texture’, ‘text’, ‘organization’. After its crossing with ‘initiative’ and ‘concern’, it leads to ‘social mobilization’ that is connected to the city.

 

The various individuals carrying different identities, memories and sensitivities have decided here to form a community, and share the responsibility of maintaining the historical programme that we call ‘society’. Such a will is the most important force upon which the city relies for its existence. The differences between the ‘Other’ and ourselves become the fountainhead of our energy. The assumption that once formed society won’t need any more work is completely unfounded. It needs continuous maintenance. Therefore protecting the Other and defending our society constitute the real solution to sustainable development.

 

7. Material resources, spiritual resources and community resources enter three funnel-shaped feeder bin and experience a series of changes before entering the ‘Reform Boiler’.

 

Under the leftmost funnel, the material resources have to go through an esophagus-shaped pipe before entering the stomach, where they will complete the process of mixing with other resources and getting digested and absorbed. In the meantime, the liver provides the processing from ‘reflection’ through ‘familiarization’, ‘instinctualization’, till ‘concentration’ through the gallbladder – does it not apply to everything in our hands?

 

On the right, the pancreas produces catalyst and impulse to change the status qua as well as dreams. After pulverization, the blowers will increase the air pressure and inject them into the boiler.

 

Under the funnel in the middle, spiritual resources reach the esophagus after learning and analysis, thus becoming the new understanding of the materials, some of which head for review while the rest lead to judgment, decision and control. As the nervous system, it furnishes the wall of the ‘Reform Boiler’ with a cooling mechanism.

 

Under the funnel on the right, community air, after being filtered and renewed in the lung structures, is divided into two parts. One is channeled into the esophagus and becomes part of the mix there. The other part becomes social consciousness that evokes a sense of responsibility and impulses and is directly channeled into the ‘Reform Boiler’ as the air needed for the combustion. This part highlights the capacity and effort on the part of art as transformer.

 

8. In the lower half of the ‘Reform Boiler’, material remnants after combustion are released downwards, and become physical ‘works of art’ after ‘plastics’, ‘rehash’ and ‘remodeling’. In the meantime, there are some material remnants in the steam. They travel down through the giant pipe ‘the atmosphere of art’, before turning left and going through a series of upside down precipitators: part of art criticism, art market and art patronage is then channeled into the pipes marked ‘art history writing’ and ‘art collection’ and eventually reaches the museum on the farthest left. The other part enters a fashion blower, and rises up through biosafety disposal in order to recycle the resources.

 

Physical art works are gathered in art collections which form the core of the contemporary art museum. A series of radiating pipes give off energy, including curating, publishing, education, exhibition, social mobilization and the biennale…their impact creates waves in the river of everyday life.

 

9. The upper half of the ‘Reform Boiler’ mainly describes ‘artistic experience’, i.e., how the audience has changed during its encounter with the art work. Initially, when the audience first enters the boiler, it remains calm. As it is heated up – the thermal energy of the fuel has been transferred onto it. During this process they experience anxiety, wonder, surprise of discovery, awakening and a sense of liberation, certainty, and freedom, and produce several specific psychological effects: stimulating physical vigor, dispelling of prejudices, moral vigor and emotional vigor, etc.

 

10. After leaving the boiler, the audience who has just undergone an artistic experience gets excited, sensitive, active, critical and imaginative. They drive the turbines, which then drive the generator to generate electricity. The generator produces ‘ideological renewal’, ‘social creativity’ and ‘spiritual renewal’ and pumps them upwards into the transformer….while ‘the steam of the art audience’ itself is condensed and channeled downwards back into the river of everyday life.

 

The generator is here deployed as a metaphor: Artists are here defined as social mobilizers, who not only consume resources in the production of objects, but also transform their work into power generation, and produces energy for the network they find themselves in. They establish their own communities and discuss the sharing, transformation, adaptation, resonances and amplification. Their activities trigger the intrinsic vigor of the social milieu. They work in fields, streets and communities, interweaving their individual creative work with the reconfiguration of social energies. And for this reason they are ready to break free of existing artistic concepts and institutions at any moment. Such art work, shot through with a holistic artistic inclination, runs through individual and collectivity, other and self, labour and creativity, the everyday and the miraculous, which are precisely the core of our concerns.

 

11. Where does the ‘cold water / audience’ come from? They come primarily from the ‘River of Everyday Life’ at the bottom of the picture. Before reaching the exhibition hall they have to cross the mountain ranges of ‘Ideological Control’ and ‘Conventional Bourgeois Life’, as well as overcoming ‘economic control’ and ‘cultural preconceptions’. After a few warm-ups in art knowledge, they are pumped into the upper half of the boiler like cold water. Here the visitor is a crucial participator of the artistic experience, since art has not happened until the entrée of the visitor.

 

12. Another set of cooling and condenser system helps to cool down those people from the excitement of the artistic experience. These are the laymen who have gained immediate artistic experience without having to enter the ‘Reform Boiler’. They pass the condenser and get into contact with people who have just obtained their artistic experience, which makes them realize that they have to return to everyday life. Yet their temperature will rise through the contact. Therefore this condensed water itself forms a mini-circulation. They enter the cooling tower of ‘art mythology’ and ‘social evolutionism’ at the down right of the picture. After condensation, some of them return to the River of Everyday Life as an art participator in waiting, and others return to the condenser and function as condensed water.

 

13. The cooled down recipients of art experience have to surmount the ‘Dam of Reason’ before reaching the ‘Deposition Pool’ and Lakes of Revival, where they reflect comprehensively on their daily life. Here, the intertwined lakes are: renovation of industrial heritage site (we can see 798, M50 and PSA Power Station Art Museum standing by the lake), rural reconstruction, handicraft movement, neighbourhood reactivation, ruin recovery, archive review, story retelling and rehearsal, community re-identification, gathering collected memory, identity reform, refreshing individuality, rehabilitation and redesign, re-evaluation, refining and reuse of objects. After life-long learning, they eventually reach the drainage system of daily rebirth and get injected into the River of Everyday Life at the leftmost part of the Lake District. Thus a cycle of participants of art is complete. Here we are concerned with how art becomes the reviewer and rewriter of history.

 

14. Let us return to the power generator at the centre-right of the picture. As spiritual power is generated by the turbine, it enters the transformer and sets off a process of connecting to the grid. This area discusses networked technologies, i.e., community technologies including the maintenance of communication channels, shunting, recoding, recalculating, regularization and refection. They have been redesigned and redistributed by the small high voltage line tower and transported through power lines to the city on the top right, getting connected to the city’s portal of ‘becoming a citizen’. Here, as a ‘community technology’, art has become a form of social

contact and organization.

 

15. In addition, the communication technologies of the community also include processes such as listening, anti-trust, resonances. A gate resembling that of an academy stands at the down left corner of this area. The academy is a community of learners, and denotes the ‘Academy of Reciprocal Enlightenment’, the education project of the 9th Shanghai Biennale, a garden where people pass through ceaselessly and engage in a sort of intellectual cross-pollination. Such an academy is of course connected to the corridor of 系xi of the community as a resource.

 

16. The top right part of the picture is obviously a city map, which corresponds to the city pavilion of the 9th Shanghai Biennale. Here you can find reflections on urban functions: the city as academia and forums, as shelter, as an ark (alluding to the special exhibition Shanghai Ark), as a stage, as a museum, etc., and of course, as a power station itself. Just as any other renovation project of industrial heritage sites, the repositioning and redevelopment of the architectural functions of the thermal power station involve not only waste recycling, but also reflections on the entire city’s ecology and redesigns. The city, a collective lifestyle engendered by man’s need to rely on one another and his wish to communicate and share, is still constantly going through renewals even after centuries of close relations between itself and the industrial age.

 

All forms of energy: velocity, multiculturalism, depth, opportunity, information exchange, and parks (alluding to the Zhongshan Park project of the 9th Shanghai Biennale), the energy of intensity (I am reminded of us huddling together for warmth when we were young) , of getting lost, of complexity, etc.

 

Such a city is also productive. It produces information, talents, capital, product, opportunity, dream and experience, etc, and spreads them to the ‘suburban areas’ of a city map. Eventually it is completely connected to the wi reless way of transmitting energy envisaged by Tesla Coil.

 

Therefore, ‘reactivation’ does not mean simply moving the power station to places further away from the city, nor does it just intends to introduce new forms of energy to generate power. Rather it provides an opportunity for us to reflect comprehensively on our lifestyles. The moment the old power station comes into use again, it injects into our social networks something of a spiritual pulse that activates the inner energy of the community rather than conventional electricity.

 

 Here I am playing with language: By man’s energy we mean ‘capacity’, and if we dissect this word then we get CAPA-city. So what is CAPA short for?

 

17. My great guide Professor Sarat Maharaj once shared with me a detail in Duchamp’s life: Duchamp never used whole notebooks. He took all his notes on paper slips deposited in a box. Over the years the box would be filled with all sorts of slips. Then, when Duchamp wanted to revisit his diaries, the ones he retrieved at random often proved to be something whose time and place of composition remained unknown. It was a painstaking job and therefore a mechanism were adopted to ensure his thinking and logic were constantly sectioned and he constantly interrupted his own thought. Such is also the composition method of writing ‘Dadaist poetry’.

 

Duchamp was a brave man, so much so that he used this to kill his thinking conventions. Of course this refers to self-discipline and belongs to ‘Total Art’.

 

18. When I drew this sketch, many of the thoughts above were not clear enough. I started to contemplate on this while I was on the beach. Actually many relations would not crystalize until you open the map on your desktop. Besides you can also shift back and forth to see how best you can maneuver these relations. Therefore, a figure elicits a string of words. There are so many erasures and blots that the papers are destroyed. These are real explorations, and painting remains a spatial thinking tool.

 

The act of drawing a conceptual map is not unlike children playing with blocks: Frist drop the items in front of you and play with them, then the relations between certain items start to appear. Certain relations exist in strict couplings; others can be random while some seem to have ulterior motives. Certain relations a highly logical with clear causes and effects. For example, the direction of the mountain range decides the direction of the river, whose upstream definitely has an impact on downstream. For some other things, there is no causal logic and only the status quo which you are forced to accept.

 

19. Cartography stands in between logic and non-logic. ‘What I find mysterious about this is that the way the world is, but the fact that it is like this.’ Maps are not intended for the production of understanding, but for the production of knowledge, by which I mean a good sense of bearing and knowing where to go and how to get there.

 

Such knowledge does not present in the form of a map an era that is no longer malleable. Rather it creates action. Therefore you are more acutely aware of a sense of responsibility. Sometimes hesitation blocks progress and becomes the worst hurdle at work. Painting like this is more like an adventure in a not-so-clearly signposted wilderness. The map is also a script for action.

 

I believe that man’s first drawing of must have been a world map: A primitive goes on hunting, and his kin drew him a picture: there is a rabbit nest under the tree by the riverside. This stone can provide safe shelter, but you have to be careful that this is the trap I dug. Today, we think that describing things is itself an event. In fact, at the beginning we were promoted to describe things by a desire to excel.

 

A map helps you to find the way out, just like curating, or art itself.

 

20. How large an area the map can cover remains a question. The real world is a continuum, and therefore there is a felt need to expand the picture frame even further. Therefore the connection between the items within the picture and a cut frame is worth extra notice. Of course maps can be even more detailed, until in the end it becomes a super-photographic realist painting that casts its eyes down. But even in that case the map remains a sign. Each figure ‘annotates’ an object’s existence. It resorts to the protocol of conceptual systems, rather than optical illusions.

 

21. I believe that without looking at the text, a reader may see these words drifting in the picture as singular isles. There are bigger empty spaces in the picture as well as invisible scripts. They live on the paper as well as in your brains. I look forward to seeing them.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
1969, born in Zhangzhou, China. Now residing in Beijing and Hangzhou.


Qiu Zhijie, artist and curator, graduated from the Zhejiang Academy of Fine Arts in 1992. He is the vice president of China Central Academy of Fine Arts and a professor at the School of Intermedia Art of China Academy of Art.

 

Qiu's artworks take a variety of forms such as calligraphy, painting, photography, video, installation and theater and have been shown a large number of art museums across the world. His works are collected by individual and institutional collectors home and abroad. His solo exhibitions are held in art museums such as Haus of World Culture in Berlin 2009, Ullens Contemporary Art Center in Beijing in 2009 and Zendai Museum of Modern Art in Shanghai in 2008. He participated in exhibitions such as the 53rd Venice Biennale, 25th Sao Paulo Biennale and "New Art in China, Post-1989".

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Shanghai Visions Dreams Possibilities was a new commission work for the 9th Shanghai Biennale, which was created and unveiled at Zhuqiao, Shanghai. Stricker used the polyfoam as the material, producing a prototype formed during negative molding. This negative molding process encapsulates the his intention: demonstrate a strong, weather-resistant material, such as the potential of concrete in casting.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b.1962 St.Gallen; works and lives in Düsseldorf


Thomas Stricker graduated from the Düsseldorf Art Academy and had spent working stays in Australia, Mexico, Africa, and China. Stricker explores the dynamics of public space and landscape, transcending conventional sculpture norms. His projects reveal intricate connections between individuals, nature, and technology, emphasizing social and ecological considerations. Stricker frequently engages in open participatory processes for his socially and ecologically oriented projects.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Standing on the 5F terrace of the Power Station of Art, this installation titled "On Becoming the Wind" is a self-balancing wing with damping. It can feel the wind of the Huangpu River while restraining itself. It constantly self-adjust to seek a balance between external forces and self-preservation, to achieve the graceful pose of opening its arms to embrace everything.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1951, Hyogo, Japan; lives and works in Kameoka City, Japan


Kozo Nishino graduated from the Sculpture Course, Kyoto City Museum of Art in 1977. In 1978-79 he traveled around many ruins in regions throughout Europe, North Africa, the Middle East, and Asia. After returning to Japan, he resumed creating sculptures. Kozo Nishino's artistic production revolves around natural phenomena such as the sky and the wind. The structural beauty of the titanium and steel of his sculptures reveals the expansiveness of time and space. Through intricate handiwork of his floating rings, horizontal bridges, ethereal wings, and the numerous large-scale public works. Highly acclaimed both in Japan and internationally, Nishino's delicate yet dynamic figurative expression originates from his deep yearning and reverence for the sky and space.

 

In 2013, Kozo Nishino installed Sky Memory, a 30-meter-diameter sculpture that seems to float 7 meters above the ground in the lobby of 4 World Trade Center, which faces the 9/11 Memorial Park in New York City. Nishino has continued to work on various projects that impart a shared sense of the preciousness and warmth of humanity living nestled in the unfathomable expanse that embraces us all. Major public museum collections include Museum of Modern Art, Saitama; and Koriyama City Museum of Art, Fukushima, Japan.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: The seemingly abstract painting is actually a reproduction of the chat history on the phone screen, with the left and right sides representing the gray and blue/green chat bubbles. The artist believes that such a structure is very interesting, like a fixed zone in which one can play freely, but cannot change the rule. It preserves the order of painting, but at the same time completely destroys, or ignores the order of painting.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
1977 Born in Shanghai, China. Currently lives and works in Shanghai.


Xu Zhen’s practice covers various media such as installations, video, painting and performance, etc. His works displayed in the 49th Venice Biennale in 2001, and won the prize for ‘Best Artist’ at the china Contemporary Art Award in 2004. Aside from being an artist, Xu Zhen is also a curator. He-curated together with other artists major exhibitions in Shanghai and was one of the initiators of Art-Ba-Ba in 2006. In 2009, Xu Zhen established “MadeIn Company”, a contemporary art creation corporate, focused on the production of creativity, and devoted to the research of contemporary culture’s infinite possibilities. In2013, MadeIn Company launched XUZHEN® which is committed to art creation and cutting-edge culture development. In 2014, MadeIn Companyestablished MadeIn Gallery and in November 2016 launched the first “Xu Zhen Store” in Shanghai.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: In “Shouting”, a moving crowd faces away from the camera until, startled by screams behind them, they spin around (a reaction that elicits laughs from whomever is behind the camera).

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
Irregular structures not only allow for improvisation, but also allow everyone to improve the structure itself. You can't easily draw plans and sections of irregular structures, you have to improvise on the site to design their shapes. Of course, models can help you realize the potential of a structure, and they are very easy to make, but you cannot easily turn a model into a whole building.


-- Yona Friedman


The last link in the macroscopic to microscopic "city-building-structure" chain is Yuna's most varied and fundamental creation - the irregular structure. Just as matter is composed of molecules and molecules are composed of atoms, the discovery and study of atoms become the basis for human to understand the properties of matter. After developing the concept of mobile buildings and cities in the air, Yuna's later work focused on inventing and experimenting with different forms of irregular structures.


Yuna distinguishes between the subtly related concepts of "irregular", "arbitrary", and "uncertain" as follows: A pattern is considered "irregular" when its constituent elements are deployed in a manner that cannot be conventionally defined; When there is no obvious combination of components, it is considered "arbitrary"; The internal structure of an "uncertain" pattern or system is not only shown as "disordered", but also its constituent elements have no combination law. In Yuna's building system, the details of the building object are uncertain, even if they can be defined with statistical approximation, as thermodynamics and chaos theory presupposed, although the details are unstable, the whole will lead to equilibrium.


Mobile buildings can be composed of a single irregular structure or a mixture of different types of irregular structures, such as partition chain structure, protein chain structure, container structure, Mobius structure...

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
1923 Born in Budapest, Hungary

Currently lives and works in Paris, France

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
Instead of the variability of architecture noumenon, Friedman's central theory, "Mobile Architecture", is to explore how to develop a framework of architecture that could respond to or contend with the varied social system.The theory echoes with the inhabitants' self-consciousness and free-expression of their spatial needs, highlighting that the existence of a city is to meet human's aspiration for changes. Hence, Yona is above all against the so-called privilege of an architect. To him, the architect is rather a technology provider and popularizer, a problem solver, sometimes a problem performer as well.Friedman describes his unrealized projects as a parabola. His autonomy world ensconced between art and legend indicates a brand new way of life in civil society.


The "Shanghai Bridge Town Project" can be seen in Yuna's future urban planning for Shanghai. In 2002, while visiting Shanghai, Yuna discovered that the water of the Huangpu River blocked pedestrians and the entire city. Thus, he proposed a "bridge town" design: a livable bridge that not only expands the urban living space, but also eliminates "barriers" and "barriers".

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Ryan Francesca Rogus will carry out a two-month "Work in progress Beijing Live Creation Project" in Beijing in mid-July 2012. During the two-month live creation period, Ryan will express his observations and feelings in China through his artworks, and also experiment with Chinese painting materials and elements.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
A contemporary Cuban artist, born in 1960 in Holguin, Cuba, currently lives and works in Havana and Madrid. From 1977 to 1982, he attended the National Art School in Havana, Cuba, and in 2001, he received an honorary Master of Fine Arts degree from the California State University, San Bernardino. His work aims to break free from traditional exhibition frameworks, combining teaching and life through conceptual art. He firmly believes that art is a tool for changing society and life, and he seeks to find community practices and educational programs for intervention.


In 2010, he was awarded the National Visual Arts Prize by the Cuban Ministry of Culture.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Cao Kai unfolds his historical thinking in an innovative form with digital technology. In 2005, to create this set of works, he cooperated with his technical team to re-create the structure of the Nanjing Yangtze Bridge. The high-definition and photorealistic image quality and the visual effects provide the image of the bridge with a sense of strangeness. As one of the generations who was born and grew together with the Nanjing Yangtze Bridge, he has always paid attention to the bridge and its multimedia representation. After thirty years, time has corroded the bridge with rust and its symbolic meaning has gradually faded, but the sense of humanism history is still intense.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: Born in Changzhou, Jiangsu in 1969, and currently residing and working in Nanjing, this individual is the founder of the CIFF China Independent Image Annual Exhibition. They graduated from Nanjing Art Institute in 1992 and worked in the film and television media industry for several years. In the year 2000, they established the "Purge Studio" in Nanjing, engaging in various aspects of work, including the creation, criticism, historical research, curation, and education of experimental film and video art. Their work also extends to a wide range of areas such as documentaries, new media art, and digital art.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: The artist continuously created the "Some Days" series since 1999 to discuss the relationship between personal memory and collective memory in history and culture. The artist created an absurd meaning through self-centered photography language in a simple black-and-white tone. The narrative photography scenes originated from his reflection based on real life. The series of work is "related to childhood, related to growth, related to family, related to memory," and the reflection of Chinese cultural memory based on personal growing experience. The work uses different symbolized photography language to share the warm moments in memory with the audience through moving psychological narratives.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: In Mushrooms, the artist trains her lens on the boreal forests of Northeast Asia. Beneath the canopy’s dappled light, the camera follows the transfer of energy and information through the micro-ecosystems on the forest’s floor, presenting the interplay of mushrooms, moss, insects, and soil as a grand dance.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b.1981, Sichuan Province; works and lives in Beijing.


Liu Yujia’s short films weave documentary footage, literature, ethnography, folklore, and travelogue into embodied and affective experiences. Taking the physical landscape of Asia for her subject matter and setting, her lyrical style unsettles the line between straight documentary and narrative storytelling. Meditative and symbolic, Liu’s work often relegates humans to the status of minor characters by focusing on other forms of life.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: The work's extensive use of plastic reflects the artist's sensitivity to plastic materials and industrial waste in the early 1990s, which was inextricably linked to the social context of China's fledgling economic development at the time. The artist takes the physics concept of "entropy" or "energy loss" in artistic creation to seize the uncertain nature of the material and its transforming relationship with nature. The constant interleaving between texture and form of the synthetic material reflects the change in society and the exploration of time.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: Born in Beijing in 1962, he was a key member of the early Chinese conceptual art groups "Touch Art Group" and "New Measurement Group" from 1987 to 1995, participating in the "Magicians of the Earth" exhibition in 1989. His artistic creations are focused on expressing in an extremely pure form, encompassing installation art, painting, works on paper, and photography. He has participated in numerous important art exhibitions both in China and abroad. Throughout his continuous artistic career, Gu Dexin skillfully uses familiar materials from everyday life, exploring the most fundamental phenomena and issues of life and society with a sharp perspective, serious and profound thinking, and the most direct language. In 2004, he received the "Outstanding Contribution Award" from the CCAA China Contemporary Art Award.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: " Art is a delicate operation of transposition, an assiduous struggle against the state of things. Be where I do not think I can, disappear from where I think I am, this is what’s important. ." Kimiko Yoshida's works are presented in the form of selfies, but one will find it difficult to recognize her original appearance from these images. Creating this series as a "bride," she used her inner examination, transcended folklore and territories to distill the ancient customs and mythologies in the same human face. At this moment, she breaks the limit of time and space and becomes everybody.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: This Japanese-French artist was born in 1963 in Tokyo, Japan. She has an extensive educational background, studying in the Literature Department of Chuo University in Japan and the Tokyo Institute of Photography. She furthered her studies in photography at the National School of Photography in Arles, France, and at the Fresnoy National Studio of Contemporary Arts. Koji Yoshida is renowned for her self-portrait works, which have gained her significant recognition. Her unique artistic language earned her the New York International Photography Award in 2005. Yoshida's art blends Baroque spatial saturation with Zen minimalism, and her distinctive style is characterized by monochromatic foundations.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: From Haikou, Shenzhen, and Guangzhou, to Shanghai, Beijing, and Chongqing, Weng Fen's photography records China's urbanization and modernization after the Reform and Opening-up as well as the mixture of dreams, desires, and impulses within it. They consist of two key elements: one is the remote landscape of cities, and the other is the girl images. The wall between them is like a boundary marker, separating from yet connecting the real world and presenting a complicated contemporary metaphor. As the artist states, "These young girls are our mirror. The remote cities are the byproduct of modernization dreams. In humans' eyes, they represent civilization and advance."

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1961, Hainan Island,; lives and works in Guangzhou

 

Weng Fen graduated from the oil painting major of Guangzhou Academy of Fine Arts and is currently teaching in Guangzhou Academy of Fine Arts. His artistic practice covers photography, video, social action, installation and other medias.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: From Haikou, Shenzhen, and Guangzhou, to Shanghai, Beijing, and Chongqing, Weng Fen's photography records China's urbanization and modernization after the Reform and Opening-up as well as the mixture of dreams, desires, and impulses within it. They consist of two key elements: one is the remote landscape of cities, and the other is the girl images. The wall between them is like a boundary marker, separating from yet connecting the real world and presenting a complicated contemporary metaphor. As the artist states, "These young girls are our mirror. The remote cities are the byproduct of modernization dreams. In humans' eyes, they represent civilization and advance."

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Ma Liuming studied oil painting in a formal education system, has never stopped his painting creation, and his paintings are an extension of the "alienation" quality in his performance art. The "Baby" series clarifies that he has wondered freely between baby bodies with "Fen-Ma Liuming" faces rather than merely living in the male body It seems that those baby bodies, different from those in our daily lives, are only placed on the enclosed pictures with pure-colored backgrounds.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: Born in 1969 in Huangshi, Hubei, this artist studied at the Hubei Academy of Fine Arts in the Department of Oil Painting from 1987 to 1991. In 1993, he settled in Beijing and, along with other artists, established the Beijing East Village. He began experimenting with performance art in 1988, creating works under the name "Fen Ma Liuming." The artist has performed in various countries, including France, Germany, the United States, and Japan, and has participated in significant exhibitions and held solo shows. His notable participations include the 48th Venice Biennale, the Gwangju Biennale 2000, the 7th Istanbul Biennial, and the 1st Guangzhou Biennale in 1992.

title: Fen · Ma Liuming Walks the Great Wall

raw.title: Fen · Ma Liuming Walks the Great Wall

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: As a member of the avant-garde artist group "Beijing East Village" in the early 1990s, Ma Liuming always conducted performances in the identity of "Fen·Ma Liuming." In this work, the Great Wall's symbolic strength is juxtaposed with the ambiguity of the artist's body: the wall divides and restricts vision borders, and the body blurs and confuses such differences.
