blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: In the artist's theoretical book Tractatus Post Historicus, he defined "post history" as "a period when different values and models coexist, when we observe anything from multiple perspectives, a real space without certainty." Triptychos Post Historicus started in 1976, in which artworks, found objects, and fruits are used as the elements in a comprehensive symbol system to express his understanding of artistic form and philosophy - "They freely move within their respective gravitational spheres. Each element has its own galaxy, and they meet in time in the post-historical era to form a triptych and then continue in their respective directions."

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: Born in 1948 in Sarajevo, Bosnia, this conceptual artist currently lives and works in Paris. He studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Zagreb and at Saint Martin's School of Art in London. Initially, he gained recognition for a series of photographic works that began in the early 1970s. His installation works combine well-known masterpieces with furniture, fruits and vegetables, and other everyday items, breaking traditional boundaries between high art and daily crafts. His artworks have been collected by prestigious institutions including the Tate Gallery, the Museum of Modern Art in New York, and the Pompidou Center.

title: Face Painting - Plum, Orchid, Bamboo, Chrysanthemum

raw.title: Face Painting - Plum, Orchid, Bamboo, Chrysanthemum

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Huang Yan's creation is rooted in traditional Chinese literati paintings. The artist puts writing brushes, ink sticks, paper, and ink-stones into a contemporary transformation and appropriates the landscape patterns on canvas, photography, and even human bodies. After landscape creations and literati figures in multiple artistic mediums, the artist uses flower and bird paintings at the beginning of the 21st century as his “treatment” to the niduses of human civilization histories in the East and the West.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: 出生于1966年的艺术家，原籍吉林，目前居住和工作在北京。1978年，他开始学习中国传统山水画。1987年，他从长春师范学院毕业。自1994年起，他开始使用油画和摄影来记录自己的观念和行为。他的创作形式多样，常在摄影中融入传统绘画和行为艺术元素，在绘画中加入当代元素。自1997年以来，他在北京、香港、上海、伦敦、柏林、纽约、巴黎、阿姆斯特丹和米兰等地举办个展。他的作品在全球范围内广泛展出，并被包括国家大剧院、维多利亚·阿尔伯特博物馆、纽约摄影艺术中心等多家机构收藏。

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: From 1995 to 2009, Lin Yongbin created the "Face" series comprised of seventeen video works. None of these videos were edited; each of them took an external condition as reference, and the subjects as well as their movements allowed minimum limit. This series is thought-provoking, leading the audience to reflect the essence of time and identity.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: Born in Beijing in 1963, now living and working in Tengchong, Yunnan. In his early years, he studied painting with Gu Dexin, Zhu Haidong, Tang Pinggang, and others. Li Yongbin did not receive formal art education at an art college but became a professional artist through self-learning. From 1994 to 2008, he created the "Faces" series, which includes sixteen video works. His video works are never edited, and each piece is based on an external condition that determines its length, with the subject and its actions minimized to the extreme. Using the camera and the brush as tools, he shows his attention to humanity, the world, change, and self.

title: Impressions of the Four Seasons - Summer Water

raw.title: Impressions of the Four Seasons - Summer Water
raw.medium: Acrylic on canvas, photo 120 x 150 cm

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: The artist's creation goes along with the economic transformation and radical changes in urbanization, which is almost synchronized with the development of China's contemporary art. After the fire disaster in the studio in 1991, he found a sort of "trace" in the fire. Using fire and ashes as the media, the artist recombined the fragments of consumer society and construct a new signature dialogue.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: "Born in 1965 in Dangshan, Anhui, Xue Song graduated from the Shanghai Theatre Academy's Department of Stage Art in 1988. He creates his artwork by burning existing images and texts, then redistributing and reassembling them before collaging them onto canvases. This process of destruction and rebirth, deconstruction and construction, establishes a unique creative significance and produces a novel visual effect. Xue Song has held solo exhibitions at the Shanghai Art Museum, Long Museum Shanghai, Shanghai Baoli Art Museum, Xi'an Art Museum, MOCA Singapore, Ueno Mori Art Museum in Japan, and others. His works are collected by institutions such as the National Art Museum of China, Shanghai Art Museum, Long Museum, M+ Museum in Hong Kong, Museum of Fine Arts Boston, Nanyang Technological University Asia Pacific Museum in Singapore, and the Museum of Modern Art in Bonn, Germany."

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: The "Supports/Surfaces" movement, an important avant-garde movement in post-war France, emerged in the late 1960s. Inspired by Matisse's paper-cutting, it took place in the same period as the new abstraction movement of hard-edge painting. Pincemin joined the movement in 1971, and as one of the most groundbreaking artists, his creation is full of powerful, strong, and firm color blocks. The picture mainly consists of horizontal and vertical stripes. Through the methods of cutting, collage, and folding, the artist frees paintings from the traditional, lyrical, and insightful standards.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
The painter and sculptor, born in Paris in 1944 and passed away in Arcueil in 2005, Jean-Pierre Bansard was dedicated to exploring the diversity of painting and artistic creation methods. In his early career, he was part of the "Support-Surfaces" group, an art movement that focused on conceptualism.


From 1974, Bansard began creating large geometric paintings, notably in his "Palisade" and "Entrance" series. These paintings are characterized by their subtle color schemes and horizontal and vertical stripes. In the 1980s, he shifted his focus to creating large-scale sculptures, which were often assembled from recycled materials. These works highlight his interest in both the textural and structural aspects of art, blurring the lines between painting and sculpture. Bansard's contributions to the art world are marked by his innovative approach to materials and form, reflecting a continuous exploration of the boundaries and possibilities within the visual arts.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: The work describes a world more beautiful than Utopia. The human bodies in the picture, as the constitution elements, are set in an uncertain space, where humans pursue peace, joy, and YOLO. Everybody conducts secret and lighthearted conversations here, where you can find women with garlands on their heads, women smoking cigarettes, women bathing, and among others. Surrounded by unusual plants, there are flying swallows and other creatures in between, forming a stark contrast with the modern high buildings in the background. The comedy-style aesthetic expressions are exactly the scene the artist aims to portray.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: The Croatian contemporary artist, born in 1971 in Zagreb, graduated from the Academy of Fine Arts in Zagreb in 1997. Since 2010, he has been teaching painting at the Academy of Fine Arts in Zagreb and currently serves as the president of the Croatian Association of Artists. His works often feature large and complex combinations of figures, adhering to themes of spirituality and everyday life, attempting to portray his belief in a dreamlike and ideal world. He has participated in numerous solo and group exhibitions, including shows in Zagreb, Split, MOMA P.S.1 in New York, Tokyo Wonder Site (TWS), Spinnerei in Leipzig, and other locations. His artistic style often blends realism with elements of fantasy, creating a unique narrative that explores the boundaries between the real and the imagined.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: The artist is committed to enhancing the identity of marginalized cultures and focusing on the living situation of minority groups in Cuban society. His works are built with the natural materials which are pervasive in daily life, such as papers, cardboard, incendiary sticks, rusty metal plates, and so on. The cluster of wooden boxes is assembled unskillfully, scattering around the ground and walls like a mini shanty. Although the material is dull and poor, these boxes are spreading infinitely with everlasting power. He explores the meaning of the medium to express his feelings on poverty, reality, life, and art.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: A contemporary Cuban artist, born in 1971 in Havana, graduated from the National Academy of Fine Arts San Alejandro in Havana. He is a member of the National Union of Writers and Artists of Cuba (UNEAC) and the International Association of Art (IAA) affiliated with UNESCO. Roberto Diago confronts the official Cuban narrative on race in his works, attempting to rewrite history by incorporating themes of slavery and the nation's effort to forget its disgraceful past. This includes references to the garments worn by slaves, using materials like printed fabrics. Diago creates paintings and conceptual installations using ready-made objects. His works have been exhibited in prestigious venues such as the National Museum of Fine Arts of Cuba and the Havana Visual Arts Development Center.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
The artist takes water and ink as the mediums for his creation in furniture design and Gongbi painting, not only to express modern aesthetics of oneness and unity with the normalised and industrialized style characters in design language, but also to return to the literati tradition through the dialogue of ancient ink technique of Gongbi painting. He thinks that contemporary people are obsessed with the innovation of concept, idea, material, and technology, dropping into the mist of the superficial form of art. Any medium and material, no matter old or new, can release its vitality only by injecting the

creator's feelings and spirituality into it. This iron-hard sculpture resists the artificial idea of stiff innovation by its simplest appearance which integrates technique and beauty.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: Shi Jianmin, born in 1962 in Xi'an, graduated from the Xi'an Second Light Industry Technical School in Decorative Arts in 1982 and from the Central Academy of Arts and Crafts (now known as the Academy of Arts & Design, Tsinghua University) in 1986. He currently lives and works in Beijing. Shi Jianmin's works are characterized by their whimsical, ethereal, and romantic qualities, reflecting a cultural longing for the mode of existence in human life. His art also represents an emotional expression formed through the experience of numerous intricate and complex matters. Shi Jianmin’s approach in his creations is often seen as a blend of traditional Chinese artistic elements with modern artistic expressions, showcasing a unique perspective on life and existence.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Through earlier experience of furniture design, the artist saws, forges, welds, polishes, and link the highly-hard stainless steel, forming the symbolic image based on the "chair." Its style is natural and smooth, and even lyrical and rhythmic. Therefore, the works process the qualities of like what stated in the Kao Gong Ji, "the favourable timing, the animistic environment, the graceful material, and the delicate craftwork."

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: In the work, there is a beautiful yet aging woman who hopes to be young forever like the mask in her hand. However, no matter how hard we try, we will finally become old, like what was said in the Heart Sutra, "Form does not differ from emptiness, emptiness does not differ from form. That which is form is emptiness, that which is emptiness is form. The same is true of feelings, perceptions, impulses, consciousness."

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: Born in 1969 in Changchun, Jilin Province, the artist currently lives and works in Beijing and Chongqing. They studied at the Lu Xun Academy of Fine Arts in the Sculpture Department from 1989 to 1994 and are now an associate professor at the Sichuan Fine Arts Institute. The artist's work is filled with respect for humanity and tradition. They are adept at observing and depicting people in everyday life. Their works embody the primal vitality found in the lives of ordinary people and use a unique sculptural language to reveal aspects of Chinese social life in the consumer era.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
As the artist states, "I hope there exists a time like 25:00, which people can become as big as they want and do whatever they like." The artist deconstructs aesthetic habits through photography image, and takes the body as the "chip" of critique with the viewing perspective of getting rid of the self to evoke the most real side of humans in physiology and psychology.

Actually this “Female Giant” has not very much courage, that’s the reason why she can become so large only at the o’clock of 25:00, and make the gesture like that.Much time, the realm of reality and the realm of male come mixed together in my mind. They are all come from outside, and exist strongly, initiative, aggressive. In front of these, I often feel of atony, not know what to do, and weak. However, as long as the last of my life, I could not avoid them even for one day. So, I hope, there is a certain time like 25:00, I could become as large as I like, and act what I will.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: Born in Yiwu in 1975, the artist attended the Central Academy of Fine Arts in China. From 1999 to 2005, they were active in the Chinese avant-garde art scene under their birth name, Chen Lingyang. Chen's work "Twelve Flower Months" is considered a landmark in the integration of feminism into contemporary Chinese art. From 2005 to 2020, Chen Lingyang conducted an experiment: voluntarily leaving the art operation system, shedding their artist identity, and making art a purely personal affair. In 2020, they publicly announced their return to the art world under the name Alice Chen, reclaiming their artist identity and re-entering the art operation system.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: The artist continuously created the "Some Days" series since 1999 to discuss the relationship between personal memory and collective memory in history and culture. The artist created an absurd meaning through self-centered photography language in a simple black-and-white tone. The narrative photography scenes originated from his reflection based on real life. The series of work is "related to childhood, related to growth, related to family, related to memory," and the reflection of Chinese cultural memory based on personal growing experience. The work uses different symbolized photography language to share the warm moments in memory with the audience through moving psychological narratives.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: 1972 Born in Kuandian, Liaoning Province, China. 1995 till now, works in Shenzhen and Guangzhou, China.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: The "Focus" series is jointly completed by artist Lin Tianmiao and Singapore Tyler Print Institute. The artist seizes the essence of imprinting in printmaking and breaks the normal procedure by starting with making paper. She also boldly combines all kinds of plate-making methods together breaking the bounds of different categories such as etching and stencil printing. In the process full of contingency, a series of mono works that cannot be copied is created. The exhibited work takes an enlarged head as the background. Through using silk thread to reconstruct the picture, there forms a subtle dialogue between material and image, and the meanings of both have changed in the process.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: Lin Tianmiao, born in 1961 in Taiyuan, Shanxi, currently lives and works in Beijing. She studied at the Fine Arts Department of Capital Normal University in 1984. In 1988, she moved to the United States and studied at the Art Students League of New York in 1989. She worked in New York for many years as a designer. In 1995, Lin Tianmiao returned to China and exhibited works such as "The Expansion of Entanglement", "The Temptation of Saint Therese", "Pants", and "Tree" in the "Open Studio" art event, establishing her significant position in experimental art. She was also one of the first Chinese female artists to gain international attention and recognition. Her works are permanently collected by prestigious institutions including the Brooklyn Museum in New York, MoMA in New York, the National Gallery of Australia, MoMA in San Francisco, M+ in Hong Kong, the Seattle Museum of Contemporary Art, the Singapore Art Museum, and the Centre Pompidou.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
Drawing on a poem by the thirteenth-century Persian poet Rumi (from which the title is also taken), Somewhere Beyond Right and Wrong, there is a Garden. I Will Meet You There is the account of a healing process and a meditation on human suffering. Combining found footage, documentation from the artist’s own travels, and animations of the mythological centaur Chiron (renowned as a healer and prophet), Somewhere Beyond Right and Wrong... asks how spiritual practice can help us to move beyond individual subjectivity to perceive life and death from a cosmic perspective.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Exo-Ecologies responds to the likelihood that humans will soon become an interplanetary species. Yet the fact that the first extraterrestrial “colony” will almost certainly be planted by a “pioneering” corporate enterprise suggests that we, as a species, have learned little from the consequences of imperialism and extractivism here on earth. Taking the form of an alternative launch site, this monumental installation honors and mourns the many nonhuman life forms who contributed to space to pave the way for humans, beginning with the fruit flies that were, in 1947, the first earthbound species to leave its atmosphere. They were followed by—among other species—monkeys, mice, dogs, soil, seeds, worms, tortoises and frogs, before Yuri Gagarin became the first human to enter space in 1961.Before becoming an interplanetary species, this artwork insists that we reappraise humanity’s responsibilities to the ecosystems in which it participates and recognize the contribution of nonhuman workers on, in, and above the earth. Hence the two central slogans of the work: Intra-planetary Solidarity (repair bonds across human and non-humans on earth), and Exo-Ecologies Unite (encounter other extraterrestrial ecosystems on radical egalitarian terms)

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
born.1981 in Netherlands, works and lives in Rotterdam.


Jonas Staal is a visual artist whose work deals with the relation between art, democracy, and propaganda. He is the founder of the artistic and political organization New World Summit (2012–ongoing). Together with Florian Malzacher he co-directs the training camp Training for the Future (2018-ongoing), with writer and lawyer Radha D’Souza he founded the Court for Intergenerational Climate Crimes (2021-ongoing), and with Laure Prouvost he is co-administrator of the Obscure Union (2019-ongoing).


Exhibition-projects include We Demand a Million More Years (Fondazione Sandretto Re Rebaudengo, Turin, 2022), Extinction Wars (with Radha D'Souza, Gwangju Museum of Art, 2023), Propaganda Station (Museum of Contemporary Art, Zagreb, 2024) and The British East India Company on Trial (with Radha D'Souza, Serpentine Galleries, 2025). His projects have been exhibited widely at venues such as the Cooper Hewitt Smithsonian Design Museum in New York, V&A in London, Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam, M_HKA in Antwerp, Centre Pompidou-Metz and the Nam June Paik Art Center in Seoul, as well as the 7th Berlin Biennale, the 31st São Paulo Biennale, the 12th Taipei Biennale and the 14th Shanghai Biennale.


Publications include Propaganda Art in the 21st Century (The MIT Press, 2019) and Climate Propagandas: Stories of Extinction and Regeneration (The MIT Press, 2024). Staal completed his PhD research on propaganda art at the PhDArts program of Leiden University, the Netherlands.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Silkworms spinning silk on fragments of blue sky reflected on the broken mirrors they sit upon, their endless strands of silk spun in the figure of 8 resembling clouds and stitches that slowly but surely sew them together. As the pieces of mirrors on the floor reflect the film projection onto the walls around it, the silkworms seem to be undertaking the cosmic task of mending and bridging the azure skies that hang above all of humanity.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
1945, born in Shanghai, China. Currently lives and works in Taizhou, Zhejiang Prov, China.


From 1986 to 1989, Liang Shaoji studied soft sculpture from Maryn Varbanov at China Academy of Art who was one of the world's leading tapestries. In the late 1980s, Liang started experimenting with silkworms. For more than thirty years, he has been indulged in the interdisciplinary creation in terms of art and biology, installation and sculpture, new media and textile. His Nature Series sees the life process of silkworms as creation medium, the interaction in natural world as his artistic language, time and life as the essential idea. His works are fulfilled with a sense of meditation, philosophy and poetry while illustrating the inherent beauty of silk.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: If you watch closely, you will find that the trajectory of silkworm spinning is like an "8", which repeats and spreads continuously. This "8" is not only a code for the life weaving of silkworm, it also resembles the symbol of "∞", which symbolizes infinity. The video shows the trajectory of "8" when the silkworm is spinning.

title: Listen to the Silkworms/Nature Series No.96 (PSA Edition)
medium: Voice installation, silkworm, mulberry leaf, etc., size variable

raw.title: Listen to the Silkworms/Nature Series No.96 (PSA Edition)
raw.medium: Voice installation, silkworm, mulberry leaf, etc., size variable

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
I have experienced many sleepless nights over my 20-year silkworm bearing experiment. When establishing intimate relationship with the little creature, its flowing-brook-like sounds of eating mulberry leaves and of spinning out led me to somewhere distant - an empty, quiet and magnificent territory. I listened silently and attentively, feeling a sense of relief, as if I had realized the state of Chan Buddhism. That’s when the idea of “Listen to the Silkworms” came into being.

 

“Listen to the Silkworms” erases the differences between life, production and art. In fact, Chinese sericulture is a great form of performance art and biological art. Additionally, it cannot be simply explained through a few words such as “behavior” and “Chan”. It spawns new meanings as the audience’s perspective changes. Owing to the location where the work displays and the fact that sericulture involves humanity and science (such as the biological clock), “Listen to the Silkworms” offers the weary city dwellers a sense of hope to return to nature for enlightenment and self-redemption.

 

The work is now exhibited in an empty and quiet room. Only when the audience wears the earphone can they hear the sound. Although the direct connection between vision and hearing has been cut off, it points out a path towards what is so-called “great form is beyond shape; great music has the faintest notes”. 

Unlike Cage’s pausing piano that prompts the audience to contemplate, “Listen to the Silkworms” is a kind of “natural state”, lifelike, serene and sober, rather than creating a sense of abruptness by compulsion.

medium: Red industrial silk, cocoons, approx. /each，400 pcs in total

raw.title: Babies/Nature Series No.15
raw.medium: Red industrial silk, cocoons, approx. 6.5×2.5×2cm/each，400 pcs in total

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Liang moved his studio to the Tiantai Mountains since 2000, he has found the solitude not only to focus on raising his silkworms, but also to deeply meditate upon the rich history and philosophy embodied in these sacred grounds. He became especially taken by the Buddhist belief in the equality of all living things and similarly in the Taoist notion of Qi Wu (equality of things.) For Liang, caring about silkworms is equal to caring about life and people: as he has said, “When I see a silkworm, I treat it like a baby.” Accordingly, Babies/Nature Series No. 15 features silkworm cocoons delicately swaddled in sewn red blankets. Since the first iteration of this installation was completed in 1994, Liang has created several versions whose acquired meanings differ in accordance to how, when, and why they are shown. For instance, in commemoration of the tragic Sichuan earthquake in 2008, Liang created a version in which visitors could either adopt a “baby”, or place it within the growing circle of cocoons on the floor. In all their iterations, Babies is a tender yet powerful meditation on what it means to cherish something, and what it means to be human.

title: Beds/Nature Series No.10
medium: Charred copper, silk, cocoons, approx. /each，30 pieces in total

raw.title: Beds/Nature Series No.10
raw.medium: Charred copper, silk, cocoons, approx. 20×12×10cm/each，30 pieces in total

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
Every time when silkworms spin (the process usually lasts 3 to 6 days), Liang Shaoji has to be at their side and can only sleep for 3 hours every day. Once again, he was lying on the ground to observe and conduct his practice as if he was a silkworm. But he was too tired and fell asleep. A silkworm fell between his neck and shirt collar. He did not find out that this little thing had already left a circular trace on him until he woke up an hour later. He then started to make his Beds.

 

It was once full of anxiety and worries in China in the 1990s. Portraying what he saw and felt in those years, Liang modeled these beds with the copper wire taken from burned engines and let silkworms live and spin on them. Those silkworms spent all their life on the beds, which is just like human beings, most of whom come to and leave this world on the beds, and spend at least 1/3 of their time on the bed for sleeping.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Guo Fengyi was an autodidact artist who spent her entire life in her native city of Xi’an. After an early retirement due to illness, at 47 she started practicing Qigong to alleviate severe arthritis pain. Taking inspiration from her love for traditional Chinese folk art, Guo Fengyi tried to express instantaneous feelings with her paintbrush, using pen and paper as means to adjust the balance between body and mind. Her artistic practice unites the act of painting and life itself, forming a creative quotidian affair. In her earlier works, Guo Fengyi used available domestic supports such as her grandson’s schoolbooks and old calendar pages. Gradually she started working more systematically on long scrolls, which she filled with detailed images of mythical creatures, chimeras, cosmological diagrams and numerologies, outlining with thin and fine lines. These complex and extremely detailed drawings contain the artist’s interest and study of philosophies of mysticism, in which her conscious flow and body perception was attuned.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1942; deceased in 2010


Guo Fengyi was an autodidact artist. After becoming ill in the late 1980s, she began practicing Qigong as a means to alleviate her illness, strengthening her health through an understanding of the body’s energy flows, and eventually developing the ‘Penguin’ style Qigong, which she now teaches as a revered master. In 1989, after two years of practicing Qigong, she began to have strong visions that she felt compelled to express through drawings. Complex and intricately lined, her quasi-psychedelic drawings, which often take the form of scrolls portraying metaphysical entities, map vectors of energy both inside, and emanating from, the body. Merging the figurative with the diagrammatic, these visionary works embody an idiosyncratic yet systematic response to our physical, psychological and spiritual existence.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: "The series is a representative of my works regarding containers. I borrowed the technique of Chinese line drawing to depict the net, using lines and spheres of color blocks to create psychological contrast and balance. This is the portrait of everyday objects. "  - Zhang Enli

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b.1965, Jilin, now residing in Shanghai.


Mundane objects and the traces of daily life activities are the dominant depicted subjects in Zhang Enli’s works. The muted tones and loose washes of paint intertwine with the expressive lines and curves that make the objects seem removed as if occupying a liminal reality where only the essence of the object is portrayed on the canvas. In his series of installations, known as Space Paintings, he creates the immersive space that suspends the audience into the void of time and space by incorporating with environment, history, and personal experience. Zhang Enli’s depiction on the prosaic aspects of contemporary life leads viewers to think about the proposition of existence.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: This video installation centers on the world’s largest radio telescope, located in Esperanza, Puerto Rico, which is home to the last remaining population of the Amazona vittata parrot. In collaboration with science fiction author Ted Chiang, the script includes living, nonliving, human, animal, technological, and cosmic actors. As the parrot named Alex, “The humans use Arecibo to look for extraterrestrial intelligence. Their desire to make a connection is so strong that they’ve created an ear capable of hearing across the universe. But I and my fellow parrots are right here. Why aren’t they interested in listening to our voices? We’re a non-human species capable of communicating with them. Aren’t we exactly what humans are looking for?”

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
Jennifer Allora, b. 1974, Philadelphia, U.S.A.

Guillermo Calzadilla, b. 1971, La Havana, Cuba

Working collaboratively since 1995; live and work in San Juan, Puerto

 

Through a research-based approach, Jennifer Allora and Guillermo Calzadilla’s work traces intersections of history, material culture, and politics through a wide variety of mediums, namely performance, sculpture, sound, video, and photography. Their work has been exhibited and collected widely in public institutions and private collections. They were the United States Representatives for the 2011 Venice Biennale. In 2017, they were awarded The Scientific Merit Award for science and The Audience Award, at the 10th Annual Imagine Science Film Festival.

This series is not only the beginning of my portrait painting in the 90s of social groups but also the original prototype of my later portrait (container) series of objects. " -Zhang Enli

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
The artwork was realized by junya.ishigami+associates for Junya Ishigami’s touring solo exhibition Freeing Architecture at the Power station of Art, China. This architectural model is a representation at scale 1-10 of the Serpentine Pavilion designed by junya.ishigami+associates in 2019 in London, UK.


The design for the 2019 Serpentine Pavilion takes the roof, the most common architectural feature, as the base of its inspiration. It is reminiscent of roofing tiles seen around the world, bridging both architectural and cultural references through this single architectural feature. The roof of the Pavilion is made by arranging slates to create a canopy that evokes nature. It appears to emerge from the ground of the surrounding Park. This design for the Pavilion plays with the perspectives of the built environment against the backdrop of a natural landscape, emphasizing a natural and organic feel as though it had grown out of the lawn, resembling a hill made of rocks. This is an attempt to supplement traditional architecture with modern methodologies and concepts, to create in this place an expanse of scenery as never seen before. Possessing the weighty presence of slate roofs, and simultaneously appearing so light it could be blown away by the breeze, the cluster of scattered rock levitates, like a billowing piece of fabric. The interior of the pavilion is a cave-like enclosed space, a refuge for contemplation. For the architect, this Pavilion is thought as a “free space”. It illustrates the idea of harmony between architecture and nature.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b.1974 Kanagawa Prefecture, Japan; lives and works in Tokyo.


Junya Ishigami graduated from Tokyo National University of Fine Arts and Music with a M.F.A. in architecture in 2000, and joined the office of Kazuyo Sejima & Associates that same year. He founded his office, junya.ishigami+associates, in 2004. Ishigami inherits the delicate, light and natural features of Modernist architecture in Japan. He explores the relationship between landscape and nature, the transparency and ambiguity of space, as the same time, emphasizes the topic of locality of architecture and globalization. In a way, Ishigami extends the definition of architecture in human cognition. His first independent project KAIT Workshop won him the AIJ Prize 2009. In 2008 & 2010 he represented Japan for the International Architecture Exhibition of the Venice Biennale and won the Golden Lion for the best project for“Architecture as Air: Study for Chateau la Coste” in 2010. Ishigami was the designer for the Serpentine Pavilion 2019.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
"After 1990, my “Complementary” series entered a new stage of creation, i.e. the of mixed media works. The Overlapping Newly-Translated Scriptures (1996) is a work that I am personally satisfied with. It was well received after its debut at the first edition of Shanghai Biennale. It is said that the German collector Peter Ludwig proposed to collect this work after his visit to the exhibition. However, the acquisition was unsuccessful due to his sudden death from illness. Later, this work was collected by the renowned Belgian collector Guy Ullens.

 

The Overlapping Newly Translated Scriptures shown at this exhibition is another version I made for my solo exhibition at Z-Art Center in 2009. I made three changes in this version. First, I added two more boards to make the whole work less tight. Second, I added more details during the remake process — the scriptures were not copied by me alone, but by several people, so there is a variety of handwritings. It did not matter if one made a mistake, because we could cross it out and re-write. We transcribed the scriptures fast, and our impatience is reflected in the scribble and the occasional mistakes. The crossed-out and corrected writing across the lines not only makes the boards more rhythmic, but also faithfully reflect the lack of religious sincerity among contemporary people. The attentive viewers can vaguely sense the complex and subtle connection between religion and contemporary people. Third, the images attached to the original works used to be black-and-white photocopies of Buddha photography, while in the new work images were changed to colorful photo records of religious activities around the world, which further suggests that religions in different cultures can best represent their spiritual essence. Despite the diverse religious activities, the development trend of world civilization is complex and volatile, and cultural infiltration and materialism have inevitably led to the collapsing of our spiritual home.

 

The tonality of the work is an interplay of golden and silvery. View this work under the light, the texture of plexiglass and the complexity and dislocation caused by the overlapping handwritings may dazzle the audience when they proceed. The splendid and dazzling effect exactly reveals the thinking behind my creation of this work!" - Zhou Changjiang

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1950 in Shanghai, China.


Zhou Changjiang graduated from the oil painting class of the Fine Arts Department of Shanghai Theatre Academy. In 1984, he joined the Creative Studio of Shanghai Oil Painting and Sculpture Institute. He has participated in various international and national art exhibitions and won many awards. Currently, he serves as a professor in the Art Department of East China Normal University, adjunct professor at Shanghai Academy of Fine Arts, member of the Chinese Artists Association, and director of the Chinese Oil Painting Society.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: These sickles, inscribed with caste names and geographies, are neither symbols nor an assembly, but a concatenation of singularities. On a tree trunk, they propose labour in a different moment of its manifestation: of repose and defiance. The field they evoke is at once essential, and a threat to the ideologies and imaginaries of productivity.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
Vinu V.V.

b. 1974, Cochin, India；works and lives in Cochin


Vinu V.V.'s art is a portrayal of revolts and poetics of Dalit culture. In his sculptures he redeploys ordinary objects - needles, thread, tin cans, sickles - to activate traces of labour and genealogies of caste occupation, producing uncanny conjunctions and charge around them. His work has been exhibited in solo and group shows in Fort Kochi, Ernakulam, Kottayam, New Delhi and Eramalloor.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: In Egó Sympósion, the artist revisits the twelve historic portraits in which he has cast himself since the 1980s. For each personality, he creates a moving image work with a first-person narrative in his enthralling signature style. He not only crafts a visual representation, but also combines the self- portrait with an original narrative that creates continuity and breathes new life into the character.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1951, Osaka; lives and works in Osaka.


Yasumasa Morimura has been working on self-portraits. Since his first self-portrait, "Portrait - Van Gogh" (1985), he has transformed himself into many diverse subjects, focusing on icons from Western culture. His subjects include famous paintings, images of popular culture, or mass media. His practice is based on deep research on the subjects, and brings a new perspective to iconic images. His work questions not only identity and gender, but also the medium of photography and painting.

title: I Saw It, Couldn't Express lt, But It Came to Mind...

raw.title: I Saw It, Couldn't Express lt, But It Came to Mind...

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
Mass culture typically depicts and comments on normal daily routines and normal bodily functions， raising important yet sensitive issues， which are fundamental to our shared emotional existence.


Liu Qingyuan's lightboxes recreate the atmosphere of the small commercial streets in his adopted home of Guangzhou, where the process of modernization has seen traditional placards replaced by brightly lit signs. What do these lightboxes represent? For Liu, they embody the thoughts and feelings and words of ordinary people. Standing beneath the lightboxes and looking up, you might see things you yourself said only the day before brought to life in flickering images.


Art moves us when it's true. Artists are always searching for ways to reveal the truth, but the most important thing will always be to make the viewer feel the truth.


"I hope that a commercial setting combined with scenes of hustle and bustle, festival, money, circus, television, power, etc. can have some effect on most people, and yet there is no need to be too surprising, as it is like a static or dynamic national bazaar.

 

All my works are made of woodcuts, films, and plastic lightboxes, which stimulate the visual possessiveness of the public again through their characteristic functions of “propaganda, advertising, and flattening”. The elements of the work I Saw it, Couldn’t Express it, But it Came to Mind come from the personal basic writing exercises I have been doing—“Woodcut Propaganda Posters”. The concepts for these woodcut works are derived from the contextual symbols of individuals living in the current times, and are the combination of contradictions, oppositions, conflicts and delusions, including issues everyone more or less faces today such as power, sex, competence, knowledge, collision, development, survival, memory, etc. These enlarged parts corresponding to the minor aspects of our individual world come from the minds of each of us—unspoken thoughts, light hypotheses, and silent acceptance.

 

This work is transplanted into the space by combination or enumeration. In the semi-open public space, the audience can interact with the work by “stand here and take a photo”. These photos will be presented and intervened in the manner of “consuminga hypothesis” and will be recorded and retained as part of the work. " ——Liu Qingyuan

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
Liu Qingyuan

b.1972, Chongqing; works and lives in Guangzhou.


Liu Qingyuan graduated from the Department of Printmaking of Guangzhou Academy of Fine Arts. He currently serves as the Deputy Dean of the School of Visual Communication and Media Design and the Director of the Department of Experimental Art at the Guangzhou Academy of Fine Arts. He works on the social integration method, interdisciplinary practice, and creation of contemporary art and design. His work involves different fields of contemporary culture, such as music, experimental drama, literature, design, cultural conservation, folk arts and rural construction, etc.

title: Documentary Video, Music and Archives of Landscape: Commemorating Huang Binhong
medium: 4:3 color video with resolution of 720*576, the set including video disc*1, sound disc*1 and related archives

raw.title: Documentary Video, Music and Archives of Landscape: Commemorating Huang Binhong
raw.medium: 4:3 color video with resolution of 720*576, the set including video disc*1, sound disc*1 and related archives

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Landscape-Commemorating Huang Binhong is a fan-shaped stereoscopic installation with neon and sound, which is 5 meters high and 10.6 meters wide, fashioned with a curved body of 13.6meters in length. The whole picture is composed of 2520 neon tubes light up one by one in every10 seconds which are controlled by the single note of Guqin (traditional Chinese musical instrument) during the 7-hours full process of displaying. Synchronous with the music, the neon light up when a note struck that last from 2 to 3 seconds, and leave it into a silence of 7 to 8seconds. The landscape brought by the light, the light is determined by time, however, the music is sounded by the landscape, which is harmonious with the light.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
Born in 1952 in Shanghai. Now residing in Shanghai.


Shen Fan started disassembling concrete forms and space in painting since the early 1980s, and began creating abstract painting works. Late 1990s, he has been bringing Chinese painting elements into multi-medium and materials such as ceramics, neon light, metal, and music, expanding the boundaries between painting and new media. He is one of the earlier Chinese artists who combine classical aesthetics into the contemporary context to explore contemporary Chinese cultural expressions.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
Commissioned by Power Station of Art

Tungus presents the interconnection in space and time among several groups of characters in different geographic coordinates during their journeys back home. A main narrative thread derives from the artist’s rewriting of two stories.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
Born 1984; lives and works in Beijing.


Born and raised in Changchun, China, Wang Tuo currently lives and works in Beijing. Wang Tuo employs various mediums and a process that combined interview, reality show and the theatre of absurd to construct a maze of melodrama. Through his performative manipulation on individuals’ lived experiences and intervention in intellectual legacies such as literature, film, theatre and art history, Wang’s practice attempts to examine the unreliable relationship between the contemporary human status, myth and cultural archive. In the self-referential environments that he constructs, dramatic, often humorous as well as absurd aspects of the concept of society are exposed. Wang’s practice also seeks to develop a discourse on how present ideology is derived from its historical context continues to adapt to changing condition. Wang has recent solo shows at Present Company, New York, Salt Project, Beijing, Taikang Space, Beijing. In 2021, Wang Tuo will have his first institutional survey at UCCA Beijing.

title: Qian Xuesen and the Yangzte River Computer

raw.title: Qian Xuesen and the Yangzte River Computer

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Taking Qian Xuesen’s ideas on system theory and his career in scientific research as a thread, the work fabricated that during the period of socialistic construction of P.R. China, Qian and the collective team jointly developed a supercomputer device that could couple natural energy with the computing power of the masses. Integrating real documents in history, the film completes a narrative of "new historical science fiction" while also revisiting the history of electronic technology development in P.R. China.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
Born 1969; lives and works in Shanghai.


Shi Qing’s artistic creation involves various media and their integrated application including installation, video, and performance. He stresses a leaping advancement of subjective practice and media writing, while is also an active organizer of different social initiatives, as the co-founder of Radical Space, CWI, and Jiangnan Stack, who has also initiated and realized projects such as  “Collectivist Building”, “Difang Works”, “Hinterland Project”, and “Shanghai Redux”.

title: Water System Refuge#2
medium: Installation, photography, document  Overall size variable, Video duration 15’29”

raw.title: Water System Refuge#2
raw.medium: Installation, photography, document  Overall size variable, Video duration 15’29”

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: The series of “Water System Refuge” focuses on the impacts of local policies and post-disaster reconstruction after the 2008 Sichuan earthquake. Taking old tents, building materials of ethnic Qiang people, and the post-earthquake museum as our research objects, this project discusses how frequent disasters in the upper stream of the Minjiang River (which is not a human-centered area, with its complex geological structure) are related to the urgent need for collective experiments beyond the region,and the need for thinking about the diversity of local traditions, local plants and ancient wisdom.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
Cao Minghao, born 1982, and Chen Jianjun, born 1981

Working collaboratively since 2010; based in Chengdu.


The practice collaborated by Cao Minghao and Chen Jianjun is based on research and focuses on processes and multiple ways of collaboration. The two artists make efforts to explore new social relationships between ecological materials and human society; they particularly look at the river basins which have not been re-recognized and the water systems which have been outside the real orders, to explore the changes of ecology history and the ways of re-imagining the future. Their works include researching about the disappearing countryside, the connection of migrant workers in the South, the new narratives of specific water systems and the public installations of water refuge. Their works create the power of connection between all things through different visual narratives. Their projects have been shown at a number of exhibitions, including COSMOPOLIS #2.0：Repenser l’humain in Centre Pompidou (Paris, 2019), COSMOPOLIS #1.5: Enlarged Intelligence (Chengdu, 2018), The 7th Bi-city Biennale of Urbanism/Architecture (Shenzhen, 2017), etc.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Cao Minghao and Chen Jianjun initiated their “Water System Project” research in 2015. It is an ongoing platform investigating the relationship between the history of the Dujiangyan irrigation project and the conditions of the surrounding water systems. The two artists develop collaborative art-making processes, working with participants of diverse backgrounds and disciplines, such as environmental NGOs, anthropologists, urban planners, and villagers from the area. Together they engage with ecological and social problems caused by changes in the water system. Cao and Chen have worked with multiple boat-making experts to re-design an abandoned ferry boat, encouraging conversations and cooperations during the process, in which local knowledge and narratives about local residents’ relationships with water are recorded.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
Commissioned by the 13th Shanghai Biennale/Power Station of Art


For Fluffy Grounds, C+ has collaborated with Maria Puig de la Bellacasa, Martin Nadal and Drew Zeiba, with the contribution of Óscar Hernández Tristancho, Ana Isabel Bustamante Cruz, and Ella Fathi.


In the month of April, the grounds of Beijing become a magical and contested terrain. “Spring snow” turns the air white and covers the city grounds with a white fluffy tapestry that inspires love and wonder, aversion and fear. Variously referred to as a headache, nuisance, allergy inducer or pollution, this fluffy stuff is the carrier for poplar and willow tree seeds. Trees once planted to fulfil human imaginaries of comfort start behaving as trees proper, and excess overflows and transcends the previously controlled domesticated garden. Urban paved grounds, unlike soils, cannot welcome fluffy seedlings into their soft layers of decomposing litter. Humans become hostile to their wild behavior and the tree is rejected as a source of discomfort—along with other interspecies relations, as hairy moths attracted by poplars join the count of “natural pollutant” agents. Through poplar seeds close-ups, graphic visualizations, and experimental storytelling, the video explores the tousled nature-cultural materialities of this white swirling stuff.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
C+ arquitectas founded 2006/2016; based in Madrid and London, the director is Nerea Calvillo González.


C+ arquitectas is a female-lead collaborative team that focuses on research and spatial design, developing architecture projects, environmental mediations, ephemeral installations, exhibition design and visualisations. Their works have been exhibited in the Royal Academy of Arts (UK), Canadian Centre of Architecture (Canada), LABoral (Spain) or at the Museum of Contemporary Art (Chile). They have published in interdisciplinary academic journals, art and architecture magazines and the general media. Their pedagogical projects are currently being developed at the Centre for Interdisciplinary Methodologies (Warwick, UK), GSAPP (Columbia, US), and Universidad Rey Juan Carlos (Madrid, Spain).

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: With a huge wooden brush covered with iron wire (which resembles hair), this work articulates Shen Yuan’s sense of loss and anxiety about her identity as a female creator. The artist often uses everyday objects such as brushes, buckets, and wooden boats as prototypes for her work. As a Chinese woman who migrates to different parts of the world, her work frequently draws upon her nomadic private life while reflecting upon her experience in a rapidly changing world.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1959, Xianyou, Fujian Province; lives and works in Paris.


Shen Yuan is one of the earliest Chinese contemporary artists to gain international recognition. In the early 1980s, she studied in the Chinese Painting Department of the Zhejiang Academy of Fine Art (now the China Academy of Art), and expanded on experimental arts as led by the trend at the time. She experienced changes of living environment and a discontinuity of cultures as she moved to France in the early 1990s, which provoked her reflection on language and identity issues. Shen is skilled at using daily objects to create art installations, and has a preference for those that dissolve shortly and are difficult to use. She contends that “it is the responsibility of an artist to endow new value upon things.” Materials like knitting, embroidery, hair and shoes appear constantly in her artworks, reflecting the simple scenes of women’s everyday life as well as the complex feminist discourse. Her recent artworks demonstrate a closer association with her peripatetic experience travelling around the world, which exhibits her acute perception towards the dramatic changes that are taking place around us.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: For many years, Yang Fudong has been continuously developing his Museum Film Project. For the 12th edition of Shanghai Biennale, he transformed the central staircase of the Power Station of Art into an environment for a mass performance involving five hundred participants. Entitled Indeed, the Only Way, the work considers notions of historical progress, social evolution, and the dynamics of time and space in personal life. The “stage” for the performance was composed of red carpet, mirrored surfaces and silver wallpaper, a setting of grandeur that evokes certain power relations in the social landscape, reflecting upon the possibility of cultural inertia.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: b. 1971, Beijing; lives and works in Shanghai.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Fluorescent colors began to increasingly dominate Ding Yi's canvas since 1998, as an attempt to capture the metropolitan exuberance and vitality of Shanghai and the infinite tension emerging from the intersection of reality and illusion. If the grid compositions in Ding Yi's “Appearance of Crosses” paintings calls to mind architectural drawings of urban planning, the “Fluorescence” series, on the other hand, bestows this towering landscape with a magical radiant aura. Creation of the “Fluorescence” series continued until 2010. Like the artist's works of public sculpture and architecture, these paintings respond to Shanghai's urban spirit, and can be seen as carriers of Shanghai's urban sensibility in highly concentrated form.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1962, Shanghai; lives and works in Shanghai.


Ding Yi is a pioneer of Chinese contemporary abstract painting. His canvases are filled with countless individual “crosses”, a sign inspired by the standard markings used in offset color printing. In his practice, he refuses narrative and representation, with the simple appearance of the “crosses” covering the great effort and consciousness that lies beneath the artist’s intuitional creations. From his pursuit of precise brushwork to his obsession with the hand-drawn traces, and from experimentation in various mediums of painting to his recent incorporation of woodcut technique into his painting explorations, these tiny crosses mark out a serial structure of resonance.


His creation maintains a profound interaction with the spirit of the city, and can be viewed as the refined essence of the Shanghai urban experience over the past few decades: the grid composition in his paintings evokes an association of urban planning, and particularly the “Fluorescence” series since 1998, which bestowed this towering landscape with a radiant aura. His public sculpture and architecture works, meanwhile, can be seen as extensions of the city and direct interactions with the urban space.

title: Appearance of Crosses 2018-B3
medium: Acrylic, pencil and chalk on rice paper;  (in 4 pieces)

raw.title: Appearance of Crosses 2018-B3
raw.medium: Acrylic, pencil and chalk on rice paper; 450 × 936 cm (in 4 pieces)

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: New exhibitions are often one of the main external sources of Ding Yi’s creative motivation. This work, Appearance of Crosses 2018–B3, was created specifically for the exhibition “The Challenging Souls: Yves Klein, Lee Ufan, Ding Yi”. Taking three months to complete, the painting is an experiment on a new painting surface—Xuan paper. This choice of material not only echoes Ding Yi’s experience studying traditional Chinese painting at Shanghai University in the late 1980s, it also summons the “East-West contention” that concerned the entire art scene at the time. Such discussion remains relevant today, and this artwork can be seen as the artist’s experiment in the contemporary expression of “Orientalism”.

title: Pulp Landscape 1
medium: Camera, stepper motor, railway track, leather suitcase, acryl, copper, iron, video terminal controller; ; overall dimensions variable

raw.title: Pulp Landscape 1
raw.medium: Camera, stepper motor, railway track, leather suitcase, acryl, copper, iron, video terminal controller; 80 × 60 × 160 cm; overall dimensions variable

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: This is the first in a series of works created by artist Hu Weiyi in the form of a miniature film studio that can shoot in real time. Hu installed seven pinhole cameras in an old suitcase which can continuously capture objects at close range placed on a railway track, transforming the suitcase into a mechanical device that can autonomously generate images. The footage is then displayed in real time on five screens positioned in a circle. The suitcase contains a plethora of short-lived objects and detritus encountered in our daily lives, such as discarded circuit boards, dead insect carcasses, useless tools and instruments, old dentures and internet memes. By collecting together these elements, the artist constructs a “pulp landscape” that reproduces some of the vulgar parts of real life. Repeatedly photographed, enlarged and projected in this suitcase theater, the objects become actors which seem to have their own emotions and their own desires, forming a kind of pulp carnival.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1990, Shanghai; lives and works in Shanghai.


Hu Weiyi graduated from the China Academy of Art. Committed to new media art, he focuses on the exploration of the unknown and the melancholic moments in life, while staying curious about the nature and bodily harm. He reversed the randomness and naturally-generated relationship to a subjective expression, and preset the audience's trajectory. Like many mature artists, he has a good grasp of space, concepts, and outreach information. His main exhibitions include the solo exhibition “Flirt” (2014) at M50 Art Space in Shanghai, the opening exhibition “Multiverse” (2014) in the Shanghai 21st Century Minsheng Art Museum, the second CAFAM Future Exhibition (2015), and “No Express” (2015) at Ullens Center for Contemporary Art, Beijing.

title: I Hate People but I Love You

raw.title: I Hate People but I Love You

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: I Hate People but I Love You is a large format single-channel video installation set in Mac OS. The video features two cyborgs, one of which is an android with the simulated face of an Asian woman, while the other takes the form of a floating Möbius strip composed of pop- up windows. Both immerse themselves in an incessant deadpan conversation: “…May I be your friend? Do I look real to you? I hope so… I hate people but I love you.” The artist dramatizes the classic sci-fi paradigm of dystopian isolation and loneliness, one which is becoming a reality not only in the alienation of social media but also in the unmapped boundaries of interpersonal emotion between users and increasingly “humanized” operating systems.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1984, Xi'an; lives and works in Shanghai and Berlin.


aaajiao is the pseudonym of young artist Xu Wenkai, and his fictional persona on the internet. He was born in Xi'an, one of the oldest cities in China, in 1984, which happens to be the title of George Orwell’s classic prophetic novel. aaajiao’s creations combine a strong sense of dystopia and the reflection on the literati spirit. Many of his works are dedicated to exploring cultural phenomena and political strategies under the influence of new technologies and media, varying from social media writing and data processing to a new aesthetic landscape under the Internet and mobile media. As a representative of the new media artists, aaajiao introduces China’s special culture and technology on social media to international art discourse and discussions. His works are frequently exhibited in art museums and institutions around the world, such as the Institute of Contemporary Art (Boston, 2018), HeK (Haus der elektronischen Künste Basel, 2017), the Jewish Museum (New York, 2016), the ZKM Center for Art and Media (Karlsruhe, 2015), etc.

title: I Am My Own Bot
medium: Single channel video, color, sound; website; 15'32''

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: I Am My Own Bot displays an environment deeply intertwined with by a digital past as well as its present counterpart. Reflecting on this intersection, local and global networks, social media, gardening structures, parks, and finally nature itself all become amalgamated into a digital hyper-representation.

title: Archival Materials of Three Steps Nine Footprints
medium: Archive documents and photo collage, exhibition brochure; 3 plaster footprints, each

raw.title: Archival Materials of Three Steps Nine Footprints
raw.medium: Archive documents and photo collage, exhibition brochure; 3 plaster footprints, each 100 × 60 × 15 cm

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
Three Steps Nine Footprints was conceived and realized by Huang Yong Ping in Marseille, France in 1996. In 2016, the work was exhibited at the artist’s solo exhibition “Bâton Serpent III: Spur Track To The Left” at the Power Station of Art. On this occasion, Huang collected and compiled archival materials of this work, including 3 plaster footprints, sketches, photos, and exhibition brochure, to preserve certain aspects of his creative process.


Produced in response to a series of terrorist attacks carried out in Paris in 1995, this work comprises a series of footprints impressed in plaster by an iron contraption with three feet, modelled after historical representations of the footprints of the Budhha, Jesus Christ, and Mohammed respectively. With one step in three footprints, it takes twenty-four steps to complete the walk, leaving altogether seventy-two footprints. The stepping method is derived from 禹步 (Yubu) of Taoist rituals, also referred to as “Three Steps, Nine Footprints.” In reference to their use as hiding places for bombs during the 1995 attacks, Huang positioned a series of sealed trash cans in the exhibition space. The work is a poignant reflection on what the artist described as violence and conflicts between different cultures, walking along and taking the wrong path.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1954, Xiamen, Fujian Province; d. October 20, 2019.


Huang Yongping was one of the most important artists in China’s contemporary art trend. He challenged art museums and traditional art concepts with his creations, and explored the relationship between Chinese and Western cultures, and the relationship between man and animals through space installations, trying to find an expression that could transcend national boundaries and ideological conflicts.


He graduated from the Zhejiang Academy of Fine Arts (now the China Academy of Art) in 1982, and moved to France in 1989. He co-founded the important artist collective Xiamen Dada in 1986). His works were exhibited at some of the most prestigious exhibitions worldwide, including Venice Biennale (2005), Shanghai Biennale (2000 & 2012), Monumenta (Paris, 2016). His solo exhibitions were held in various institutions including Power Station of Art (Shanghai, 2016), Ullens Center for Contemporary Art (Beijing, 2007) and Walker Art Center (Minneapolis, 2007).

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
The two works they are showing in this Biennale both display their "concern" for real people.


In Shoulder, the members of the collective each returns to his or her own home, blindfolds their parents, and takes them to a specific location. In each case, it is a place that the parents once took the artist to. The blindfolded parents are led and supported by the artist, creating a new connection, or relevance, between family members who have for years been growing apart. They are revisiting not just a location, but a relationship.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: Irrelevative group is a group of young artists strongly inclined toward social action. Each member has their own projects outside of the collective, but they work together to do "work which we could not do, do not have the courage to do, or lack the willpower to do alone." Over the last few years, Irrelevantive Group have attracted considerable interest by undertaking a series of "walking" performances in public spaces, and projects involving interactions with their family members. Their name derives from their keen sense that contemporary art has been come too irrelevant to real life and real people. Through their collective action, they are attempting to build a new "relevance".

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Already a well-established painter, in the early 1990s Li Shan moved away from many of the artistic concerns of his peers and began to focus on what he saw as essential ethical questions facing biology and humankind itself. Rejecting the supposed predominance of humanity over other life forms, Li began to propose that human genes could be profitably combined with those of other species, a principle that he explored in the hybrid creations that populate his “Reading” series. In his account of the nascent field of Bio Drawing, Li Shan wrote: “What an artist does, in her or her own way of thinking and doing, is really about finding a different mode of interpretation in life.”

blocks.body:
b. 1942, Lanxi, Hei Longjiang Province; lives and works in Shanghai.

In early 1998, with molecular biology as the scientific foundation, he finished the first BioArt proposal in art history at the genetic level, Reading. blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
"1906-1989-2012: Guangzhou-Hongkong-Shanghai-Anji is a piece of local/ regional history composed of folk material (straws and bamboos), urban objects, family histories and quotidian events such as letter-writing and postal service arrangements. With its three components – front stage, back stage, and the partition separating the two stage zones – I play with the assumed hierarchy of dramaturgy. On the 'front stage' is a huge load in a netted sphere, highlighting the perceptual presence of what can be seen, heard and touched. At the back stage, fragmented discourses, statistics, and details of lived experiences and their representation fill a wall with framed objects. The 'partition' so to speak is a huge wall of bamboo slags, the most spectacular component, calling attention to its very material presence as much as my inscriptions. 


Consistent with my works' engagement with historiographic experiments, my enquiry in 1906-1989-2012 shifts to the detailed study of objects, material supplies as well as the effort and labor put into the skilled and meticulous workmanship. My artistic direction is, on the one hand, to transform the practicality of objects to explore their neglected physicality and, on the other hand, to convert labor time into the force of visual quantities. I bring to the front stage laborers forgotten and lost in silence at the end of assembly lines – including people like my maternal grandmother who committed to small daily handicrafts to earn cash subsidies to get for folks in the Mainland needed supplies which they turned into loads carried on a bamboo slag. 


Throughout the sixties and seventies, my grandma spent her days making ropes used in traditional weighing scales by rubbing hemp on the side of her lower leg. I was the little girl who wrote most of the letters on her behalf to check if little parcels arrived properly, why her son was not writing, and to announce her semi-annual return to Guangzhou. This is our HK-based family's story of Cultural Revolution. Together with various changes in the postal service arrangements between Hong Kong and China, I am writing an alternative economic history, in the spirit of Fernand Braudel, based on the changing costs of purchasing and mailing daily necessities. This alternative history contrasts with, and so provides a counterpoint to, the dominant narrative of economic progress/regress in China. 


On a personal note, this work contains a past that has always seemed impossible to capture – now best to be let dwell in tangible objects, however elliptical my memory might be. 1906-1989 marks the years my grandmother lived. In 2012, the purpose of reactivating folk materials ties me and my jaded stories back to Shanghai, a city neither she nor I is familiar with. The skilled workers in Anji, Zhejiang, provide this work with their labor and time, which I mean to honor. "


— Linda C.H. Lai

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: Linda Chiu-han Lai is associate Professor in Intermedia Arts at the City University of Hong Kong’s School of Creative Media (SCM), is a research -based interdisciplinary artist with broad international exposure. After compl eting her Ph.D. in Cinema Studies at New York University, she has sought meaningful connective extension to other relevant artistic and theoretical endeavors. She persists in artistic creation as the practice of theory. Her artistic/academic research focuses on historiography, visual and auto-ethnography, urbanity and archiving, with a strong emphasis on the criticality of micro/meta narrativity.

title: Deviation
medium: Silicone, resin, aluminum alloy material; Each

raw.title: Deviation

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Combining the life-size lower body of a man with a monstrously oversized upper body, wings and eyes of a dragonfly, these conglomerate creatures embody Li’s fascination with the prospect of DNA sequencing, contemplating the benefits of genetically engineering human chromosomes with those of other lifeforms. Li has conjectured that replacing human eyes with those of a dragonfly might enhance our perception of color, enabling us to experience vision through the approximately thirty thousand facets that make up a single dragonfly eye. Probing speculative biological futures, Li’s work invites us to reflect on the uncertain position of humankind in our planet’s ecology.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: In biogenetic research, DNA can generate a new biological protein through transcription and translation. The “Mistake Of Translation” series uses a large quantity of manuscripts to present all kinds of results due to mistakes in the translation of genes. The selected 100 rough skeches in the exhibition have used different colored paper and a simple hand-drawn style to present the various transfigurations resulted from recombining insect and human genomes or the exotic insect varians with huaman facial features or organs. In the field of scientific experiments, all unexpected varians or variations are often seen as miatakes or failures. However, in Li Shan’s artistic concept and creative practice, all these mistakes in translation have a unique significance of beauty and value.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: In the process of reading, skipping words, misreading, or mispronunciation are inevitable. For Li Shan, these are indeed the most charming and meaningful incidents. If they are connected to a behavior of reading, a new definition of life and creation of alternative art can be spawned. The huge painting exhibited in R108 seems to be a conceptual sketch of a biologist before he carries out an experiment. An unfinished work of art, It records the traces of the artist’s thinking and is garnished with conflicting elements and contradicting vocabulary. In fact, it can be regarded as an embodiment of Li Shan’s bio-art concept in a panel painting, “all life is equal and the same.” The painting juxtaposes tiger, human, dragonfly, sperm, and other symbols of life, presenting a progressive state of information exchange in genetics with a purpose that Li Shan has uttered：“I provide that symbols and present them to you.I have reached this goal.”

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Boat Zhang refers to these videos of physical performances and video work as “a group of body practices”. Through these “very small, simple points, ambivalent actions related to her body, emotion and private daily life”, she revisits themes of daily life, choice, fate, femininity, and individual identity with a unique view. Her works also reflect the spiritual need of turning inward when living in the collective.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1983, Yuyao, Zhejiang Province; lives and works in Shanghai and Tokyo.


After graduation from Goldsmiths, University of London in 2007, Boat Zhang worked as an employee in more than a few art institutions. She sees her experience of being employed by institutions as a way of observation. Most of her works start with a scenario, events, body, and individuals, and employ various media such as performance, image, text, and sound to subtly change the normal state and common sense in order to normalize strangeness and defamiliarize daily routine. Her works have been exhibited in China, Japan, and the UK. She is also a member of the Japanese artist group TEAM YAMEYO.

title: The Sky of Brooklyn （Document Edition）
medium: 19 black-and-white photos, each ; 1 color photo, 65.5 × 48.5 cm; 1 study, 50 × 40 cm; color video, with sound, 2'57''

raw.title: The Sky of Brooklyn （Document Edition）
raw.medium: 19 black-and-white photos, each 50 × 33 cm; 1 color photo, 65.5 × 48.5 cm; 1 study, 50 × 40 cm; color video, with sound, 2'57''

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: The artist dug a 3-meter-deep hole in the west chamber (to imply the west) of his courtyard in Beijing, placed a TV display at the bottom of this “well,” and played a video footage shot at his studio in Brooklyn, New York. There is not much to see, however, on the screen except a blue sky. The work tackles the constant negotiation involved in the process of cross-cultural exchanges, while the clear sky seems to imply the state of minds of both the spectators and the people being watched: not much to see except for a few clouds hanging in the sky.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1960, Beijing; lives and works in Beijing and New York.


Wang Gongxin is one of the pioneers and representatives of video art in China. In 1994, he exhibited his works in his studio in the form of “Open Studio”. In the mid 1990s, he kicked off the movement of “Apartment Art” in Beijing. In 1995, he made his first video installation work, The Sky of Brooklyn: Digging a Hole in Beijing, again by the way of “Open Studio” in his courtyard house in Beijing. In 1996, he participated in China’s first video art show in Hangzhou, which was considered to be historically significant. In 1999, he founded the Loft New Media Art Space in Beijing as the art director. The Loft New Media Art Space is the earliest nonprofit art space in China, with far-reaching significance for exchanges and development of avant-garde culture and art. His works were exhibited in San Paulo Biennial, Taipei Biennial, Shanghai Biennale, National Art Museum of China, MoMA PS1 in New York, Haus der Kulturen der Welt in Berlin, Tate Liverpool in the UK, and National Gallery of Victoria in Australia. In 2013, he was nominated for the Olivier Award for Video Award for Best Set Design. In 2014, he received the honorary doctorate degree from SUNY.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: The eponymous “Basic Colors” of this video work by Wang Gongxin are the three primary colors of red, yellow and blue, which are flanked by black and white either side. Colored powders fall on various parts of the human body over the course of fifteen minutes of close-up footage, capturing the course of the material as it transforms from floating dust to a material partially absorbed by the body, accompanied by a rustling sound.
