blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: The night taxi passes over the earth's surface, via, over, across, and through borders that delineate our foreignness. The viewer is suddenly, unexpectedly, addressed directly, intimately. Stranger, how closely can I know you? Devotion departs from religion, implies a persistent openness of vision. Night Taxi seeks a new groundwork for closeness.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1973, Buffalo, USA; lives and works in Beirut.


Rheim Alkadhi collects intimate, social, and self-reflexive knowledge of people and places as a way of research. In her works, physical surroundings, objects, and human relationships attest to the overwhelming and contrasting states of disequilibrium and tranquility. Her works have been shown in Jerusalem, Sharjah, Amman, New York, Seoul, Cairo, Los Angeles, and Ramallah. She was a fellow in visual art at the Akademie Schloss Solitude (Stuttgart, 2015).

title: Off Takes
medium: HD single-channel color video, with sound; 21'18''

raw.title: Off Takes
raw.medium: HD single-channel color video, with sound; 21'18''

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Since 2012, Hao Jingban has been conducting research and compiling footage for her “Beijing Ballroom Project,” focusing primarily on the evolution of the ballroom dance tradition and its historical popularity in the early 1950s and the post-Cultural Revolution era in the late 1970s. Over the course of three years of filming, Hao experimented with different expressive methods to explore interwoven historical narratives. Off Takes originated with the discarded footage from the “Beijing Ballroom Project,” depicting personal life stories bound up with the shifting courses of political climates, which once defied interpretation due to their historical distance and poignant absurdity. Through the reorganization and reactivation of these previously abandoned fragments, Hao meditates on the semiotic and affective relations between images and meaning.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1985, Shanxi; lives and works in Beijing.


Hao Jingban completed a BA in Media and Communication from Goldsmiths, University of London in 2007, and a MA in Film Studies from University of London in 2010. She reveals the sub-cultural groups that are obscured under popular culture in the form of videos, such as middle-aged ballroom dancers and factory workers. She is good at using video as the medium of rich, three-dimensional expression. She frequently employs time-space fragments in her works, and juxtaposes multiple audio-visual media such as documentary videos, textual discourse, and film and television works to form a narrative language with polyphony and variation of multi-dimensional videos, which gives the audience a unique viewing experience. Her solo exhibitions include “New Directions: Hao Jingban” (Ullens Center of Contemporary Art, Beijing, 2016) and “Over-Romanticism” (Taikang Space, Beijing, 2016). She won the Huayu Youth Award Grand Jury Prize in Art Sanya 2016 with An Afternoon Ball and Off Takes from her Beijing Ballroom Project. In 2017, she was granted the Young Artist of the Year award at the 11th Award of Art China and the International Critics’ Prize at the 63rd Internationale Kurzfilmtage Oberhausen.

title: Journals
medium: Ink on Xuan paper; varying sizes circa

raw.title: Journals
raw.medium: Ink on Xuan paper; varying sizes circa 41 × 38 cm

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: In 1992, at the age of 45, the artist decided to leave his corporate life to dedicate himself to art. He started Journal in 1997 and this has engaged him in an ongoing dialogue with himself. He shared, “…after I’ve had a few years of my journal behind me, I realised that perhaps this was the true legacy I’ll be leaving behind: personal, consistent and with no motive other than to continue on the habit of a daily monologue.” He almost never reads his journal entries again. When he has finished making them, they are placed in folders. He added, “…the loose slips of paper which I found in my mother’s kitchen drawer had had a profound effect on me. She had written many words—single words, complicated words. Without knowing their exact meanings, these words told me of her sadness and her sufferings……As I doodle and write spontaneously one can see, without any difficulty, the paucity of some of my drawings and words. They contain illogic, churlishness, childishness, not to mention approximate grammar and spellings. The warts are human because there’s no such thing as perfection—only persistence, even in one’s failings.”

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1946, Shanghai; lives and works in Lausanne and Sainte Croix in Switzerland.


Franklin Chow attended the Académie de la Grande Chaumière in Paris. Having been born into an influential family which has fostered lots of outstanding talents and been raised in a paternal education encouraging an appreciation for art, Chow grew up with fine artistic sensibility and taste. His upbringing, as well as rich life and work experience contributed to his multicultural awareness, and was reflected in his artistic creation. His art practice combines the form of traditional Chinese art with the vision and concept of Western contemporary art. His works were exhibited in Switzerland, France, and Singapore, and collected by private collectors and art institutions in Switzerland, France, Germany, the UK, including the Teo Jakob art foundation (Bern), the Inez & Yves Oltramare Foundation (Geneva), and Rolex S.A. (Geneva).

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: This shirt made from Mexican paper is at once an installation and a painting. The dense motifs on the shirt resemble a calendar on which days are being counted. When the shirt is filled, it indicates the end of a period. The passage of time cannot be stopped. Life is limited and fragile like paper.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
Light, floating down like a feather. These words are written on the exhibition wall. The artist creates a virtual environment in the computer with it's own weight and gravitational pull, with in this environment, a fluorescent light tube falls much like a feather. Within this environment the falling progress of the tube can be precisely documented with accurate calculations and figures. Therefore, the artist will use one set of these calculation to make a stop motion sculpture that shows the falling process of the tube, as in from from point a to point b, and in between there are over thousands of tubes installed that represent the position of the falling at given time. At the same time, the process of falling is as organic in his virtual world as in the real world, therefore, there are many variables that produces many different results in the process of falling, these many processes are then calculated to printed out through out the exhibition and pasted onto the wall to represent the numbers of potential different out come.


On view, the viewer will see one giant light installation that represent the falling of the light tube (feather) made from the virtual environment. And also a computer that continually calculate and produce drawings of different out comes and processes of the falling tube.


The idea is to make the concept with tenable data from a supposed virtual environment, therefore, grounding something that is theoretical to reality.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: WANG Yuyang (b.1979) graduated from China Central Academy of Drama and the Central Academy of Fine Arts. Currently lives in Beijing, he has taught at the School of Experiment Art at the Central Academy of Fine Arts since 2008. WANG Yuyang creates works using emergent media but does not deliberately emphasize the novelty of technology. He is more interested in the artistry brought about by “outdated” technology, “destructive” aesthetics and material waste. His work has employed all possible media. He often uses humour, fiction and spectacles to explore and reflect upon the relationship between the human body, experience and cognition. At the same time he also investigates the relationship between artificial reality, media technology and historical perception.

title: Blind Prose
medium: 50 braille books on wood base, inked and varnished; Each , variable configuration

raw.title: Blind Prose
raw.medium: 50 braille books on wood base, inked and varnished; Each 50 × 50 × 28.5  cm, variable configuration

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Like many of Franklin Chow’s artwork, the installation Blind Prose finds humor in wordplay and metaphor, presenting a series of inked and varnished braille books. The books are sealed and incapable of being opened, reducing their content to illegible symbols. Each braille book varies slightly from the other, and some were published more than a hundred years ago. While people with unimpaired vision can no longer see the books, they can still access them through other sensory channels; after all, perception does not stop at the level of sight. The dialectical tension between the visible and invisible, permanence and ephemerality informs Chow’s larger philosophy: rather than mourn the transience of history, it is better to thrive in the midst of change.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: This work was created during the first day setting up the retrospective exhibition “Cai Guo-Qiang: The Ninth Wave” held at the Power Station of Art. Using his trademark medium - gunpowder - Cai created a work in homage to Ivan Aivazovsky’s The Ninth Wave (1850), a classic of Russian art history. Aivazovsky’s painting famously depicts survivors from a shipwreck clinging to a drifting mast in the last throes of survival, expressing human helplessness in the face of natures’ unforgiving power. Cai’s impression imparts a further dimension of elemental force, channeling the volatile potency of gunpowder to convey the violence of the storm.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1957, Quanzhou, Fujian Province; lives and works in New York.


Cai Guo-Qiang was trained in stage design at the Shanghai Theatre Academy, and his works have since crossed multiple media within art, including drawing, installation, video, and performance. While living in Japan from 1986 to 1995, he continued to explore the potential of gunpowder in drawing, and scaled up the explosion in his practice step by step, which eventually led to the development of his signature outdoor explosion program. He builds his work concepts on Eastern philosophy and contemporary social issues, and depicts local history and culture with a creative, adaptive attitude and methods. Viewers can therefore talk to society, nature and the universe through his works.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
Developed for the 11th Shanghai Biennale, Play the Host 客人 poses the question: could contemporary art provide a space for fictional discoveries with real consequences? The project refers to the rich mythological world of the Ming dynasty text Journey to the West (1592), exploring problems of cross-cultural translation in the first substantial and highly popular English translation, Arthur Waley’s Monkey: A Folk-Tale of China (1942).


This performative project features four characters who confront the exhibition audience with questions and statements that encourage stories to emerge in conversations and disputes. Each performer wears specially designed costumes in response to the protagonists’ magical and metamorphic characteristics in Journey to the West. The audience is both co-producer and co-author of the work, with their responses recomposed into a semi-fictional future folk tale by the artist.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1966, Helsinki; lives and works in London, Vienna, and Hong Kong.


Verina Gfader is an artist and researcher (London–Vienna–Hong Kong) currently affiliated with the City University of Hong Kong on the research project Meaning and Narrative in Abstract Animation (2018-2020). Working from within a vocabulary of experimental animation and independent publishing, she orchestrates her practice as organized fields of research aided by drawing and animation, printed matter, text performance and fabulation. She completed her doctorate in 2006 at Central Saint Martins in London, followed by a research residency at Tokyo University of the Arts (Geidai) to explore the structural coherence between independent Japanese animation and geographical, institutional and social ideas.

title: Pigs, Time and Space
medium: Single-channel color video, with sound, 21'12'';  installation dimensions variable

raw.title: Pigs, Time and Space
raw.medium: Single-channel color video, with sound, 21'12'';  installation dimensions variable

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: In Pigs, Time and Space, a native Chinese speaker tells a tale of migration and identity through the lens of ancient mythology and historic events, intertwined with the experience of the Pig, voiced by a Danish-accented narrator. In circular movements of time and space, this transcendental story starts and ends with the Pig, our protagonist, travelling through times ancient, present and imaginary in order to confront the paradigm shifts that connect intertwined histories.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
Founded in 1993, Copenhagen.


SUPERFLEX was founded in 1993 by Jakob Fenger, Bjørnstjerne Christiansen and Rasmus Nielsen. Through its diverse and extensive art practice, SUPERFLEX challenges the role of the artist in contemporary society and explores the nature of globalization and power systems. Their works address serious social and cultural concerns by posing witty and ironic questions. SUPERFLEX describe their works as a "tool", thereby suggesting multiple areas of application and use.

title: TAI CHI - 迪斯科
medium: multi-channel video, installation; Video, 20 TV, Shikumen Old Bricks, Music, Sound Interactive Dance Floor;  4:3, black and white, sound, looping； 07'28”, 11'46”

raw.title: TAI CHI - 迪斯科
raw.medium: multi-channel video, installation; Video, 20 TV, Shikumen Old Bricks, Music, Sound Interactive Dance Floor;  4:3, black and white, sound, looping； 07'28”, 11'46”

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
Six years after I left Shanghai, I returned to my hometown in 1995. It was in the early stages of reform and opening-up... when a brand-new “social landscape”, and an abrupt connection between tradition and modernity, between what was Chinese and what was foreign (mainly Western), corresponded to people’s desire for modernization.The way of thinking determines the behavior.I filmed the collective “迪斯科 (Disco)” by a group of people with uniform movements in a street of Shanghai, while “Disco” originated from the West is extremely personalized and random. In this work, I focus on a state of sincere misunderstanding during Eastern and Western cultural exchanges, and the trajectory of cultural extension is often based on this state. As for the title, “太极”became “Tai Chi” when introduced into the West from China, whichturned out to be very different as it used to be when it was brought back to China. Similarly, “Disco”,known as “迪斯科”in China, would make people feel awkward if it returns to its birthplace.This work was first exhibited in 1996, with 50 old-fashioned televisions placed around the exhibition room, simultaneously playing the video I filmed, to enhance the visual effect of collectiveness. The video was accompanied by the disco music recorded in the street and traditional Chinese music. The floor of the room was covered with two layers of used bricks from demolished Shikumen. In the center, there was a circular glass lightbox with a diameter of 2.2 meters, which could change its color combination of the Tai Chi patterned light according to the strength of the live music. (The glass lightbox was designed in the fashion of a ballroom light for the audience to dance on it.)

---Zhang Jianjun

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: Zhang Jianjun is an internationally known artist with exhibits worldwide, having recent shows in China, the United States, and Europe, including the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York; the China National Art Museum in Beijing; Shanghai Art Museum Biennale; Venice Biennale, Italy; Gwangju Biennale, Korea; Power Station of Contemporary Art, Shanghai; National Contemporary Art Museum, Rome, Italy; Dresden National Art Museum, Germany; Caixi Forum Museum, Barcelona and Madrid; Pera Museum, Istanbul; Royal Academy of Arts, London, England; etc. Teaching at NYU in New York since 1997, Professor Zhang has received many honors and grants including First Prize at the First Shanghai Youth Art Exhibition, Shanghai Art Museum (1986); the Asia Cultural Council Fellowship (1987-1988); two Pollock-Krasner Foundation Grants; two New York Foundation for the Art Fellowships (2007 and 2014); Artist-in-Residence, Royal Academy of Arts and K11 Art Foundation (2019), etc.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Lin Ke uses the laptop as his canvas and the mouse as his brush. Lin’s work focuses on the interaction between a human and a computer as he explores the entanglement of the operator and the operated. In the performance video Fly, the artist sits cross-legged in front of his computer, controlling it with a touchpad while using the front camera to record an interaction between himself and the mouse cursor (which resembles a fly). Blurring the boundaries between what is seen onscreen and reality, Lin explores the hazy threshold between the virtual and the real. Just as language can transcend its basic function of communication, Lin utilizes various functions of computer software in ways never imagined by their creators, which carries the rhythm of poetry.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1984, Wenzhou, Zhejiang Province; lives and works in Shanghai.


Lin Ke graduated from the New Media Art Department of the China Academy of Art. Since 2010, he has turned his attention to the performance art in the Computer Age by making himself his own guinea pig. Converting his laptop into an art studio, Lin extracts materials and forms from computer software and the Internet as the source for his artwork. The mundane act of exploring the internet and various application software becomes the catalyst for his art making and self-portraiture. He records operational behavior and conceptual images by using screenshots and screen recording software. His works take the form of installation, image, sound, text, video and computer painting. He was awarded the OCAT - Pierre Huber Art Prize in 2014, and The 9th Award of Art China (AAC)—the Most Influential of the Year in 2015, for his creative practice with materials. His works has been shown at the ZKM Center for Art and Media Karlsruhe and the Museum of Contemporary Art Tokyo among other well-known art institutions.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Zheng Bo investigates the past and the present from the perspective of marginalized communities and marginalised plants. He has founded a botanical garden, as well as an online course that he co-produced with scholars in ecology, literature and cultural studies. He has also enquired into the role of plants in the history of the Chinese Communist Party. He received his Ph.D in Visual & Cultural Studies from the University of Rochester, and teaches at the School of Creative Media, City University of Hong Kong.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1974, Beijing; lives and works in Hong Kong


Zheng Bo investigates the past and the present from the perspective of marginalized communities and marginalised plants. He has founded a botanical garden, as well as an online course that he co-produced with scholars in ecology, literature and cultural studies. He has also enquired into the role of plants in the history of the Chinese Communist Party. blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
A curator once asked me if there was something invisible whose presence could only be perceived through sound.


My answer was "the wind."


Several pedestal fans were arranged in a rectangle, alternating between operation and rest at five-minute intervals. The arrangement was designed to ensure that the wind generated by the fans moves and dissipates within the confines of the

rectangle. As the opposing fans face each other, their intersecting airflows create a collision of winds, producing a unique blend of sound. Here, the movement of air simultaneously produces sound and wind, intertwining the generation of sound with the dissipation of wind.


Generation was dissipation, and dissipation was, in turn, generation.


While the invisible, intangible wind is being dissipated, the audible wind is being generated.


Ocean Waves, featured in the main section of the 11th Shanghai Biennale, expanded this concept into a 7 x 7 grid of 49 electric fans. After the Biennale, the fans were distributed for free to 49 of my friends for collection, accompanied by an agreement: the fans must be used in their daily lives, and if the work were exhibited again, the collectors would lend the fans free of charge. In this way, I enabled the transformation of the fans between daily objects and art exhibits, redirecting the generation of meaning in artworks to the performative act of discourse.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: b. 1978, Shanghai; lives and works in Shanghai. A Shanghai native, Yin formed the Dead Poets Society in 1998, a slowcore band in which he was the lead singer and also a bassist. Yin turned to digital music three years later and his musical creation started to cover a wide range, e.g. live music performance, contemporary dance, and physical theatre. In recent years, Yin starts to focus on laptop music performance, field recording, and the functional exploration of music within a social structure. In the creation of sound art, YIN Yi is known for his philosophical and poetic ideas. His observation and reflection on public space is both acute and deep, and his works are both avant-garde and critical. Exhibitions that Yin Yi participated in are RAM Assembles (2023), Shenzhen-City of Design (2022), Echigo Tsumari Art Triennial (2018), the 11th Shanghai Bienniale (2016) and Sound Art China (2013). As a curator, he recently curated the music section of the RAM Assembles, "Composing for" (Shanghai Rockbund Art Museum, 2023), "Listening Path: Contemporary Sound Art Practice in China" (Shanghai Duolun Museum of Modern Art, 2024).

title: As Long As You Work Hard

raw.title: As Long As You Work Hard

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: The artists assemble tools from workers and farmers in Longshui into a cellular form, suggestive of growth and multiplication. The genius of Longshui's cottage industry of tool making, and its form of life, stand in uneasy confrontation with the industrial production of tools over the last two decades. The work draws its name from a Chinese proverb, "You can take enough pains to grind an iron rod into a needle", which metaphorically links labour, perfection and liberation.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: Estd. 2011, Chongqing. Cell Art Group was founded by Than Young (b. 1980) and Dong Xun (b. 1984) to engage in cultural study and artistic production. The group draws its inspiration from cells - how they reproduce, infect, mutate and regenerate - and sees this as an analogy for the relationship between artists and the society.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: "Riyaaz" references musical learning through repetition, interruption, persistence, and dis- and re-engagement. When in "Riyaaz", one reflects on one's practice, with an attention to how one is moving through music. This work rehearses moments of listening, reflection, and self-instruction through which musical habits are honed.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
B. 1970/Rawatbhata. Surabhi Sharma & Tejaswini Niranjana have made the films Jahaji Music: India in the Caribbean (2007), and Notes from a Global City (2009), together.


Sharma has also made Jari Mari: Of Cloth and Other Stories (2001), and has directed and scripted fiction films, and science programming for children. A guest lecturer at the National Institute of Design (Ahmedabad) and Tata Institute of Social Science (Mumbai), her films have been screened and awarded at various international and national festivals.

title: Delicate Cycle
medium: Kinetic sculptures, washing machines, video, performance

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Sasamoto plays on things that exercise gravitational force, and reimagines their axes and movements. The kinetic environment created through her installation and performances is a scientific exploration of orbital mechanics referred to, in physics, as the "three-body problem".

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: B. 1980, Yokohama. In her installation/performance works, Aki Sasamoto moves and talks inside careful arrangements of sculpturally altered objects, activating bizarre emotions that underlie daily life. She has collaborated with visual artists, musicians, choreographers, scientists, and scholars, and is co-founder of the nonprofit Culture Push (New York). Her works appear in galleries, theater, and in odd sites, and have been shown in the Whitney and Gwangju biennales, and in cities including New York, Tokyo and New Delhi. She teaches at Rutgers University and Columbia University. Aki likes food.

title: Strange Views
medium: Miniature street lamps, concrete slabs; Each  (× 11 pieces)

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Na Buqi often explores subjects of urban landscape, city dwellers, and the unique feeling of estrangement one feels in the company of others. In this work, she restructures the formal relation of two familiar artefacts of daily life - concrete and street lamps. The towering concrete edifices that populate cities around the world have been translated into podiums to be topped by miniature street lamps, arranged in a tight grid like an abstracted network of streets. In this play with the scale and composition of architectural structures, Na presents a surreal and poetic perspective on life in the city.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1984, Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia; lives and works in Beijing.


Na Buqi graduated from the Central Academy of Fine Arts. Her work embodies an extended thinking about “objects” and explores object-centric ontology: the objects around us do not exist because of their relationship with humans, but exist independently from human perception. She held her solo exhibition “Parallel” at C-Space (Beijing, 2015), and participated in group exhibitions such as the 11th Gwangju Biennale (2016) and “Soft Haze” (Thomas Erben Gallery, 2016).

title: Disguise
medium: Five-channel video installation, color, sound; 3D printed masks; Four channels, each 9'20''; one channel, 32'36''

raw.title: Disguise
raw.medium: Five-channel video installation, color, sound; 3D printed masks; Four channels, each 9'20''; one channel, 32'36''

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Using 3D scanning and printing techniques, Yang Zhenzhong fabricated 50 masks after 50 factory workers’ faces, and then asked them to wear the masks while performing their daily routine at the factory. While documenting working conditions in the factory, the video dramatizes the process of production. In contrast to the frozen expressions of the masked workers, the movement of their bodies is liberated in a kind of dance. Though it still retains the atmosphere of regular production, the factory is suffused with the magical potential of an uncanny theatre.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b.1968, Hangzhou; works and lives in Shanghai.


Yang Zhenzhong has been working with various art forms such as photography, installation, video, multimedia, and interaction since 1994. He is adept in analyzing the relationship between people, space and their living conditions in a straightforward and sarcastic attitude, and satirizing moral values in modern Chinese society. With metaphors and paradoxes, he tries to question the spirit of the times, and condemn a host of problems people have to face in modern society in a humorous manner.

title: Across the Burning Track
medium: Two-screen video, Housed in a structure by Nikolaus Hirsch/Michel Müller

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Ritwik Ghatak's last film Jukti, Takkoaar Gappo (Reason, Debate and a Story, 1974), which tells the story of an intellectual caught in the turmoil of 1970s Bengal, is re-scripted. With images, texts and voices spectrally connecting moments from history with current flows of a city, viewers dive into the recesses of what the film's protagonist calls "life for the living"; journey with a consciousness embedded in a "burning universe".

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: B. 1961, Kolkata. Moinak Biswas is writer and co-director of the award-winning Bengali feature film Sthaniya Sambaad (2010). His books on Indian cinema include Apu and After, Revisiting Ray's Cinema (2005) and Ujan Gang Baiya (1988, 2012). He edits Journal of the Moving Image and co-edits BioScope, South Asian Screen Studies. A professor in the Department of Film Studies, which he co-initiated at Jadavpur University, he is also initiator and coordinator of the Media Lab at the university.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: The image 'Anthropogenic Landscape' questions the ongoing socio-ecological transformations of the landscape of planet earth, use of land, the loss and destruction of fertile soil, forests, water, biodiversity and politics of knowledge and severe impact on the existence and identity of indigenous rural communities and their rights to decision making, forced and undesired displacements ,marginalization of their way of life,cultural environment in which both human, non-human and nature could prosper and cultural dynamics not destroyed.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: B. 1949, Meerut. Navjot Altaf began her career in the 1970s. Her imagery comes out of her theoretical and methodological innovation combined with deeply engaged readings of historical and contemporary art, film, and cultural theory. Her works have been shown in innumerable cities over four decades, with solo shows in New Delhi, Mumbai, New York, Florida, Lancashire and Fukuoka.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: The installation is challenging dialogues surrounding the response of "nature," as a strong atavistic feminine presence, to war conflicts. The artist develops a voice to bring the presence of this magic, that of ancient female living forces, through the superposition of techniques in drawings and paintings evolved into photography and video. As such, interposing parallel ages and realities and developing a remote and suspended time. In Search of Vanished Blood claims a place for the victims among whom there are those that transcend the human sphere.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1946, Karachi; lives and works in Mumbai.


For more than five decades Malani, as a senior feminist artist, addresses social, political and ecological issues. In her experimental art Malani broke out of the classical painting frame in 1969 with film and photography, continued in the late eighties with theatre, ephemeral wall drawings, erasure performances and video/shadow plays.

title: Eclipses for Shanghai
medium: HD video of performance with sound 15'00"

raw.title: Eclipses for Shanghai
raw.medium: HD video of performance with sound 15'00"

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: For the fourth installment of the Eclipses series, a group of students will represent the two total eclipses of the sun that will be visible over the area of greater Shanghai in the next thousand years. During the live performance, the shaft of the Power Station chimney becomes a sound artifact where the eclipses of June 9th, 2309 and June 7th, 2635 can be seen and heard. This series of works was initiated in 2009 under the premise of creating a site-specific work that could address an event in the distant future that is guaranteed to take place. Total eclipses of the sun, being rare and enigmatic astronomical events that can be predicted with accuracy hundreds of years in advance, proved to be the perfect subject matter for the project. In previous iterations, the work was staged in a football stadium in Austin, Texas in 2009 and later in Mexico in Cholula and Mexico City in 2014, where the piece took place at the foot of a pre-colonial pyramid and a modern concert hall, respectively. These paradoxical happenings engage a group of people in a collective ritual that commemorates an event in the distant future. Eclipses for Shanghai is an exercise in recalibrating our sense of time and geography, compelling participants and viewers to imagine what the world, especially the cities and the lives of people in them, will be like in hundreds of years. Simultaneously, the work grounds us in the small slice of space and time that we occupy in our lifetimes.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b.1968, Mexico City; lives and works in Mexico City.


His work comprises a variety of mediums such as installation, sculpture and video. Since 1991 his work has been shown extensively in Mexico, South America, the U.S. and Europe. His most recent projects include "Naj Tunich," La Tallera, Cuernavaca (2018); "Atlas," Museo Universitario del Chopo, Mexico City (2018).

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: The poem in Popol Vuh, an ancient narrative from the Mayan-Quiche people in Guatemala, this version by the Guatemalan author MiguelÁngel Asturias says on the lunar face: “ All this happened to us, all this happened, the sky fell twice.” This mysterious work seems to refer to the sky as a forgotten language and representation far from modern common horizons, but still always there above us.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1938, Buenos Aires; lives and works in Buenos Aires and Los Angeles.


Leandro Katz is an artist, poet, and filmmaker. Especially known for his films, he invented alphabets and photographic installations which include specific long-term projects dealing with Latin American subjects that incorporate historical research, anthropology, and visual arts. They include The Catherwood Project, Lunar Alphabet, The Vortex, and Project for The Day You'll Love Me, among others.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Kadder Attia's work as an artist, thinker and researcher orbits around the importance that the concept of "Repair" has in all kinds of cultural, spiritual, political and social practices. His works are a constant reminder of the significance that physical and material scars have as a record of trauma and a component of history. By calling attention to the fascination we have for all forms of reparation, Attia makes us aware of the power of our ambivalent fascination for the cracks that grant uniqueness to a place.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
Born in 1970 in France, grew up in Paris and in Algeria, and now lives and works in Berlin and Paris. 


​Preceding his studies in Paris and Barcelona, he spent several years in Congo and in South America. Kader Attia's intercultural and interdisciplinary approach of research explores the perspective societies have on their history, especially as regards experiences of deprivation and suppression, violence and loss, and their traces in collective memory. His socio-cultural research has led him to the notion of Repair: Describing an infinite process closely linked to loss and wounds, to recuperation and re-appropriation. Repair reaches far beyond the subject and involves it in evolutionary processes in nature, culture, myth and history. In 2016, Kader Attia founded La Colonie, a space in Paris providing an agora for vivid discussion. Focusing on decolonialisation of knowledge, attitudes and practices, it aspires to de-compartmentalise knowledge by a transcultural, transdisciplinary and transgenerational approach.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: An important work from the “Mr.Quan's Image Biography” project, this video is an autobiographical film by Ma Guoquan that records his family life and personal thoughts during a struggle with mental illness. Against a backdrop of the ubiquitous construction sites of Northern China, which developed under the region’s urbanization policy, the film captures the emergence of religions that had come to serve as an emotional and spiritual support for local people.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1990, Baoding, Hebei Province; lives and works in Beijing.


Ma Haijiao studied at the China Academy of Art (2009-2016), and graduated with a BA and then an MFA. He constantly addresses the “everydayness” of life in his works, based on which he traces the logical clues to shape working forms and video texts.

title: Collective Memory: Power Station of Art

raw.title: Collective Memory: Power Station of Art

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: In the series of Collective Memory, Chen Shaoxiong digitally reduced photos of worldwide public cultural institutions - the Louvre, the British Museum, the Museum of Modern Art New York, the Centre Pompidou, the CCTV Headquarters in Beijing, and the Power station of Art, etc - to pixels of various sizes, and then invited residents of the respective area to complete the paintings with their fingerprints. Collective Memory commemorates a shared living experience while referring to the democratization of image and intellectual production.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1962, Shantou, Guangdong Province; d. November 26, 2016.


Having grown up in South China, Chen Shaoxiong developed eclectic imagination and creativity in an unorthodox regional environment. He entered the Guangzhou experimental art scene in the mid-1980s and became a member of the Big Tail Elephant Group, the most important art group in South China in the 1990s. The Group maintained each member’s individuality while taking collective action in “dual marginalization”, and made a series of landmark creations in alternative urban spaces in the fashion of “guerrillas”.


Some of Chen’s works were independent, the others were cooperative along a development trajectory parallel to his personal creations. For example, he worked with Ozawa Tsuyoshi from Japan and Gim Hongsok from South Korea on “Xijing Men”, and Liu Ding on “Project Without Space”. His works employ image, installation, photomontage, painting, performance, and collective participation, following up closely on challenges faced by Chinese society in the wave of globalization. He also invited the public to participate in the creation of some of his works in order to inspire and share the common memory and ideals of urban and social changes.


His works were featured in the Venice Biennale (2003), Guangzhou Triennial (2005) and Shanghai Biennale (2002), and exhibited in PS1 Museum, the International Center of Photography in New York, the Victoria and Albert Museum in London, Kunsthalle Bern in Switzerland, Mori Art Museum in Tokyo, Hamburger Bahnhof in Berlin, and Tate Liverpool in London.

title: The Views
medium: Four-screen projection installation,  overall; color video, silent, 27', 3'58'', 3'30'', 5'42''

raw.title: The Views
raw.medium: Four-screen projection installation, 740 × 740 × 290 cm overall; color video, silent, 27', 3'58'', 3'30'', 5'42''

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Familiar scenes in the quotidian life can be found in this work: lotus pond of no lotus in winter, night sights outside of the window, abandoned railways, trees with no leaves on...These fleeting views evoke a poignant sense of loss and transience. Occasionally, moments of change break the stagnant view, be it the passing-by magpies or flickering lights, further rendering the nihility of existence and the brevity of life tangible.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1946, Shanghai; lives and works in Lausanne and Sainte Croix in Switzerland.


Franklin Chow attended the Académie de la Grande Chaumière in Paris. Having been born into an influential family which has fostered lots of outstanding talents and been raised in a paternal education encouraging an appreciation for art, Chow grew up with fine artistic sensibility and taste. His upbringing, as well as rich life and work experience contributed to his multicultural awareness, and was reflected in his artistic creation. His art practice combines the form of traditional Chinese art with the vision and concept of Western contemporary art. His works were exhibited in Switzerland, France, and Singapore, and collected by private collectors and art institutions in Switzerland, France, Germany, the UK, including the Teo Jakob art foundation (Bern), the Inez & Yves Oltramare Foundation (Geneva), and Rolex S.A. (Geneva).

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Since 1984, the circle has been a prominent motif in Yu Youhan’s painting, and it has gradually become an integral part of his approach to abstract form. This series of works takes the circle as its primary compositional device, which is articulated by an eclectic use of dots and lines. Yu’s expressive use of grey tones makes reference to handling of ink washes in the history of Chinese landscape painting, while the repeated linear strokes recall the gray-tiled houses that characterize the region of Jiangnan south of the Yangtze River. Works in the series exploring a wider color palette develop new lines of aesthetic inquiry. Though Yu’s artistic approach has undergone significant changes throughout his career, the creation of the “Circle” series has been a notable constant, which the artist is continuing to develop today.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
“My motive of starting this project was to make Japanese portraiture. I started with Kabuki actors and moved on to Bunraku puppets and I did Noh masks as they are the three major traditional theatrical arts in Japan. Usually Noh masks are photographed on a flat surface such as wall and treated as still materials and therefore approached two dimensionally. I started the FACES series of various subjects and they are about human faces with personalities, characters, emotions, and I loved the subtleties that facial expressions carry with them. I also wanted to expand my approach into ‘faces’ of non-humans such as heavy make-ups, masks, even animals, and I still treated them as human faces. I tried to photograph Noh mask as if they are faces of living humans. I put them on a mannequin head that were covered with black cloth and I photographed them three dimensionally.” 

——Hiroshi Watanabe

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1951, Sapporo, Japan; lives and works in California, USA.


Hiroshi Watanabe graduated from the Department of Photography at Nihon University. He moved to Los Angeles after graduation and became involved in the production of TV commercials for Japan. He later established his own production company. In 1995, his passion for photography rekindled, and he traveled worldwide extensively, photographing what he found intriguing at that moment and place.


In 2000, he closed the production company to devote himself entirely to photography. His works have been published and exhibited around the world, and received numerous awards. His works are in the permanent collections of Philadelphia Museum of Art, Santa Barbara Museum of Art, J. Paul Getty Museum, and Los Angeles County Museum of Art.

title: Standard Family
medium: Inkjet prints、documentary video  (produced by NHK in 2001); Each  (× 200 pieces)

raw.title: Standard Family
raw.medium: Inkjet prints、documentary video  (produced by NHK in 2001); Each 20 × 35 cm (× 200 pieces)

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: The background of this work is China’s one-child policy and its subject, three-person nuclear families. Wang utilizes visualized photography to expose the universal pattern of life during these times, reflecting upon the present and the future from multiple perspectives through the presentation of the “current” state of each individual family (such as their clothing, professional characteristics, life experiences, genetic traits, and even forms of family organization) and trying to understand this profound and particular era of reform.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1963, Suiling, Heilongjiang Province; lives and works in Beijing.


Wang Jinsong graduated from the Chinese Painting Department of the Zhejiang Academy of Fine Arts (now the China Academy of Art). In the 1980s, he shifted to work with different concepts, media, and methods after exploring the modern forms of ink paintings. In the early 1990s, he began to see painting as a way of revealing life and society at a deeper level. He extended the connotation of “blank” in a teasing way, and appropriately reflected the social atmosphere in the special context at that time. After a series of exhibitions abroad, he quickly broke through the boundaries and took up the challenge of working with more different methods and media. Since 1993, he has devoted himself to various forms such as painting, performance art, and conceptual photography.


After 1995, he was fascinated by the repetitiveness and expressiveness of photography. In more than a decade, he created a number of conceptual photography series on social phenomena, such as Standard Family (1996), Parents (1998), and One Hundred Signs of Demolition (1999), making people face up to the reality highlighted by the similarly and repetitively composed and expressed photos. The images in these photos seem to be an unretouched record of objective reality, or “a bystander’s ‘presentation’” according to him, which the artist gives no interpretation or judgement. The large-scale photography installation exhibition Tianwen (2010) of 600 photos pushed this expression technique to the extreme, showing the care for humanity and concerns for living conditions of the grassroots in a stunning manner.

title: The Bedroom
medium: Metal, quilt cover, pillow, light fixutre and lightbulb;

raw.title: The Bedroom
raw.medium: Metal, quilt cover, pillow, light fixutre and lightbulb; 500 × 200 × 100 cm

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: The Bedroom was created for the 10th Shanghai Biennale on the theme of the “Social Factory,” which responded to the past life of the Power Station of Art. Made up of a street lamp and a bed, four steel legs elevate the bed to the height of the lamp, rendering it unreachable and transforming the streetlight into something akin to a “bedside lamp.” With the transformation of Shanghai's industries in recent decades, the factories that once lined the Huangpu River went derelict, forcing workers to find work elsewhere. Chihying captures the entanglement of the life of the factory worker with that of the city, a relationship which continues to undergo rapid change today.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1985, Taipei; lives and works in Berlin.


Musquiqui Chihying is a member of the art group Fuxinghan Studio. He works with a range of creation forms to explore topics such as the relationship between human living status and the environment, and how artistic production transforms everyday life. Musquiqui has participated in several international exhibitions and regularly contributes to art magazines.

title: The Fear of Math
date: Sketch made and  published in 1998, installation realized in 2015
medium: Resin and steel; L700 × W500 × H

raw.title: The Fear of Math
raw.date: Sketch made and  published in 1998, installation realized in 2015
raw.medium: Resin and steel; L700 × W500 × H110 cm

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
Datong Dazhang often utilized readymade objects and instruments from day-to-day life, with simple modification or combination. Whether it is an installation or a performance, language and text (including titles and proposal instructions) play a key role in his projects. One example is the word play between “beads” (pronounced Zhu) and “pigs” (also pronounced Zhu) in The Fear of Math. This installation of an abacus with beads made from pig heads indicates a sense of powerlessness of traditional techniques being taken over by new technology. The installation The Fear of Math was first realized at the occasion of Datong Dazhang’s posthumous retrospective at the Power Station of Art in 2015.


Note from the sketch:

Welded with square stock, angle iron, and steel pipes Use fresh pig's heads


Datong Dazhang’s interpretation of his works:

1.I found that rotor is a useful stuff, because it can avoid being suspected of blocking the traffic, and at the same time, force you to be present any minute.

2.I have been afraid of mathematics since I was a child, as I would be considered an idiot as people said, “Look! This boy is as stupid as a donkey.” if I failed to count. I’m more frightened of computers now, which means I’m frightened of modernization drive and the future.

3.The relation between the works and the ancient abacus is nothing but a coincidence. I have no interest in elaborating on it.

4.What really attracts me is the entertaining aspect of this work.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1955, Datong, Shan'xi Province; d. January 1, 2000.


Datong Dazhang, whose real name was Zhang Shengquan, born in Datong, Shanxi Province. He was called by many “Dazhang” (Big Zhang) because of his height of 1.9 meters. Over time, he simply adopted the sobriquet of “Datong Dazhang.” Datong Dazhang stood as a rare model for a significant life within the thirty-year course of Chinese contemporary art. He was a gifted talent, a martyr to art, a wise man who adhered to pure art spirit and independent thinking, and a lonely free soul. On the New Year’s Eve of 2000, while the whole world was cheering for the arrival of the new millennium, Datong Dazhang hung himself in his apartment. In his short yet prolific life, he produced a great number of works in the form of installation, performance, painting, poetry, mail art, etc. His art fantasies shone with sharp thoughts. As an important figure documented in the Wen Pulin Archive of Chinese Avant-Garde Art, Datong Dazhang truly adhered to an avant-garde spirit about never reversing the course. In our increasingly commercialized present, a careful reading of his message can help us reflect on the current situation of Chinese contemporary art, and its destiny.

title: The Expansion of Details Leads to the Collapse of the Whole Entity
date: Sketch made and  published in 1998, installation realized in 2015
medium: Wood and steel; L2640 × W55 × H

raw.title: The Expansion of Details Leads to the Collapse of the Whole Entity
raw.date: Sketch made and  published in 1998, installation realized in 2015
raw.medium: Wood and steel; L2640 × W55 × H4 cm

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
Most of Datong Dazhang’s installation proposals take their cues from daily appliances, and are in no way self-mystifying. They do not stress the volume or the quality of material, nor do they emphasize the complexity of the production process. Nevertheless, the wisdom, humor, and charm revealed in his works is distinctly pulpable. The Expansion of Details Leads to the Collapse of the Whole Entity consists of a pickaxe with a sharp head and a handle that keeps on extending; even if the pickaxe handle keeps on extending, the pickaxe head would still refuse to retreat. This installation was first realized at the occasion of Datong Dazhang’s posthumous retrospective at the Power Station of Art in 2015.


Note from the sketch:

The Expansion of Details Leads to the Collapse of the Whole Entity

The length can be 30, 50, or 100 m.

The pickaxe head is hard and strong, with the will of iron; so even if the pickaxe handle extends past ten meters, it would still refuse to retreat. This makes the connecting and disassembling of the handle very thought-provoking...

It needs to produce power and rhythm. The bolts need to be big.

title: Questioning the Weight of Scales
date: Sketch made and published in 1996, installation realized in 2015
medium: Wood, steel and nylon wire; L3160 × W1280 × H40 mm

raw.title: Questioning the Weight of Scales
raw.date: Sketch made and published in 1996, installation realized in 2015
raw.medium: Wood, steel and nylon wire; L3160 × W1280 × H40 mm

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: For every edition, he created about 50 copies and each contained about 13 pages. Despite the limited number printed, it reached important art critics and artists in the big cities across the country, including Yuanmingyuan, Dongcun, and Songzhuang. In 1994, he divided his mail art into two parts: one includes drafts of installation and performance which he called “things,” and the other mostly includes poems, notes, and proposals, which he called “The Right Guard.” The installation Questioning the Weight of Scales was first realized at the occasion of Datong Dazhang’s posthumous retrospective at the Power Station of Art in 2015. Composed of several connected scale beams, the work creates a delicate balance that only exists on a theoretical level. The work presents a series of inquiries, unceasingly calling the standard, fairness, and justice of determined values, and even truth into doubt.

title: Friend Watan
medium: Single-channel video, with sound; wood structure theater, aluminum-mounted Prints; 36’47''

raw.title: Friend Watan
raw.medium: Single-channel video, with sound; wood structure theater, aluminum-mounted Prints; 36’47'', 153.4 × 94 × 208.5 cm

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: In an approach that resists the conventions of both biography and documentary filmmaking, Chen Chieh-jen captured the story of his friend Watan Uma in a filmic assemblage framed within a wooden theatre. Also an artist, Watan belongs to the Taiwan Atayal community and only began to embark on a creative career in his middle age after leaving his job at a factory. Working from the photographs and notebooks that Watan provided in addition to Chen’s own observations, the artist attempted to discover a notional “past” while reconstructing Watan’s personal history.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: Born in 1960, Taoyuan, Taiwan Province; lives and works in Taipei.

title: The Bianwen Book I
medium: 24 aluminum-mounted prints, video installation of People Pushing;

raw.title: The Bianwen Book I
raw.medium: 24 aluminum-mounted prints, video installation of People Pushing; 500 × 200 × 100 cm

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Chen Chieh-jen’s Transformation Text is a creative reimagining of bianwen. Not only has he extended the significance of bianwen into contemporary art by transforming, translating and rewriting contemporary realities via audio-visual narrative; in keeping with the nature of bianwen, he has also formed a collection of his audio-visual creation over the last decade by reassembling blueprints of social production, photographic records, symbolic objects and texts, video clips, and a temporary movie theatre as a three-dimensional spatial book with six chapters.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body: Born in 1960, Taoyuan, Taiwan Province; lives and works in Taipei.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: In 2006, White began creating tapestries with photographic images of plumes of smoke. Berlin B, one of her more recent smoke tapestries, captures what White describes as the cotton’s “dream of becoming something other than itself” by arresting these transient, fleeting tendrils of smoke in a physical medium. While tapestries are often associated with epic chronicles in Western art history, here White reframes the medium as a monument to ephemerality.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1963, California, USA; lives and works in Los Angeles.


Pae White’s practice traverses sculpture, tapestry, graphic design, and large-scale installation. Probing both material and motif, she explores the limits of the possibility of a given medium, and often expands its established associations. Her works perfectly combine scale and delicacy, repurposing everyday substances into sensory and revelatory new arrangements.

title: Those Times II
medium: 20 pieces of knitted and embroidered cotton fabrics sourced from ordinary households, cotton thread;

raw.title: Those Times II
raw.medium: 20 pieces of knitted and embroidered cotton fabrics sourced from ordinary households, cotton thread; 700 × 500 cm

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Hu Xiaoyuan collected a large amount of second- hand embroidered or knitted household textiles, which she repurposed to produce new tapestries. Mostly made between the early 1960s and late 1980s by female members of the family, her collection includes door flaps, tablecloths, curtains, pillow cases, quilt covers, teacup coasters and sewing-machine covers. While these furnishings were made by different hands, their makers often utilized similar methods or techniques, either knitted, crocheted, woven, or embroidered, creating an impression of visual consonance.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1977, Harbin Province; lives and works in Beijing. 


Hu Xiaoyuan graduated from the School of Design of the Central Academy of Fine Arts. Her works take various forms, including installation, video, painting, photography, etc. She stays away from specific experience and turns to discuss more abstract topics such as time, space and existence, revealing a somewhat extreme sensitivity. From the topics of her works, she obviously tends to analyze knowledge rather than express personal feelings. These topics are closely related to the knowledge from within, forming an island of thinking.


Her works have been widely exhibited at home and abroad, such as at Documenta 12, Kassel (2007) as the first invited Chinese female artist, and the 2nd New Art Museum Triennial, New York (2012), and the 9th Taipei Biennale (2014). Her works were featured in exhibition projects of art institutions and spaces such as Le Palais de Tokyo in Paris, Bonniers Konsthall in Stockholm, Kunsthaus Graz, and Orange County Museum of Art in California; and were collected by M+ Museum in Hong Kong, Rockbund Art Museum in Shanghai, Hammer California, among other public institutions.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
These natural objects have always been there. They have never been ignored, and they do not need people to remember them in order to continue to exist. But they record every passage of the shared history of humankind. Every time I go to explain, I find that my own knowledge and analytical capacities, placed next to the oceans, are pathetic. So I think I can only try to express them in painting.

—Shi Zhiying

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1979, Shanghai; lives and works in Shanghai.


Shi Zhiying graduated from the Oil Painting Department of the Fine Arts College of Shanghai University. Since 2005, she has been working in the Oil Painting Creation Department of the Shanghai Oil Painting and Sculpture Institute. Her paintings are free of exaggerated shapes and flamboyant techniques, but employs light and ethereal brushwork to reveal the depth of nature hidden under life. Focusing on natural things such as the sea, grass, erg, and cosmic nebula, she creates a scene and space of both breadth and depth by tiling and extension, and transforms passive reception to active observation of the most original feelings and experience one obtains when facing the world.

title: Parading Project - Shouder, Family Letter
medium: 8 color videos, with sound; 8 high-power microscope, each ; microcarved whole grains

raw.title: Parading Project - Shouder, Family Letter
raw.medium: 8 color videos, with sound; 8 high-power microscope, each 12 × 18 × 31 cm; microcarved whole grains

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: For the installation Letter from Home, the collective members of the Irrelative Group inscribed letters from their parents onto grains of rice and beans using microcarving techniques, which visitors can read through microscopes. This estranged process of observation imbues these often-ignored commonplaces with a new dimension of significance. In the video Shoulder, each member of the collective returns to his or her own home, where they proceed to blindfold their parents and take them to a specific location, a place that each artist was once taken to by their parents. The blindfolded parents are led and supported by the artist, creating a new connection between family members who have grown apart. They are revisiting not just a location, but a relationship. The group’s name is derived from their keen sense that contemporary art has been come too irrelevant to real life and real people. Through their collective action, they are attempting to build a new “relevance” for art in modern society.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
Founded in 2011, Beijing.


Irrelative Group is an art group of nine, who are Chen Zhiyuan, Feng Lin, Gao Fei, Guo Lijun, Jia Hongyu, Li Liangyong, Niu Ke, Wang Guilin, and Ye Nan. Since its establishment in 2011, Irrelative Group has been committed to integrating life and creation with an “irrelative” attitude. Every irrelevant action is irrelevant to what seems relevant, so it becomes relevant to irrelevance, and irrelevant to relevance.


They are still creating art or whatever else that is irrelative to these expressions.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: At the opening ceremony of the Shanghai Biennale at Power Station of Art, a ball filled with blue paint hanging inside the chimney at 30 meter above the ground was released from its net and dropped onto the floor. When the ball finally collided, the paint inside escaped and splattered in all directions. Meanwhile, two high-speed cameras, one from overhead and the other at floor-level, managed to capture the entire experience. Upon viewing the footage in slow motion, one is able to appreciate the full concerto of violence and beauty contained within a sublime moment that otherwise would have been too fast for the naked eye.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1938, Appenzell, Switzerland; lives and works in St. Gallen, Switzerland.


Signer’s creations encompass sculpture, installation, photography and video. His “time sculpture” includes presupposition, implementation, and recording of these "experiments" that are important to aesthetic achievements, and even events. They have not only inherited the three-dimensional modeling of physical materials that traditional sculptures value, but also extended the focus of creation to the so-called fourth dimension: the dimension of time. By combining three-dimensional objects, real-time actions, still photos and moving images in various ways, Signer’s time sculpture captures the containment and release of energy in different scenes. His creations are always ingenious, full of charming and interesting lightness and irresistible humor. His works have been widely exhibited in art museums in Europe, North America and Asia, including the 37th Venice Biennale (1977), Documenta 8, Kassel (1987), and the Swiss Pavilion at the 48th Venice Biennale (1999).

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Pascale Column like erections raises the perpetual issue of human existential. A concentration of frustration leads me to this contemporary ritual I always wonder if there really a difference between hell and paradise. Although Men live for happiness, it is nevertheless clear that misfortune is part of happiness. Pascale Column finally to probe the soul of the living, the paradise, Whether it is in China, in Japan, in America, in Mali or ... in Syria.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1966, Nkongsamba, Cameroon; lives and works in Ghent, Belgium and in Yaoundé, Cameroon.


In the middle of the 1990s Jean Apollinaire Tayou changed his name, declining it in the feminine form to become Pascal(e) Marthin(e) Tayou. This marked the beginning of an unceasing artistic, geographic and cultural nomadism that has brought Tayou to prominence on the contemporary art scene.


Tayou’s work, like his name, is deliberately fluid and eludes pre-established schemes. Multiple, ungovernable, gripping, profound, unexpected, proliferating and varied, it is always linked to the idea of travel and the encounter with what is other to self. Being a traveler is not just a condition of life for Tayou, but also a psychological condition capable of subverting social relations and the political, economic and symbolic structures of our lives. Tayou’s works are conceived in situ, in close association with the here and now.

title: Wallwave Vibration (Asyncronouse motions) (Radially Polarized Zero Azimuth)
medium: Polyester resin, wall paint; diameter  × 12 cm thickness

raw.title: Wallwave Vibration (Asyncronouse motions) (Radially Polarized Zero Azimuth)
raw.medium: Polyester resin, wall paint; diameter 220 cm × 12 cm thickness

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
The “Gaps” are sculptural elements in relief (sort of “scarification”

- tattoos in relief, which then are scars), appear as memory elements

subcutaneous skin of the wall. In this sense, many elements such as

windows, books, heaters, push the area of architecture as a memory

of the object in a place and its presence in the architectonical surfaceskin,

appearing like shadows of the originals, such as sudden changes in

architectural surface, suggesting expressiveness intrinsic to the wall in a

movement as possible.

In the most recent sculptures, one loses the element more properly object.

The deformation concerns more particularly the physical manifestation

of the vibrations, expressed each time with different frequencies and

intensities, wherein the visual pattern becomes “echo” of a phenomenon

more purely physical, as a succession of waves on a liquid surface. In this

direction it is as if the entire architecture, or a portion of it, would suffer

the consequences of a phenomenon that affects it, modifying it in an

organic symbiosis between sculpture and the wall.

The yield of these surreal elements and while their formal complexity in a

more purely sculpture, put these works in the double ground of abstraction

and sublime, expressed as the artificial glare of a “expressive diagram.”

Specially, the works are performed starting from a study of physical

phenomena and reported physically by three-dimensional modeling,

using numeric control cutting machines and the moulds for the final form.

The work is then installed in the space so camouflaged, looking for a

perfect blend with the architecture that houses it. The extreme edges of

the sculptures are “welded” to the surface to the walls in order to fully

standardize the surface and make it in a visual continuum.

The general title of “Gaps”, refers to the term “gap” between one element

and another, more specifically, the strange relationships in “intervals” of

consecutive prime numbers in mathematics.

The project for Shanghai Biennale is the installation of 4 kinds of

“frequencies,” each of them realized in polyester resin and fixed to the

wall, in a sort of sampling of different forces and reactions.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1969, Milan; lives and works in Prato, Italy and Beijing.


Loris Cecchini is one of the most outstanding Italian contemporary artists around the world. His works combine photography, painting, sculpture, installation etc. and form a more uniform and changeable basic element with each other. Growing up in the ancient city of Siena and influenced by the cultural concepts of the Renaissance, Cecchini’s creation is devoted to exploring the intersection of poetry, nature and technology, and uses the institutional drawings in sculpture to provide a personal interpretation of space. His works have been featured on solo exhibitions in art museums and institutions such as Le Palais de Tokyo in Paris, the Musée d’Art Moderne de Saint-Etienne Métropole, MoMA PS1 in New York, and the Shanghai Duolun MoMA, and shown on international exhibitions such as the 49th Venice Biennale (2001), the 6th and 9th Shanghai Biennale (2006, 2012), and the 13th and 15th Rome Quadrennial (1999, 2008).

blocks.title: Description
blocks.body: Joseph Beuys developed the 100-day Dialogue Series Blackboard Drawing on the basis of the program “Organization for Direct Democracy through Referendum” (Büro für Direkte Demokratie durch Volksabstimmung) at Documenta 5 in Kassel in 1972, which had since evolved into a range of installation works. The form of Beuys’ Blackboard Drawing series was deeply influenced by the social philosopher Rudolf Steiner, but Beuys truly transforms “blackboard” into an icon of his own works. The diagram on the blackboard illustrates his vision on a new society and “social sculpture” (Soziale Plastik) theory, the core of which is to regard art as a way of social transformation and even human evolution.

blocks.title: Artist Bio
blocks.body:
b. 1921, Düsseldorf, Germany; d. 1986.


Joseph Beuys was one of Germany’s greatest post-war artists. In a well-known story, Beuys was shot down while in service as a pilot in the Crimea, and was saved by Tartar nomads using carpets and animal fat. This experience inspired him to make frequent use of these materials in his later work. After WWII, Beuys studied monumental sculpture at Düsseldorf Academy of Fine Arts, and stayed on to teach at the same school. He was in close contact with the Fluxus movement, and developed an artistic style that combined sculpture, performance and social action. He also created the concept of “social sculpture”. In this “expanded conception of art”, art is seen as a path for social transformation, even human evolution. Beuys was deeply influenced by Rudolf Steiner. He believed implicitly that humanity must find a balance between the spiritual and material worlds, and that art was a force for transmitting “warmth”.


His speeches, teaching and political actions were as shocking as his artistic creations, and they became a part of his social sculpture. At the heart of Beuys’ art is the drive to unleash potential, to improve society; thus, teaching was very important to Beuys psychologically. He often saw the giving of talks as a form of creativity itself. In his work for the 1972 Documenta at Kassel, he discussed the possibility of Germany developing direct democracy with visitors to the expo over the course of 100 days. His blackboard explanations and pictures served as memorials to the spirit of that dialogue, and were exhibited as an example of “social sculpture”. Here, we are showing three of his blackboards out of respect for this radical teacher.
